ALFRED F. BRESLAUER
Grand Ma ster
September 30. 1960 - September 29. 1961

ALFRED FISHER BRESLAUER
GRAND MASTER

The 95th Grand Master. Alfred F. Breslauer, a native-born Californian, took office as a man with a message. Immediately upon his
installation he announced the theme for his year as Grand Master:
"The Year of the Master Mason." The philosophy of this theme was
the motivating force of the activities for the year.
The Grand Master brought Grand Lodge closer to the individual
Master Mason. The Master Mason was urged to attend Grand Lodge
and •See it in operation. He was given the opportunity to attend Special
Communications of the Grand Lodge in his home area, as regional
meetings celebrating historical even.ts were scheduled throughout the
state. These sectional meetings also gave the Grand Master the opportunity to "democratize" Grand Lodge by giving the individual Mason
the opportunity to know intimately the officers of the Grand Lodge.
While giving prominence to the importance of the Master Mason,
the Grand Master likewise tried to impress upon the individual Mason
his responsibility to the Craft. He emphasized the reciprocal obligation
of a Mason to at.tend his Lodge and actively participate in the a.ffairs of
the constituent Lodge as well as the statewide Masonic activities of
Grand Lodge. This was .the message of the Grand Master, not merely
evidenced by a formal pronouncement at the beginning of his term, but
energetically supported by his activities ducing the entire year, so that
the words of !!he message became a reality.
The busy year which accomplished the purposes of The Year of the
Master Mason was in a great measure made possible by the rich
Masonic background and experience which Grand Mas.ter Breslauer
brought to the office. His seventeen years as an Inspector, his service
as a member on Public School and Grand Lodge Week Activities
Committees. his authorship of the Master\s Handbook. and numerous
o~her Masonic activities, enabled him to put into action some of his
theories for the advancement of Masonry.
This same Masonic experience also assisted in making the I 12th
Grand Lodge Communication a meaningful, efficient, and well directed
session. The briefing session for new attendants at Grand Lodge, rhe
tiiming of reports and important items of business, the distribution to
the Lodges of recommendations of the Grand Master prior to the session .
the creation of a fair system of computing multiple non-ballot votes. all
bore evidence of his years of Masonic experience.
This biographical sketch should contain some of the statis.tical facts
of his personal life. civic activities, and the Masonic experience com-

CORN, WINE AND OIL
Psalm 23:5; Psalm 104:15
THE VERY REVEREND CLARENCE REIDENBACH, D.D.

Grand Chaplain
During my year as Grand Chaplain, I have heard a good deal about
corn. wine and oil. These symbols are familiar and important in Masonry. I have been impressed and intrigued by them. I decided that I
wanted to do some thinking and research on the subject. In addition
to being important in Masonry. there is a good deal about these symbols
in the Bible. Moreover. the ideas that they stand for are important in
life.
Corn, wine and oil were staple crops. They were something that
the people had a good supply of. and they had them year after year.
We think in terms of those things that are at •hand in our daily lives.
The ancient Hebrews used these everyday things as offerings to their
God. What better offerings can we make than to give of what is important to us personally? Common things, also, take on a new meaning
when they are consecrated to God. What is holy and what belongs to
practical living become one. They are not forever separated in two
different worlds, These symbols came out of living nature. There is
something mysterious about life, and it is good for us to think of how
close we are brought to the great mystery of life by the things that we
call common because they are close at hand, but which are not so common after all. These fruits of nature were made holy by being offered
to God, and they were also used to make holy the lives of the worshippers. Holy, by the way, means hallowed or sacred, but it is also
the modern form of the old Anglo-Saxon word halig, which meant
whole or healthy. Whatever makes us holy is supposed to make us
healthy in spirit.
The corn was not merely what we call corn. which is Indian corn
or maize. Maize is an Indian word. Our Pilgrim and Puritan fathers
were helped to eat better because the Indians taught them how to grow
and utilize maize. Corn primarily means grain. In England, the word
refers to wheat; in Scotland and Ireland, it refers to oats. In Bible times,
it referred to wheat and some other grains. People differ, and their
differences do not always lead to trouble.
Corn and bread are, naturally. mentioned often in the Bible. We
can all remember how Joseph had grain stored up against the seven
years of famine. In Deuteronomy l l : 14, God promises his people that.
if they will keep his commandments, he will "give the rain of your
land in its season, the former rain and the latter rain, that thou mayest
gather in thy grain, and thy new wine, and thine oil." Psalm 65:13

Com or grain refers to nourishment. It was a basic food, as corn
and frijoles are basic foods in Mexico today. Bread has come to signify
all food, as when we speak of our daily bread. Psalm I 04: 15 speaks
of "wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face
to shine, and bread that strengtheneth man's ·heart." The Pilgrims, at
their first Thanksgiving, were basically thankful for their crops. There
is the story of an old woman who lived to be one hundred years old.
The reporters went to ask her to what she attributed her long life. She
gave a classic reply. She said, "Vittles." We cannot discount victuals.
In this life, we cannot get very far away from food, and we cannot,
therefore, actually get away from the source of all life and food.
Corn is a symbol of the solid things of life. It stands for necessities,
foundation factors. There are, for instance, basic values: to make the
most of oneself, to have a good work. to maintain a good home, to be
sensitively aware of the people around us in our human environment, to
be sensitively aware of our total environment, God. There are solid
and basic virtues, the kinds of virtues that we Masons exalt: truth,
honesty, honor, temperance, prudence. fortitude, justice, brotherly love.
These are the bread, meat, and potatoes of personality and character.
There are solid men, like George Washington, so greatly honored by
our country and also in Masonic history. He hardly seems to have had
genius, like Jefferson and Hamilton. but he had a mind that saw things
steadily and saw them whole. He was a man who could say that it would
require little ·beyond common sense and common honesty to make ours
a great and prosperous nation. He was noted for his courage and his
character.
We now come to the wine. If I were of the same mind that I used
to be, I would at this point make a pitch about prohibition. But I shall
not do that. I do not believe that it would work. Alcohol. by the way,
is only one of the causes of alcoholism. I am an honorary member of
Alcoholics Anonymous, and I have known hundreds of rhem. They are
nervous, and have severe emotional problems; these facts are basic in
their alcoholism. Of course. I believe in control. Temperance is one of
our Masonic virtues. The Bible also discusses excess. That leads to all
sorts of distressing human problems.
The Hebrew wines were light wines. A distinction was made between wine and strong drink. 0£ course. wine can cause trouble; one of
the worst cases of alcoholism is the "wino". That is probably because it
is relatively cheap and also. I think. because of its sugar content. The
alcoholic can go longer on it without eating, and that causes much of the
trouble. But the idea among the Hebrews was to restrain themselves
to light drinking.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The use of wine was practically universal. The book of Second
Maccabees says: "It is hurtful to drink wine or water alone, but wine
mingled with water is pleasant." The Twenty-third Psalm says: "My
cup runneth over," and that referred , no doubt. to the wine that was
served to the guest. Wine came under the head of refreshment. We
Masons believe in refreshment; we are called, on occasion. from labor
to refreshment. There must be labor in our lives, but there must be refreshment as well as labor. I remind you that the 104th Psalm speaks
of "wine that maketh glad the heart of man."
I am strong for making people glad and merry. and I like it that we
have a symbol that suggests the joyful side of life. People do not laugh
and play enough. Laughter is a fine medicine for the soul. It spreads
joy and good will. I have noticed, over the years, that the people who
are most popular in any social group are the jolly ones. The glum ones
are mostly on the sidelines. I feel that I have a fundamental duty to make
people happy. If they are happy. they have less trouble in being good.
Good people should be genial people; if they are not. they are not the
best kind of recommendation for goodness. I sympathize with the little
boy who prayed that God would make all bad people good and all
good people easy to live with. Humorless people get old too fast, and
they are all too often a source of danger to others.
Of course. we need more than wine to make the heart glad. We need
decent and stable lives. We need to be free from regrets and guilt
feelings . We need to know what we are doing well enough to have
poise. We need a sense of accomplishment and of being worth while.
We need to be concerned about others enough to keep our minds from
dwelling too much on ourselves. We need faith. which is another word
for confidence. The most inclusive and stabilizing faith is our faith in
God.
Now we come to the oil. It was olive oil. I am glad that it was not
petroleum. That would not smell so good, and the struggles over oil fields
would not be so very pleasant to contemplate. Olive oil was very important, and it had many uses. It was used in cooking food. for lighting and
for making cosmetics. It had medicinal purposes. Isaiah 1 :6 speaks of the
wounds of the people because they had not been obedient to their God:
"There are wounds, bruises. and fresh stripes: they have not been
closed, neither bound up, neither softened with oil." The good Samaritan poured oil and wine on the wounds of ehe wayfarer who had been
beaten and robbed. Of course. oil was used for religious purposes.
Genesis 28 : 18 tells what Jacob did after his dream at Bethel: "Jacob
rose up early in the morning . and he took the stone that he had put
under his head, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil upon the top
of it." Those set aside for places of leadership would be consecrated
by being anointed with oil.

Oil. as well as wine, was a symbol of joy. Isaiah 61 :3 speaks of the
oil of joy taking the place of mourning. Once more, let me cite Psalm
I 04: 15. It speaks there of ~he oil to make man's face to shine. Oil was
used to protect the skin against the weather. It was used also because
they thought that it beautified the face ; it made the face to shine. That
looked good to them. And this applied to men.
Oil was particularly a part of glad feasts . The good host had a
supply of oil with which to anoint his guests. The oil also had perfu me
in it. !hat helped. Proverbs 27: 9 says: "Oil and perfume rejoice the
h~art . . ~he grea~ Twenty-third Psalm says: "Thou anointest my head
with 011. We still use oil on our heads. The barber puts in on. There
is a kind of oil of which a little dab'll do you. Two dabs are dangerous.
Oil is a symbol of smooth and friendly relations. lack o f friction.
We pour oil on the troubled waters. We know that we have to use
just the right kind of oil in our automobile engines. I once heard a
Negro preacher compare life to an old Ford car. It was one of my
unforgettable sermons. He had a lot of good points. One of them was
derived from the oil: life among people had to be smooth. There had
to be brotherly love and harmony. As a matter of fact. we need to be
free from friction within. Fears and guilt feelings can rub us raw. And,
of course, if. we do not have harmony with our fellow human beings.
we are ·h eading for mutual destruction .
Well, it takes more than oil to make the face really shine. The light
comes from the inside out. Love will make the face to shine. I marry
a lot of people. They talk with me in preparation for their marriages.
!hey a~e ~ ?appy lot, and their faces do shine. One of the greatest days
m my lifetime was Armistice Day, in 1918. The people poured out from
their homes to be together. It was like one great prayer meeting of
thanksgiving. Everyone was jubilant. I have never at an y other time
s~en so many faces shining so much. I would like to see it again some
time. The sense that one has lived up to t'he dictates of his own conscience can give the heart and the face a glow. Psalm 15: 7 says: "Thou
hast loved righteousness, and hated wickedness; therefore God, thy God,
hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fello ws." We can
remember, a·lso, how the face of Moses shone when he ca me down
from the mount, because he had been with God.
Life has various sides. There is what we call the solid and substantial. There is that which is light and joy ful. There is that which is
sublime. We really want to have these various interests mixed in their
due proportions. In Masonry. we have the variou s sides represen ted
by our symbols. We have more than one symbol. We want more than
a one-sided life. We have the corn, and the wine, and the oil. I hope
that we can have th e great realities represented to us by our symbols.
I hope that really you may have the nourishment of the corn . the refreshment of the wine, and the joy of the oil.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ceremonies and public building dedications. The administrative and
executive duties of the office become more numerous and complex. The
visit of any Grand Master to a Lodge or District is an important event.
The Brethren of the Constituent Lodges look forward to hearing a
message from the Grand Master and greeting him personally. In a
Jurisdiction as large as California. with approximately 243,000 Master
Masons, 705 Lodges and 178 lnspectoral Districts. it is of great
assistance to have a consolidation of districts for meetings. Those
Lodges or Districts which traditionally ·have had separate meetings
for the Grand Master should join, if possible, with other Lodges and
Districts. An outstanding example of this cooperation occurred this
year in the 5th Division. consisting of 47 Inspectoral Districts. comprising approximately 190 Lodges. This Division is located in Los
Angeles and the surrounding area and includes about 80.000 Master
Masons. If the Grand Master devoted an evening to each District
it would take approximately two months of the Grand Master's time
to visit these Districts. With the cooperation of the Masters of the
Lodges. the Inspectors of the Districts. and the Assistant Grand Lecturer of the Division, a series of six Sunday morning Breakfasts was
arranged. The Grand Master thus had the opportunity to visit every
lnspectoral District in the 5th Division (except two located east of
the Sierra Nevada Mountains), and had the opportunity to talk to
and greet personally hundreds of Master Masons who attended these
Breakfasts. Similar cooperation was experienced in other parts of
the Jurisdiction. A particularly outstanding Breakfast was the one
held at Anaheim at which 900 Master Masons were present. This
was the .first time such a Breakfast had been held in Orange County.
My sincere gratitude goes to the Brethren who have been so considerate
of the Grand Master.

THE YEAR OP THE MASTER MASON

16

It should not be a prerequisite for selection as Grand Master
that he be a person who has reached retirement. It would be helpful.
no doubt, if the Grand Master were not required to spend any time
to earn his livelihood and could devote every hour of his term to
Masonic activities. However. not all Grand Masters can do that.
nor should they be required to do so. Your present Grand Master,
the Deputy Grand Master, and Senior Grand Warden, were and
are actively engaged in their professions and business. The assistance
and cooperation of all Brethren to lighten the requirement of Lodge
visitations were and will be. I am sure, most welcome. This year the
assistance was outstanding and I am forever indebted for this aid.
I bespeak the same consideration for my successors.

17

It was most pleasing to the Grand Master to see so many Master
Masons present at these Breakfasts, receptions and ceremonies. Thcir
presence gave meaning and emphasis to the Year of the Master M ason,
which was the theme adopted for this year. My hopes and aspirations
for this year were set forth in the messages I wrote for the fou r
issues of the California Freemason for 1960-61. In the JanuaryMarch issue I told how the theme happened to be chosen and the
importance of the Master Mason in the Masonic framework. The
April-June issue carried the story of how this theme could be implemented by Grand Lodge, and what Grand Lodge and its officers
planned to do to make this year meaningful for the individual members. The next issue , July-September, pointed out what consti tuent
Lodges should do to enrich the objective. and contained specific suggestions for Lodge activities for the 2,500 Smiths. 2.000 Johnsons
and 1,400 Browns, among other Master Masons in this Jurisdict.ion. The final issue emphasized that this was not a one-way road
and ~he Master Mason had certain corollary obligations. The obligations of the Master Mason himself were spelled out in that article.
In order that the whole story be presented, I am taking the liberty
of attaching the articles referred to as exhibits to this message. It
would be presumptuous on my part to characterize the year as a
successful one. Only my Brethren can answer that inquiry. I did
find that many Lodges adopted the theme for their activities during
the year, and implemented the objectives in accordance w ith the suggestions of th~ Grand Master. If it has helped in any measure I
have been well repaid.

This year the Master Masons of Ca lifornia contribu ted the magnificent sum of $645,453 .76 to the Endowm ent Fund, evidencin g continuing interest in our Masonic Homes for the Aged and the Children .
The Correspo ndence Committ ee, publishin g the Californi a Freemason, continue s to gain high praise from the other Masonic Jurisdictions for the quality of this publicati on. Our magazin e is one of the

year ma intained that high standard .
Masonic educatio n always moves slowly. This seems to be its
essential character istic. However , I feel that the Committ ee on Masonic Educatio n has made real progress this year. In addition to the
continue d distribut ion of the candidat es' booklets, there has been published a nd distribut ed to the Lodges a brochure comprisi ng three plans
for Masonic Educatio n. This has been a real step forward, and the
use of the brochure by the individua l Lodges will make Masonic Education a reality rather than merely a project. Excellen t regional meetings with well-info rmed panelists , held in various parts of the state,
have been of great assistanc e.

A new committe e. that of Masonic Informat ion , was created this
year for the purpose of proper dissemin ation of Masonic news to the
daily periodica ls througho ut Californ ia and Hawaii. Its formatio n
and work this year were in the nature of a n experime nt and a very
modest budget of $1.500. primarily to cover secretari al work, was
set up. The members of the Committ ee have given unstintin gly of
their time. and Masonry has received most favorable news coverage
in the press. The exhibit of the Committ ee at this Commun ication
shows some outstand ing example s of this favorable action. It is
planned to publish material which will be of assistanc e to the Constituent Lodges in the preparat ion of proper new releases to local
newspap ers. This Committ ee should become one of the most valuable
in Grand Lodge.
Through the question naire prepared by the Committ ee on the
Relation ship between Temple Associat ions and Constitu ent Lodges,
we have obtained a current roster of the Temple Associat ions existing
in our Jurisdict ion. The importan ce of this compilat ion is realized

problems involving Temple Associat ions is under way and the results

After many years of planning . our Grand Lodge Library was
brought into existence this year in the Library and Museum Room on
the second floor of the Californ ia Masonic Memoria l Temple. There
are more than 2.000 volumes dealing with Masonic subjects. The Library Commiss ion is making a special effort to collect all possible Masonic Californ iana. It is hoped that in time we will have in our Library the finest collectio n of Masonic material dealing with the early
Masonic 'history of Californ ia and Hawaii. The Library Commiss ion
has also set up, for the first time in our jurisdicti on. a series of books
which are available on loan to all brethren . More than 1,000 Masonic
books are available for a three-we ek loan merely on request of a
Brother. The report of the Board of Library Commiss ioners will give
full detail of this fine project and work.
Californ ia and Hawaii have a rich heritage of early Masonic activity. It would be criminal if we did not take some steps to preserve
the documen ts, material. parapher nalia, furnishin gs . and memento s
which are approxim ately one hundred years old. A start 'h as been
made this year for the preserva tion of these irreplace able items. During the past years there have been many instances when valuable
items have been lost through fire and other casualtie s. Let us not be
dilatory in this matter. but act promptly , so that we may save these
historica l documen ts for future genera tions.

On M ay 15, 1861 , the Grand Lodge of California met at Sacramento. California. On that day Grand Lodge was called off and at
the invitation of the seventh Governor of California. Brother Jdhn G.
Downey, a member of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42. marched to the
State Capitol to lay the cornerstone for that building. Almost one
hundred years to the day, namely on May I 3, I 961, Grand Lodge
again convened in Sacramento. Hundreds of Masons attended, and
clad in their white aprons. marched again to the State Capitol and,
at the invitation of the present Governor of California, re- laid the
cornerstone at a most impressive ceremony.
Masonry received most favorable comments in the press for these
events.
On Februa ry 3. 1961. a reception was held in El Centro by the
Imperia l Valley Officers Association for the Grand Master. This
event was given international and interstate significance, as the Grand
Master of Baja California, Most Worshipful Joaquin Aguilar Robles.
and the Grand M aster of Arizona, Most Worshipful Earl A . Spitler.
attended. Grand Lodge met in Special Communication and our visiting Grand Masters were received with due honors. Our Masonic relations with our neighboring Grand Lodges were strengthened by this
meeting.
A like interstate aspect occurred at the centennial celebration of
Lassen Lodge No. 149 at Susanville. California, on May 6, 1961. At
our invitation, the Grand Master of Nevada. Most Worshipful Stanley D. Sund een, and the Grand Master of Oregon , Most Worshipful
Julius M. Swanson. were in attendance and received with honors.
These meetings without doubt created a great interest in Masonry
in the areas involved.
As Grand Master, I participated in a very interesting ceremony
at Santa Rosa. California. Luther Burbank, w ho had gained worldwide fame as a horticulturist, had been a member of Santa Rosa Lodge
No. 57. On his death his gardens, which had been used for man.y of
his experiments with plants, were established as the Burbank Memorial Gardens. A request was made that there be a Masonic dedication
of these gardens, and your Grand Master. on May 19, 1961, ded'icated a plaque which was erected at the entrance to the gardens in
memory of Luther Burbank by his Masonic brethren. Luther Burbank

23

There was another centennial event which deserves special mention. On Washington's Birthday in 1861. Thomas Starr King gave
a n a ddress at Platt's H a ll in San Francisco. Although his topic was
" Washington, Father of His Country," the oration he gave was the
first of a great number which urged the citizens of California to keep
our state in the ranks of the Union. From that date on he traveled
throughout the State of California, and it is recognized that largely
through his efforts, California was saved for the Union. The physical
strain of these efforts resulted in his early death. He was Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge of California at the time of his death. His
remains were cremated and the ashes are contained in a marble sarcophagus in the churchyard of the First Unitarian Church, Geary and
Franklin Streets, San Francisco. Many years later, when the Hall of
Fame at Washington was suggested and each state was called upon
to name its two most illustrious sons, 'I1homas Starr King was named
by California as one.
On the centennial of that historic address, February 22, 1961,
your Grand Master placed a wreath at the statue of Thomas Starr
King in the Hall of Fame. Many legislators from our state were in
attendance, including the two California Senators, Brother Thomas
H . Kuchel and Brother Clair Engle. At the same time, Past Master
H al Curtis of Starr King Lodge No. 344, and an eminent authority on
the life of Thomas Starr King, placed a wreath at his sarcophagus in
San Francisco.
We should always remember one of rhe finest expresisons, significantly M asonic, which Thomas Starr King used, "Do not build
your denominational fences so high that you cannot shake hands
across the top of them."
Some years ago the Juvenile Court Institute was established by
juvenile court judges, members of the Masonic Order in Pennsylvania. Fellows of the Institute are those judges who have attended
one or more of the annual sesions held in connection with the Annual
Convention. During the last week in June, 1961, this convention of
the Annual Council of Juvenile Court Judges of the United States met
in San Francisco. Because of the Masonic bac kground leading to the
formation of this group, the Grand Lodge of California was host at
a breakfast to those attending the convention. Your Grand Master
brought the greetings of the Grand Lodge to those present and told
of the interest of Grand Lodge in aiding youth groups, and our con~
cern with the current problems faced by young people.

VISITS TO OTHER JURISDICTI ONS

in between the Grand Lodge of Japan, whiCh was formed approximately five years ago, and the Grand Lodge of California . It comes
about in this way: The Grand Lodge of the Philippine s was formed
in 1912 by three lodges, which were then under the Jurisdictio n
of California . When the Grand Lodge of Japan was crea ted it
was formed by Lodges under the Jurisdictio n of the Gra nd Lodge
of the Philippine s. On my visit to Japan I found that there were
many brethren a nd some officers of t'h e Grand Lodge of Japan who
are members of Lodges in California and hold Dual Membersh ip in
Lodges under the Grand Lodge of Japan. As the economic reports
show, Japan -is now enjoying the greatest industrial activity it has
ever had. It is hoped that Masonry will likewise expand. Our
Brethren in Japan connected with the Grand Lodge of Japan are
doing a wonderful missionary work and deserve every encourage ment and support. In order to insure s tability it is essential that
petitions be received from Japanese nationals in addition to applications from members of the Security Forces in Japan and affiliated
services. It will take a great deal of ~ffort to make the ideals and
purposes of Masonry so well known to the native-bor n Japanese
that they will seek admission into Masonry. They are making excellent progress. In a very s'hort period of time the Grand Lodge of
Japan has been officially recognized by practically every Grand Jurisdiction in the United States and the great majority of Jurisdictio ns
throughou t the world. Brother Togasaki, whose term as Grand Master was completed a short time before my arrival. was born in San
Francisco and I was privileged to present to him the official greetings
of the Mayor· of the City and County of San Francisco set forth in
a resolution adopted by the Boa rd of Superviso rs. Although the
Lodges were dark on account of the summer period, it was my pleasure to meet with most of the Grand Lodge officers. I particularl y
enjoyed meeting the Master of the Constitue nt Lodge of Kyoto,
Brother Yokoyam a, and visiting with him and his family in his home.

Visits were made. as usual, to other Grand Jurisdictio ns. The
Deputy Grand Master attended the Annual Communic ation of the
Grand Lodge of Washingt on and also the Grand Masters' Conference at Washingt on , D.C. The Senior Grand Warden attended the
Annual Communic ation of the Grand Lodge of Arizona. Your Grand
M aster, in addition to attending the Grand Masters' Conferenc e at
Washingt on , D.C.. also attended the Centennia l Communi cation of
the Grand Lodge of Colorado at Denver, and the Annual Communi cation of the Grand Lodge of Oregon, at Portland . It was my pleasure, at the invitation of the Grand Masters' Conferenc e at Washington, D.C., to present a paper on the affirmative side of the question,
"Should this Conferenc e endeavor to organize an Internatio nal Masonic Conferenc e?". As usual, in accordanc e with the establishe d
rules of the Grand Masters' Conferenc e, no action was taken on
these proposals. although I extended an invitation to hold such an
internatio nal conferenc e at our beautiful Masonic Temple in San
Francisco, because San Francisco is a recognize d internatio nal center.
As Grand Masters have done in the past. I visited the Lodges in
the Hawaiian Islands. The kindness and courtesies extended to the
Grand Master and his family during this visit were without limit.
'Ilhere are now ten Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands, seven located in
the vicinity of Honolulu, on the Island of Oahu , and one on each of
the outlying islands. The total membersh ip of these Lodges as of
June 30, 1961, is slightly in ex·c ess of 3,000 members. I found Masonry flourishing there and the Lodges making good progress.
The visits of an Assistant Grand Lecturer or Grand Lecturer to
Hawaii are of inestimabl e value to our Lodges in that area and should
be continued .
After Hawaii, the Grand Master went on a postman's holiday.
He visited Japan with his family (at his own expense. of course)
to see how Masonry in Japan, and the Grand Lodge of Japan in
particular . w as progressin g. An unusual set of circumstan ces initiated
the trip. In 1959, while serving as Deputy Grand Master I was
invited to attend a luncheon in San Francisco for the Deputy Grand
Master of Japan who was then visiting here. The Deputy from Japan
was Brother George Togasaki, and during luncheon we discovered
that we had gone to Lowell High School together here in S an Francisco in 1915 and had not seen each other for 44 years. Brother
Togasaki urged me to come to Japan while either of us was serving
as Grand Master. My busy calendar was such that I had to delay
the possibility of a trip until my vacation time. There is a definite tie-

In this message I have discussed the importance of protecting and

their fine Masonic spirit and the enthusiastic participation of their
members in Lodge activities, but recognized the problem they face as
to size of membership because of the limited population of their respective areas. I believe there is a clear necessity of giving both moral and
actual assistance to these veteran Lodges, representing the cradle of

landmarks. What better way is there than for Master Masons to seek
plural membership in one of these Lodges. There are a number of Lodges
which have less than l 00 members, and a few with even less than
50 members. It is recommended that Master Masons visit these Lodges
and become acquainted with the wonderful Masonic spirit which exists
there, and by such visits the Master Mason can determine in which
Lodge to seek plural membership.

RELIEF To iCuBAN MASONS

I need not re-count here what has happened to the institutions
of freedom in Cuba. When dictatorship becomes supreme, Masonry
is a target for persecution. A number of our Masonic brethren from
Cuba were fortunate in being able to reach a place of safety in
Florida. We who live here in a land of freedom should be prepared to assist our brethren and their families who are forced to
flee from persecution in their native land, without any of their belongings or property, and seek refuge here. Our obligation to those
brethren who reached Florida required immediate action. Accordingly, the Grand Master directed that the sum of $1,000.00 be forwarded from the Grand Lodge of California to assist in alleviating
the plight of these families in Florida. If the condition continues
for any lengtlr of time, it may be necessary for us to make further
contributions.

III.
The Office of Judge Advocate is a relatively recent one in the list
of Grand Lodge Officers. It was created by legislation adopted in 1953.
For several years there was no one appointed to this office. No appointment was made for this year. and the office has remained vacant during
my term as Grand Master. When your Grand Master wanted the

advice or assistance of competent Masonic lawyers he sought and received such advice from the Chairman and members of the Jurisprudence

me to the conclusion that the Office of Judge Advocate is unnecessary.
With members of the Jurisprudence Committee located in various

One of the hardest working committees of Grand Lodge is the committee referred to as the Committee on Lodge Financing. Actually. its
scope of activities has nothing to do directly with the i~come a~d e~­
penditure of Lodge funds, except in a few instances. This committee is
concerned with those Lodges which own and operate real property or
have a Temple Association carrying on such activity. The name of the
committee is misleading and is often confused with the Committee on
Finance. For this reason it is my recommendatio n that the name of the
committee be changed to " Committee on Temple Construction and
Operations."
The importance of the work of this committee is realized when we
consider that the value of property involved is approximately twentyfive million dollars. The work is constantly expanding. The committee
should be ready to advise Lodges and Temple Associations regarding
the benefit of incorporating as a non-profit corporation and the correct
procedures to accomplish this. Then there is the question of tax status
of the Temple Associations and the filing of the required tax returns.
All of this demands more time from a committee already doing a full
time job. In addition, the number of Masonic Temples is increasing
each year.
These facts impel me to recommend that the size of the committee
be increased from 9 to 11 members. It is also my suggestion that because
of the technical legal questions regarding incorporation. and the tax
problems involved. that the personnel of the committee include. several
attorneys and accountants. It is, therefore. my recommendatio n that
Section 192, C.M.C.. be amended by striking the words "on Lodge

v.
It has been called to my attention that Temple A ssociations and
Lodges owning real property are handicapped by a decision adopted by
Grand Lodge in 1959. Section 199-i, C.M.C.
In that year this Grand Lodge determined that a department store
leasing the ground floor space of Temple property would not be permitted to maintain a package liquor department. That decision was based
upon a previous decision adopted in 1936, Section 199-B, C.M.C. and
one adopted in 1934. pages 26 a nd 27 of 1934 proceedings. When the
1934 and 1936 decisions are examined we find that they applied to
a beer garden. in the one instance, and a pool ball where liquor was
served, in the other. In the 1931 decision, the statement was made that
such decision did not apply to the sale of package liquor.
There is no question that saloon keepers and barkeepers are not
eligible for admission to Masonry and that the leasing of Lodge property
for the purpose of conducting a saloon or bar business. except in connection with and as part of the operation of a bona fide hotel or restaurant. should not be permitted. On the other hand , under Section 513-c,
C.M.C.. the operator of a retail bottle (package) liquor store is eligible
to apply and the Lodge may receive his application. If we permit an
applicant to engage in the business of selling bottled liquor. then we
should likewise be consistent and permit a Temple Association to lease
stores on the ground floor for such purpose.
For these reasons I recommend tha t Section 199-i, C.M.C.. be repealed.

VII.
There is an addition al recomme ndation , requiring legislation . which
feel also should be made. It deals with the problem of Multiple and
Plural Members hip. In order that the seriousn ess of the situation may
be realized. permit me to give a hypothet ical case : Brother Watson is
a member of "X" Lodge in Californi a. Under our law permittin g multiple members hip he subseque ntly joins "Y" Lodge in Mexico. He then
becomes active in lodge affairs and becomes involved in a dispute in
"Y" Lodge regardin g the election of certain officers. Under some summary proceedi ng he is expelled from "Y" Lodge. "Y" Lodge, through
the Grand Secretar y of its Jurisdict ion, notifies the Grand Secretar y of
Californ ia and, under our law as it exists at the present time, Brother
Watson is automati cally expelled from "X" Lodge. his Californ ia
Lodge. without the benefit of any trial. What provision of our Californ ia
Masonic Code apparent ly permits this drastic procedur e? It is not found
in the section dealing with the Trial of Masons for Masonic Offenses ,
but is found in the section dealing with Multiple Members hip. Section
432, Par. 6, of the Ordinan ces, as amended at the Annual Commun ication in 1960, reads as follows:
"6. Suspensi on for non-paym ent of dues or otherwis e, or
expulsio n of a multiple member shall immedia tely. and of
itself. terminat e his members hip in all Lodges in this jurisdiction , and the Secretar y of any Lodge suspendi ng or expelling such a member shall immedia tely notify the Grand
Secretar y and also every other Lodge in which the multiple member holds members hip. Like notice shall be given

GRA ND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

33

in case of reinstate ment, which shall immedia tely and
automati cally restore him to members hip in every other
Lodge in this jurisdicti on of which he was a member. "
Prior to 1960. Sub-Sect ion 6 of 432 did not use the phrase "multiple members hip," but permitted the action as set forth in said section
to be taken in reference to a plural member. Paragrap hs. 1, 2 and 3 of
Section 432 distingui sh between a Dual Member a nd a Plural Member .
Briefly. a Dual Member is one who belongs to a lodge in this jurisdiction and also a lodge in another jurisdiction. A Plural Member is one
who belongs to more than one Lodge in this jurisdicti on. Multiple membership, under the terms of the section, is defined to be either Dual
or Plural Member ship. The rather drastic provision s of Sub-Sect ion 6
can well and properly be applied to a Plural Member. In other words,
if a Mason is tried in one Californ ia Lodge for a Masonic offense and
expelled therefrom by the final action of Grand Lodge, there is no
good reason why he should have the opportun ity of another trial in
some other lodge in this jurisdicti on. On the other hand, if a Dual
Member is expelled in a foreign jurisdicti on. he should not be automatically deprived of his Masonic members hip in Californ ia without
a hearing before his own Lodge. As a matter of fact, our law is to the
contrary. Section 731-A of our Californ ia Masonic Code reads:
" Section 731 was enacted to give effect to the judgmen ts
of other jurisdicti ons. In the absence of any provision on
the subject, the judgmen t of another jurisdicti on suspending a Californ ia Mason cannot be given effect here,
and his Lodge cannot suspend him without a trial on the
basis of such a judgmen t."
We realize the judgmen t of another Masonic jurisdicti on gives
prima-fa cie evidence of the guilt of the accused. but Masonic justice,
in all fairness, should permit the accused to make his defense in his
own Lodge and to have the opportun ity to present facts as to the unfairness of the trial in the other jurisdicti on, and to submit any other
defense he might have.
For these reasons it is my recomme ndation that Section 432, Par. 6,
of the Ordinan ce be amended by deleting the word "Multipl e" and
substitut ing therefor the word "Plural" so that the paragrap h will read
as follows:
"Suspens ion for non-pay ment of dues or otherwis e, or expulsion of a plural member shall immedia tely, and of itself.
terminat e his members hip in all Lodges in this jurisdiction. and the Secretar y of any Lodge suspendi ng or expelling such a member shall immedia tely notify the Grand
Secretar y and also every other Lodge in which the plural

member holds membership. Like notice shall be given in
case of reinstatement, which shall immediately and automatically restore him to membership in every other Lodge
in this jurisdiction of which he was a member."

DEc1s10N No. 2

I received an inquiry from "X" Lodge giving the following facts: In
December, 1958, the Lodge elected Brother "P" as Master of the
Lodge. Brother "P" served approximately three months before his
death. First Query: "Is it proper for the Lodge to list Brother ' P' as a
Past Master?" Second Query: "Is it proper for the Lodge to place
Brother ' P's' picture alongside of the other Past Masters in the anteroom with the notation 'Died while in office'?'' The law applicable to the
first question is found in Section 490 of the California Masonic Code.
This section provides that the title of Past Master applies to one who
has been regularly elected or named in a charter and installed and has
served a term as Master of a chartered Lodge within this jurisdiction.
This has been interpreted to mean that the Master does not become a
Past Master unless he has served to the end of the term for which he
was elected. Of course. a Master should not be entitled to this honor if he
voluntarily resigns or does some act for which he is removed from office.
When death, however, prevents the completion of his term it does
not seem fair that he should be penalized. But that is the law. The
Grand Master has no power to change it. However, I can recommend
its change. which I have done. and the final determination is to be made
by Grand Lodge. Under the present law the answer to the first inquiry
is that it is not proper to list the deceased Master as a Past Master.
The answer to the second question is that I see nothing improper
in placing the picture of the deceased Master alongside those who have
served in office as Master of the Lodge with the notation that he "Died
while in office."
DEc1s10N No. 3

In a lodge an application for the Degrees was received at a stated
meeting in June. At both the July and August stated meeti~gs t~e Committee was granted further time. In September the committee s report
was made, an unfavorable one, and the applicant was declared rejected.
At the October meeting a Past Master requested that the facts found
by the committee be read . basing his request on Section 530 of the California Masonic Code. This section reads as follows:
"530. Report of Committee. The report shall set forth in
detail the facts ascertained respecting the applicant and
the conclusion of the committee, which conclusion shall be
read to the Lodge. The facts ascertained shall be read
when directed by the Master, or when request therefor is
made by any member of the Lodge. The names of the
members of the committee shall not be made known. The
report must be returned to the Master."

GRAND LODGE OF CA LIFO RNIA

37

The Master ref used to read the report and sounded his gavel. The
Past Master has appea led to the Grand Master from the ruling of the
Master.
The appeal involves an interpretation of Section 530, C.M.C. The
purpose of reading the facts, when requested by a member, is to inform
the Brethren thereof prior to a ballot. before which there may be such
discussion of the qualifications of the applicant and of the propriety of
receiving him into the Lodge as may seem proper. (Sec. 535, C.M.C.)
There would seem to be no such purpose in reading the facts to the
Lodge when the committee report is unfavorable, since Section 532 ,
C.M.C. provides that "if the report of the committee, or any member
thereof, be unfavorable, no ballot shall be had, but the Master shall,
upon the reception of such report, declare the applicant rejected."
Nevertheless, Section 530 gives any member of the Lodge, without
qualification, the right to request that the facts s ha ll be read.
It is my opinion that any member of the Lodge may request the facts
ascertained, whether the candidate is reported on favorably or unfavorably. The request. however, must be made at the meeting at w hich
the report is given to the Master. It cannot be made at a subsequent
meeting of the Lodge. It is my opinion and decision that the Master
correctly refused to read the facts at a meeting subsequent to the
one at which the applicant was declared rejected.

I hope that the accomplishments of this year will continue to be of

accord, without continued and determined effort by the Master Masons.

At the close of this annual communication, my duties as Grand

Some time ago I had occasion to review the life of M ichael Faraday,
the father of electrical science. This great scientific mind, involved most
of his life with complex principles and laws, nevertheless devoted a
great portion of his time to encouraging the interest of young people
in the world of science, and was able to express his thoughts in terms
that they found challenging and could understand. He ga:e a s~ries
of lectures at the Royal Institute of London, the final one bemg entitled
"The Chemical History of a Candle." He closed his detailed scientific
explanation with a philosophical statement which should be a guide to
Masons, even though as far as I can ascertain, Michael Faraday was not
a Mason. He said in closing:
"All I can say to you at the end of these lectu~es (and
we must come to an end at one time or other) 1s to express the wish that you may, in your generation, be ~t to
compare to a candle: that you may, like it, shin~ as. lights
to those a bout you; that in all your acts you may iustify the

"THE YEAR OP THE MASTER MASON"

My Brethren:
For centuries the Chinese h ave followed the custom of designating
each of their years with the symbol of some animal and element. According to the Chinese calendar, each year has its own characteristics, according to that yea r's animal symbol and the influence of the particular
element. There are twelve animals and five eJements which rotate and
fall into different combinations from year to year.
In California, Masons have occasionally described or designated
the Masonic Year. This occurred in 1958, which was called "The Year
of the Temple," being the year when our magnificient Memorial Temple
was completed and dedicated. We still have an obligation in connection
with the Temple, and it will be a yea r of rejoicing when the final payment is made on the loan due the banks. We shall certainly continue our
efforts this year to rid the Temple of this indebtedness.
What name shall we select to designate the 1960-61 Masonic Year?
Too little emphasis has been placed on the role of the 242 ,000 Masons
who comprise the body of Masonry in California. I would therefore
like to characterize this year in California Masonry as "The Year of
the Master Mason."
This suggestion is really not so unique. The importance of the Master
Mason was evidently in the minds of those who conceived the beautiful
endomosaic window w hich beautifies the foyer of our Temple. It depicts
many historic events and symbols of Masonry, but the central figu re in
that magnificent work of art i! the Master Mason, clothed in his white
apron. He is the primary and dominant representation. There stands
the Master Mason. symbolic of the 242,000 Masons who belong to the
Grand Lodge of California. He is s tanding upon the soils actually taken
from each of the 58 counties of California and from Hawaii.
It is fitting that a Grand Master designate the year as "The Year
of the Master Mason," because the Grand .Master is the direct representative of the 242,000 Master Masons in this jurisdiction. Those of
you who have attended a reception for the Grand Master in a constituent lodge. know how he is received. He is not received as the Grand
Master of C alifornia n or as the Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of
California. He is received as the Grand Master of Masons in California.
Note that his title is Grand Master of Masons in California-not Grand
Master of the Grand Lodge or the constituent lodges, but of the individual Masons themselves. No one can reach the high station of Grand
Master without feeling with all humility the honor and responsibility
which comes in being the representative of 242,000 Master Masons in
California.

40

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is sometimes thought that Grand Lodge is oblivious of the interests of the individual Mason and that it is a super-organization controlling the activities of all Masons in California. Grand Lodge is not
a self-perpetuating body. It is the representative of the 242,000 Masons
in this state. Each Master Mason attending his lodge has the right to
vote for the Master and Wardens of his lodge. The Master and Wardens or a duly elected representative attend the Annual Communication
of the Grand Lodge. At each Annual Communication the Grand Master
and other officers are elected. Thus Grand Lodge is the direct representative of all Master Masons through the duly elected officers of the 700
constituent lodges in this state and Hawaii.

ileges-material and spiritual. Spiritually, Masonry can be a way of life
for him. He is entitled to material aid and assistance in time of need and
distress. In return, each Master Mason has the duty of performing his
obligations-to live his Masonry realistically and objectively. in a creditable manner, to act honorably and deal fairly with all men, and to
support his Masonic lodge with sincere and active participation.
Granted Masonry is our way of life-then attending lodge is an
integral part of the pattern of our day-to-day activities. May the Year
of the Master Mason be a year of Renaissance of Masonic interest,
devotion and inspiration on the part of the quarter million Master Masons in California and Hawaii.

It has been pointed out in a-recent Masonic editorial that the general
public has the mistaken idea that there is some supreme authority in
Masonry which controls the activities of all Masons. Brother Luther A.
Smith, Sovereign Grand Commander of the Scottish Rite, Southern
Jurisdiction, states in that editorial t'hat the source of Masonic Power
is in the individual Mason. He writes, "Grand Masters and Grand Commanders are, in truth, merely teachers, the educators of the Craft who
have been invested with the authority to inform and remind their Brethren of their duties and responsibilities to God, their country, their neighbor, and themselves. It is the higih calling of every Mason to keep alive in
the hearts of men the love of freedom and the willingness to fight and die
for it if necessary. <It will be seen, therefore that the source of power in
Masonry, is in the individual Mason. Furthermore, if Masonic power
is to be used to promote the welfare and happiness of the community
and to safeguard the freedom of the people, the individual Mason must
exercise it whenever and wherever it is needed."
The real strength of Masonry is not in the Grand Master, nor in
the elected officers, not in the Grand Lodge, but basically in the individual Master M,ason. What a tremendous source of power-almost a
quarter million in California. In this Year of the Master Mason, what
a wonderful accomplishment it would be if that reservoir of strength
were used for the benefit of Masonry in our jurisdiction. What a great
step forward it would be if the quarter million, or even a fair percentage
of them, would attend their lodges. That should be the start-a reawakening of Masonic interest and activity-which would in turn affect
Grand Lodge and make Masonry a more potent force in our state. The
source of Masonry is in the individual Mason, and when we speak of
attendance at lodge, it does not mean "the other fellow" but you, and
you, and you--each and every individual Master Mason.
'Dhere is a principle of law which states that for every right there
is a corresponding duty. A Master Mason enjoys many rights and priv-

EXHIBIT No. II
GRAND LODGE WoRKS FOR You
My Brethren:
In the Winter issue of CALIFORNIA FREEMASON, I designated this
year as "The Year of the Master Mason." Since then I have given much
thought to methods of implementing this theme. What can Grand Lodge
and its officers do to make this year meaningful for the Master Mason?
What can the constituent Lodges do to enrich the objective? What can
the individual Master Mason himself do to attain the goals we have in
mind?
The opening ceremonies of Grand Lodge have been limited to members of Grand Lodge. By resolution amending the California Masonic
Code this restriction has been removed, and Master Masons are now
welc~me to attend except during the short period on the last day when
the elections are hekl. It is hoped that many Master Masons will be with
us at the next annual communication, in the fourth week of September,
1961, and observe Grand Lodge in operation-for it is your Grand
Lodge.
A criticism of the Craft has been that we make Master Masons proficient in the candidates' lectures, but impart little fundamental knowledge of the history or philosophy of Freemasonry in general. or the
Grand Lodge of California in particular. Steps are being taken to
remedy this situation. Reprints have been made of a series of booklets
-Address to the Candidate, Book of the Entered Apprentice, Book
of the Fellow Craft, Book of the Master Mason. These are d·i stributed
to the candidates, the first immediately after election, and the others
after each degree has been conferred. Further revision of the pamphlets
is contemplated by the Ritual Committee. In addition, the Ritucl Com-

43

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mittee is planning a course of instruction through the Inspectors of the
Districts and the candidates' coaches in the constituent Lodges, so that
each candidate will have a better opportunity to know something more
about Masonry than just the ritual. This, then is the picture as regards
the education of the candidate up to the point of his proficiency examination in the Master Mason degree.

Also in May. the Sacramento Valley area will observe an outstanding centennial. in which the entire state will join. This will recall the
events of May 15, 1861, when our Grand Lodge was meeting in Sacramento. The proceedings were interrupted so that the brethren could
march to the State Capitol, where the cornerstone of the Capitol was
laid in accordance with our traditional Masonic ceremony. The tentative date for this celebration is May 13, 1961.
This summer the San Joaquin Valley area will be asked to take part
in a meeting to be held at Columbia, where tribute will be paid to the
Lodges in the southern Mother Lode mining region. For the large number of Master Masons in the Los Angeles area, a city-wide Masonic
event is now on the planning board. These activities, sponsored by
Grand Lodge, are aimed at providing the individual Master Mason
with an opportunity to join his fellow Masons in celebrating memorable
events in the history of Masonry in California.
Th:is message to the Craft has dealt with the question of what Grand
Lodge and its officers are doing and intend to do, to make this year
meaningful for the individual member. In the next issue, we will discuss
what constituent Lodges can do to enrich the objective. I am the first
to admit that I do not 1have "all the answers." and will welcome your
letters suggestings methods of implementing this Year of the Master
Mason.

How about the quarter million Master Masons now on our rollswhat is planned for them? All Master Masons desiring enlightenment
in matters Masonic will have many opportunities to gratify this desire.
The Masonic Education Committee (formerly called the Masonic Research Committee) has prepared a brochure setting forth various voluntary plans which can be adopted by the Lodges. As soon as the text
has been approved and plans completed for its publication, it will be
placed in the hands of the Lodges. Each Lodge has been requested to
appoint a Masonic Education chairman who will spearhead the program
in :his individual Lodge. The Research Lodges are planning seminars
and meetings to discuss vital and interesting Masonic subjects. With
all of this, California should be in the forefront in the field of Masonic
education for our 242,000 Master Masons.
There are many members :in our jurisdiction who have not had the

since they are occupied in their vocations or professions on weekdays,
and their time does not permit them to come to the Temple during the
regular visiting hours. The officers of the Temple have now made it
possible for Lodges and groups of Masons to visit on week-ends, and
those interested should contact the office of Grand Lodge.
A new Grand Lodge committee has been created this year-the
Committee on Masonic Information. Its objective will be to provide the
press witih data concerning the activities of Grand Lodge. News items
and pictures are prepared and distributed to news channels for publication. There is no doubt that good public relations will result from this
service, as the general public will have a better opportunity to know
something of the positive approach of our Fraternity. Likewise, the committee will keep all Master Masons informed about the program for
the year, wh:ich is geared to participation by all Master Masons.

Grand Lodge will be convened in a special communication to receive
the Grand Master of Nevada and die Grand Master of Oregon. All
Master Masons in the vicinity are urged to take part in this event.

III

2500 SMITHS, 2000 JoHNSONS, 1400 BROWNS!!

My Brethren:
Did you know that there are about 2500 Smiths who are Master
Masons belonging to Lodges under the Grand Lodge of California?
We also have 2000 Johnsons and 1400 Browns. We are accustomed
to talking about the Joneses, but here the Johnsons seem to outnumber
them!
Every one of our 700 Lodges has its proportionate number of Smiths,
Johnsons and Browns. each of them a Master Mason, not just a page
full of names in a telephone book. In this Year of the Master Mason,
what are the constituent Lodges doing to make this year meaningful
for each member?

The aim of each activity of a Lodge should be to make the Smiths,
fohnsons and Browns something more than a statistic. They are all
Master Masons, and each one should lie assured that he is recognized
as such. The outstanding constituent Lodges are those where there is

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

full participation by all of the members in all of the activities of the
Lodge. Such interest is not just accidental-it is nearly always the
result of adequate and efficient planning, as to programming; publicizing
and general encouragement of participation.
Good programming covers both the ritualistic and business meetings
and balances these with proper entertainment features. Plans should
not be made haphazardly as the year progresses. At the very outset of
the year, major events should be mapped out as to tentative dates, so
that the year's program can be built around them. No successful Lodge
year can be like Topsy who "just grew."
As to the meetings and entertainment features themselves, it is imperative to remember that they must be varied. Any program, no matter
how carefully arranged, may be dull and uninteresting if presented
every year in the same way without change. Brethren are attracted to
the meetings when the presentation is novel.
The manner of conducting every meeting is all-important. Start the
program on time: avoid lengthy preliminaries; if there is a speaker, give
him a suitable introduction to his audience: and CLOSE ON TIME.

It is universally recognized that undignified or careless degree work
has a bad effect on attendance. Punctuality and promptness on nights
when degrees are being conferred as on other meeting nights. In planning the programs, and in carrying them out, the interest of the individual Master Mason should be kept foremost in mind, as his interest is
the reason for all of these efforts.
After programming, the next step is sufficient publicity. The finest
program in the world will be poorly attended if the members are not
fully informed about it.
Beyond publicizing the program the Lodge bulletin can serve as a
strong medium for encouraging general participation in Lodge activities,
if it makes frequent reference to the individual Master Mason members
of the Lodge. The bulletin should not be used exclusively for news items
about the officers or the Past Masters (or even Grand Lodge officers!).
Everyone likes to see his name in print.

It is unfortunate that the feeling has developed in Masonry that
the average member is merely an "onlooker" and not a participant in
the work of the Lodge. The degree work is almost exclusively restricted
to the officers. When and where possible, the members should be given
some part. At business meetings the members should be encouraged to
take part in debates and discussions. The educational programs afford
an excellent opportunity for member participation. There can be no
greater boon to good attendance than to make each individual Master
Mason--each of the Smiths, Johnsons and Browns-feel that he has

45

an active part and is actually needed in the Lodge, and is not merely
a dues-payer and a watcher!
Of course, we all recognize that this is not a one-way street. The
constituent Lodge can do all of these things to implement the purposes
of the Year of the Master MasoR, but there are certain obligations and
duties which the Master Mason himself must perform. What the
Master Mason himself can do will be the subject of my message to
you in the next issue of the CALIFORNIA FREEMASON.

ALFRED F. BRESLAUER
Grand Master

EXHIBIT No. IV
To ALL MASTER MASONS

My Brethren:
As an indication that the office of Grand Master is a full-time job,
you may be interested to know that this message is being written while
on a flight from San Francisco to Portland. The Grand Master is on
his way to represent you and the Grand Lodge of California at the
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Oregon, which convenes
tomorrow morning, so I am glad to have this time "up in the air" to prepare this message for the CALIFORNIA FREEMASON.
It is a temptation, as I glance out of the plane window, to talk to
you about the scenic wonders, from Mt. Shasta to Mt. Hood, which
seem to be on full display today just for our benefit! However, while
this plane may be "up in the air," I will try to keep my feet on the
ground in writing this message, for this has been a grount!l-level year,
the Year of the Master Mason. When we meet on the level state-wide,
there are 243,000 Masons symbolically assembled at the first step of all
Masonry in California, the Master Mason degree.
In this, my fourth message in this significant year, I address my
remarks to all Master Masons in California. Your Grand Master and
the Grand Lodge are indeed proud of the fine response of the Master
Masons this year. We observed the Centennial of the laying of the
cornerstone of the State Capitol at Sacramento, on May 13. The Brethren responded most admirably to our request for their participation in
this ·celebration. One thousand Master Masons, wearing their white
aprons, joined with the Shrine Band, the Knights Templar and the
Grand Lodge officers in marching through the streets of Sacramento
to the Capitol as their predecessors had done a hundred years before,
to commemorate this historic anniversary. We often hear the phrase
"stand up and be counted." Well, 1000 Master Masons did so in Sacramento, and it was a most rewarding and reassuring sight' to your

Grand Master. In another recent event, the same evidence of support
and genuine interest was given in Coronado, when 350 apron-clad
Master 1Masons marched from the Lodge Ha11 to the site of tjhe laying
of the cornerstone of the Coronado High School. A fine response was
also seen in the great number of Master Masons attending the Centennial celebration of Lassen Lodge at Susanvi11e. In fact, there have been
many outstanding meetings of Master Masons throughout the entire
state.

EXHIBIT XII
PROCLAMATION
PORTY-SECOND ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

Although fantastic strides have been made in the field of automation by electronics in recent years, it is still a basic fact that you cannot
have a public school system without public sc:hool teachers.
What is a teacher? First of all, an educator; then a psychologist,
and in many cases, a foster parent; clearly, not a machine. The person
must have a sympathetic nature and a genuine love and respec~ for
children. In short, the public school teacher is one of the most important
people in our national life - entrusted as the teacher is with rhe education of the future citizen.
For this reason, the theme adopted for the 1961 Annual Observance
is "The Public School Teacher - Builder of Tomorrow's Leaders."
During this week, let us all visit the Public Schools, where all
children may attend, without charge, and without regard to race, creed
oc religion. Let us pay honor to all those who 'have the responsibilty of
operating our schools: the administrators, staff personnel. principals
and teachers.
In accordance with our annual custom, I hereby proclaim the last
week !n April, 1961 - being April 24 to April 28 inclusive - as
Public Schools Week.
I direct that no meetings be held during that period except Stated
Meetings, if they fall therein, and meetings for Public Schools Week
observance.
This Proclamation is to be read at the Stated Meetings of each
Lodge in the months of March and April. 1961.
Dated: January 26, 1961.
ALFRED F. BRESLAUER

Grand Master
Attest:
EDWARD H. SIEMS

Grand Secretary

DEMOLAY WEEK

March 13-18, 1961
Youth - Key to the Future! The mantle of responsibility will, in a
few short years, be in the !hands of the young people of today. These
young people must be prepared for that responsibility.
The way of life that we cherish is being threatened from every side.
Those that would destroy it are devoting a great deal of time in their
efforts to control the thinking of our young people. If we are to preserve
those heritages which we hold so dear, we must see that the youth of
today are influenced by the principles of right thinking and right
living.
The idea for DeMolay was generated in the mind of a Mason. The
formation of the Order of DeMolay was projected and made effective
by the late Frank S. Land, one of the outstanding Masons of this

of our way of life. This young man's organization, with our help, can
be the means of assuring that the citizens of tomorrow will follow in our
footsteps.
Today there are 270 Chapters of the Order of DeMolay in California and Hawaii. Each Chapter is sponsored by a body of Master
Masons. Well over half of them by constituent Lodges of this Grand
Jurisdidion.

playing in die future of our communities and our nation, I proclaim that
the week of March 13th through March 18th of 1961 shall be observed
as DeMolay Week throughout the Jurisdiction of this Grand Lodge.

bulletin or otherwise, and to include some recognition of the Order of
DeMolay during that week.

MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND LoDGE, F. & A. M OF CALIFORNIA

To all Masonic Brethren within the Jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons of California:
In commemoration of the one hundred seventy-fourth anniversat'}
of the signing of the Constitution of the United States of America, that
momentous event having taken place on September 17, 1787, I do hereby
designate the month starting September 17, 1961, and ending October
14, 1961, as Constitution Observance Month.
Each Lodge fo this Grand Jurisdiction is requested during this
period, either independently or in conjunction with other Lodges, to
set apart at least one day to memorialize this occasion. It is suggested
that other organizations ('Masonic affiliated or not). service groups,
youth groups, schools, churches, etc., be urged to participate.
I direct that when more than one Lodge shall join in the same program for the purpose stated, none of said Lodges shall hold a meeting
or schedule any event for the Lodge on the day appointed for this occasion.

sponsorship.

REGULATIONS

I. ADVERTISING
No organization as herein defined nor any member thereof sb.all
solicit oc accept advertising of any kind for publication or insertion in
any roster, program, bulletin, or announcements to be printed or pub~
lished.
No such organization nor any member thereof shall sponsor, insert,
place or pcint advertising of any kind in any publication claiming to be
MasGnic in name or character. (C.M.C. 334).
This regulation does not prohibit the placement in bona fide news~
papers of legitimate news items of grganization, group or club activities
or advertisements in s2id newspapers in connection with rummage
sales which do not use the name of any of the organizations hereinbefore
named or any group thereof.

II. PUBLIC SUPPORT
No organization as herein defined nor any agency thereof sucb. as
social clubs, mothers' clubs, sewing circles or other clubs or groups
within such organization, nor any member thereof, using any name
whatever shall sponsor any event, project, scheme or plan wherein
public suppart is requested or solicited on behalf of such organization or
any agency or group thereof. Tickets or other items may not be sold
to the general public. ( C.M.C. 333.) Rummage sales wherein public
support is solicited in the name of the organization or of any group
thereof are forbidden, and these sales may not be held in a Masonic
Temple. Howeve , organ:izations may hold rummage sales which are
open to the public but the place of sale may not display the name of the
organization conducting the sale. News stories or advertisements of the
sales may be used but may not contain the name of the organization

III. SOLIQTATION OP GIFTS
T•he solicit~tion of merchants, firms, business houses, or the public
for gifts of merchandise, money or prizes of any kind for or in connec~
tion with the general activities of the group or organization, such as
dinners, parties, and meetings, is strictly forbidden. This regulation does
not · prohibit a member of any organization from voluntarily donating
such a gift or contributing to a Charity, or furnishing entertainment for a
meeting of the organization, either individually or through his business.
If the organization wishes to announce the name and business of the
member who sponsored or furnished the entertainment at the meeting,
it may do so.

IV. COMMERCIAL VENTURES
No organization herein denned or any agency or group thereof shall
directly or indirectly engage in any business, project, venture, promo~
tion, scheme or plan which is unethical, misleading, fraudulent or illegal.
No such organization shall knowingly receive money or property as a
donation or contribution from such operations ( C.M.C. 332).

rafRe, lottery, or other gambling enterprise or accept any of the proceeds
or profits therefrom. ( C.M.C. 685).

(3)
To the Most W orshi'pful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS the world in which we live moves faster and faster,
and
WHEREAS many of those who attend our Lodge sessions leave
early in the evening, and
WHEREAS studies indicate a desire on the part of the brethren
for short Lodge sessions,
NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED. that
1. The incoming Grand Master is hereby directed to appoint a Spe~
cial Committee, consisting of not less than seven members, to study the
possibilities of shortening our ritualistic work by eliminating duplica~
tions; by making reference in lectures to materials printed in the monitor,
or other authorized printed material; and by such other suitable and
proper devices as the committee may determine, provided always that
nothing shall be proposed or considered which alters the body of Ma~
sonry, or weakens its teachings or conflicts with its ancient charges.
2. The study shall include the opening and closing ceremonies, the
ritualistic work of each of the three degrees, and such other ritualistic
work as the committee may determine.
3. The Committee is directed to consider, on their merits, certain
"short forms" now in use in some of the other jurisdictions in the
United States.
4. The Committee may take not more than two years for its work.
It may, if it so decides, terminate its work in one year.
5. The necessary expenses of the Committee shall be paid by the
Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
J. WILSON GETSINGER, Master, Lodge No. 518

nance and on Ritual.

63

(8)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, there are many worthy and well qualified men who
have been wounded, maimed, otherwise physically disabled in the
defense of our country in its wars, and others similarly worthy and well
qualified who, through misfortune or tragedy have also become physically disabled or maimed, and who are literally unable to comply with the
physical requirements of our laws and are therefore denied participation
in our privileges, and,
WHEREAS, this is contrary to our teachings and precepts, particularly that of Brotherly love, and,
WHEREAS, we no longer work in operative Masonry but speculative only, these physical requirements are obsolete,
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that all references .to physical
sufficiency or physical qualifications for the degrees contained in our
laws, rules, regulations, edicts, decisions, O·r any other matter on this
subject, written or unwritten, having the force of law, be rescinded.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the prescribed ritual for the
various degrees remain unchanged but that in the event that an accepted
candidate is unable to physically execute or perform acts prescribed in
the various degrees, that the conferring Lodge be vested with the power
and authority to assist the candidate, either actually, by demonstration,
or other appropriate means, to perform or execute those physical requirements which his disability prevents him from performing or executing without such assistance or demonstration.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that any prostheses usually worn
or used by an accepted applicant, for his safety, comfort, physical
improvement, well being, or necessity, be permitted to be worn or used
during the conferring of the degrees.
Respectfully submitted,
RusSELL J. BRAASCH, Master, Lodge No. 651

RESEARCH LODGE OFFICERS
(12)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Relative to the Resolution adopted at the 1960 Grand Lodge session,
to the effect thpt "None but a Past Master of a California Lodge is
eligible for election as Master, Senior or Junior Warden of a Research
Lodge" (now Paragraph 18 of Section 385 CMC), it is now felt, after
more mature deliberation, and after seeing the crippling effect this
Amendment has had on the prospects for Officer material in the
Research Lodges, that this provision operates to the detriment of the
Research Lodges, without offering any compensating advantages. There
is in actual reality no connection between the knowledge and capabilities of a Past Master of a Degree-conferring Lodge and the requirements for leadership in a purely Research Lodge.
Accordingly, a Motion was passed at the March Stated Meeting of
the Northern California Research Lodge reading as follows :
"MOVED that it is the sense of the Northern California Research
Lodge that the Resolution adopted at the 1960 Communication of Grand
Lodge, limiting the eligibility of Masters and Wardens of Research
Lodges to Past Masters only, is not in the interest of California Masonry,
and would only serve to impede the progress of our Research Lodges and
the service they are capable of rendering Freemasonry in California,
and that therefore the Resolution referred to should be rescinded at the
next Communication of Grand Lodge.''

STUDY OF SUBVERSIVE TECHNIQUES

MEMBERSIIlP IN SUBVERSIVE ORGANIZATIO N

(16)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS the penetration by subversive agents of an alien
ideology into every phase of public affairs is threatening the continuation of the American way of life, and
WHEREAS this penetration has been made possible by a lack
of understanding on the part of loyal citizens to the seriousness of the
communistic inroads, and
WHEREAS the most effective weapon against any subversive force
is an informed, alert electorate, thoroughly imbued with the positive
political theories upon which our government was founded, and
WHEREAS the existing practices have not been adequate in the
dissemination of counter information to cope with the advancing communistic penetration, and
WHEREAS Masonry has traditionally opposed all totalitarian
philosophies and has represented freedom from oppression throughout
the world, and
WHEREAS the dissemination of knowledge is a basic function of
Masonry
THEREFORE BE IT NOW RESOLVED that the Grand Lodge
of the State of California approve and encourage the formation of a
voluntary committee in each of its constituent Lodges for the express
purpose of serving in these capacities:
1. To study the techniques and methods of Communism:
2. To act in the capacity of a resource group to promote and direct
the distribution of information to the public in each community
of the techniques and methods of Communism:
3. To use every opportunity to stress to the citizens of our country
the importance of our political heritage.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that a copy of this resolution
be transmitted to the several Grand Lodges of the United States of
America.
Respectfully submitted,
FRANK H. VONDERAHE, Past Master, Lodge No. 345
FABIN F. RICHART, JR., Past Master, Lodge No. 345
THOMAS L. HENNINGER, Past Master, Lodge No. 345
GLENN M. HUTCHISON, Master, Lodge No. 345
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes, and on
Education.
