(17)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS the Masonic Fraternity from time immemorial has
established, supported and fought for individual freedom and liberty
for all peoples and is recognized throughout the world as an organization of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth, and
WHEREAS the Masons of the United States of America carried
on and strengthened these basic concepts of their Masonic Forefathers
by a Declaration of Independence, a Bill of Rights and an establishment
of a duly constituted government, and
WHEREAS there exists throu9hout the world today various organizations, groups, parties and nations which are attempting to intimidate,
subvert and destroy duly constituted and representative government
and to supplant the same with dictatorial regimentation and
WHEREAS many people belonging to these subversive groups are
infiltrating into all organizations including our own and
WHEREAS our normal investigation reports may fail to expose
one of subversive intension because there is nothing now included on
our present application form for the degrees of Masonry which would
pose a discussion of such an activity,
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the following
question be added in our "Application for Degrees": "Would you be
willing to take an oath that you never were, or are, or ever will be,
knowingly aff!liated with any subversive group or organization inimical
to the government of the United States of America."
Respectfully submitted,
DOUGLAS M. CRAIG, Master, Lodge No. 381
}AMES L. LoGSDON, Sr. Warden, Lodge No. 381

called collateral Masonic organizations has been terminated by the
ruling in 1955 by the Most Worshipful Grand Master that the game
of BINGO is against Masonic law and policy, it is
RESOLVED, that the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M.
of the State of California, adopt the following policy regarding the
playing of BINGO and that annotation ( d) of Section 685 of the
California Masonic Code be amended accordingly:
BINGO games may be conducted by Lodges or so-<:alled collateral
Masonic organizations subject to the following restrictions:
1. Attendance must be limited to members of the lodge or organization and their families and guests.
2. No charge can be made, directly or indirectly, for attendance
or participation in the game.
3. Prizes awarded must be of nominal value, such as boxes of
candy, or items of similar value.
4. The event cannot be advertised or publicized other than in the
regularly published bulletins to members of the lodge or organization.
Any lodge or organization conducting or participating in a BINGO
game in which the foregoing restrictions are not complied with shall
be regarded as violating Masonic law and policy.
Respectfully submitted,

(as hereinafter described) was one of the most popular social events
in many California Lodges and so-called collateral Masonic organizations, and

to arrange enough diversified events in which the members and their
families can join in social activities, and
WHEREAS, when the game of BINGO is planned by the lodge
or organization solely as a social activity for the entertainment of its
members and their families, no charge is made for admission or to play
the game, the public is not invited and the event is not publicized outside the lodge or organization, and the prizes are limited to those of
nominal value; the game has no public connotation of gambling because
the public is in no way involved and the members and their families
are folly aware of the noncommercial nature of the event, and

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
One year ago the brethren of California accorded me the honor and
privilege of serving as Grand Treasurer. Herewith is my report covering
the activity of the office for that period.
Immediately upon taking office, an audit was conducted by Lybrand,
Ross Bros. & Montgomery, C. P. A.'s and all funds and securities were
properly accounted for and placed under my custody by Edward H.
Siems, P.G.M .• my predecessor.
In conjunction with the Grand Master, Grand Secretary and the
Chairman of the Finance Committee, the fidelity bonds of the Grand
Treasurer, Assistant Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and Assistant
Grand Secretary were reviewed and were increased to the sum of
$50,000 for each officer.
With the exception of the period of my illness early this year, I attended all meetings of the Investment Committee as well as the Homes
Board where the Grand Treasurer serves as treasurer by virtue of his
office.
Following precedent all financial reports and audits of the Grand
Lodge and its agencies are submitted in one folder. I urge each delegate
to carefully review the statements and audits as they give in detail the
story of the operation of the Grand Lodge and its various activities.
All appropriations and disbursements have been carefully reviewed
by the professional auditors as provided in Section 194 C.M.C.
Detailed rec;ords and vouchers are on file in the office of the Grand
Secretary.
The year just passed ·has been a splendid one and the budget as
presented one year ago has been strictly adhered to. The only supplemental appropriations granted were the following:
Grand Lodge Officer's Travel... ............................... $ 2,500
Inspectors' Apron & Stationery.............................. 1,200
Legal Services·-·-··--------·-----·-----------------·--------------·--·-·· 1,000
Workmen's Compensation Insurance.................... 1,000
Current Liability on Pension Fund.......................... 6,000
Social Security Taxes..............................................
800
Capital Additional Replacements............................ 1 ,500
$14,000
These were more than offset by savings in several categories. Actual
expenditures for the year were $4,308.49 less than the original budget
adopted one year ago.

This has been an interesting experience and I have enjoyed tremendously the privilege of serving with such men as our Grand Master,
M. W. Alfred F. Breslauer, Grand Secretary, M. W. Edward H. Siems,
W. Paul A. Pflueger, Assistant Grand Treasurer and W. Henry D.
Oliphant, Assistant Grand Secretary. Our friendships go way back and
being a part of this year's team has been most gratifying.
I express to the brethren my deep appreciation for the privilege of
serving them and sincerely hope that my efforts have been fruitful for
the Grand Lodge.
ARTHUR M. WARREN
Grand Treasurer

REP ORT OF GRA ND SECR ETA RY
To the Most Wors hipfu l Gran d Lodge F. o A. M. of Califo
rnia:
In prese nting my first annua l repor t as your Grand Secre
tary I wish
to emphasize that this past year has been a most active
one.
The real task of the Gran d Secre tary has tradit ionall
y been the
implied dema nd of exercising a sixth sense to recognize
the needs of the
Gran d Lodge, where ver they exist, and to minister to
those needs . The
experiences of the past Maso nic year, which developed
throu gh this
dema nd, have contin ued to follow the patter n. New proble
ms, for which
there are no clear- cut solutions in the Code, have had
a way of prese nting themselves almost daily. There are no ready -made
answe rs. In addition to the many new ones, old problems with new
ramifications have
appea red for conclusion.
This, then, is the challe nge to the Gran d Secre tary and
his staff. It
is the solution of these every day problems which offers
the greate st
oppor tunity for service to the Frate rnity. With the
many and varied
duties and responsibilities of the office the possibilities
for service are
unlimited.
The attem pt to familiarize myself with all the detail
s of the office
has been a confining one. The rewar ds, however, in friend
ships formed
with so many of the finest men on earth, as they conta
ct our office,
makes each day's effort a real joy and privilege.

MEMBERSHIP ANALYSIS

Again, as in past years, I present an analysis of the applications for
Degrees accepted during the year. As far as possible the same standards
were used for arriving at the occupations, and it is interesting to note
the changes over last year.
In presenting a membership analysis this year, we have again covered
only applicants for degrees. Part of the variance in percentages is due
to a closer adherence during this past year to a prescribed schedule of
designated occupations for clarification on the returns.

MEMBERSHIP

In presenting the membership figures this year I am using comparison
figures for the last forty years by ten-year periods beginning with 1921.
You will note that 1921 and 1951 show the largest number of initiates.
However, in 1961 we initiated more than in 1931 and 1941 and the
number of affiliates from other jurisdictions was the largest of the five

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

87

years shown. The gain in 1961 was only 1527, but it exceeds 1931 when
we had only 360 and 1941 when we had an actual Joss of 342.

Man~ Grand Lodges have been showing membership losses for
years. Figures prepared by the Conference of Grand Secretaries of
North America in February 1961 show New York with a total membership of 302,572 and a Joss of 2832, Pennsylvania with a membership
of 257,711 and a gain of 448, Ohio with a membership of 282,397 and
a loss of 396, IJlinois with a membership of 239,913 and a Joss of 3435,
and. Te~as with a membership of 244,078 and a gain of 1402. Only
California, Texas and Florida of the 49 jurisdictions in the United
States show a gain of more than one thousand members. California had
the largest gain with Florida, whose total membership is only 68,551,
a close second.
On the surface it appears that Masonry in California is losing ground
in membership in spite of the tremendous increase in population. However, we must remember that a great many of the people coming here
are women and children, none of whom are potential members. Many
are senior citizens hoping to establish the five year residence necessary to
qualify them for one of the highest old age pensions paid by any state
in the Union. Of this latter group it is a known fact that a number of
them are members of Lodges in other jurisdictions.

In conclusion I want to express the deep sense of gratification which
I feel as Grand Secretary. The job is a challengin g one, and, as is
usual when changes are made, new thoughts and new ideas are brought
into the picture. Perhaps this is good. We seek ever to progress.
The membership in general, and the Secretarie s of the Lodges in
particular, have been most gracious in accepting innovations. The
Ritual Committee and the Inspectors have worked most diligently in
helping me "over the hurdles," and putting into effect the ideas which
have been developed.
It is my earnest wish that we go forward together, and that all of
you remembe r-THE DOOR IS ALWAY S OPEN. I welcome suggestions, and will most certainly give careful considerat ion to all ideas.
My sincere apprecition to our loyal staff, and to all those with
whom we are privileged to work.

Referred to Committee on Distribution.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTUR ER
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
When you elected me Grand Lecturer in absentia last Septembe r I
anticipate d the opportuni ty of proving to you shortly that your trust
had not been misplaced. Indeed, as the first meeting of the Ritual Committee was held in Pasadena on December 2nd and 3rd, 1960, I felt
again the satisfactio n of working in the ritual of our Fraternity . At this
meeting, all the work of the three degrees was exemplified by the
Assistant Grand Lecturers, with complete agreemen t on ~e work as
handed down to us by our predecessors.
By the new year, returning strength enabled me to resume all duties
of the office and the opportuni ty of again seeing old friends at our
ceremonies and receptions presented itself.
A meeting of tJhe Ritual Committee was held in Sacramen to on
February 25th and 26th to review the administra tive duties of the
Committee members in relation to the Inspectors of their respective
Divisions. Here, too, furtheranc e of cooperatio n in carrying forward
the Grand Master's program was a prime topic.
Your Grand Lecturer was again prevented by coincidence from

108

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

directing the activities of the Committee and by C?rder of the Grand
Master the active duties of the Grand Lecturer were assumed March
1'1, 1961 by Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis, Past Grand Lecturer.
Much of the remainder of this report must, therefore, reflect the work
which Bill so ably performed. Few friends in life are as constant as
those whom we are privileged to meet in Masonry and your Past Grand
Lecturer Elbert W. Davis has proven his mettle so frequently that mere
reiteration of his merits seems futile. My heartfelt thanks go to him for
his devotion to Masonry as well as his proven friendship.
As has been customary in past years, the lodges of Hawaii received
special instruction in the ritual. Worshipful Clare B. Campbell, Assistant Grand Lecturer, made the trip in January on behalf of the Grand
Lecturer, spending nine days working with the lodges, the officers'
coaches and the Inspectors of the three districts. He reports steady improvement in the work and I believe that his attention to their needs is
appreciated by our brethren of th~ Islands.
Divisional Conferences were held as follows:
Divisions I and II at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 16-18, 1961, conducted jointly by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell, Assistant Grand
Lecturer, Division I. and Worshipful Harold N. Richards, Assistant
Grand Lecturer, Division II.
Division III at Santa Rosa, May 19-21. 1961, conducted by Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division III.
Division IV, at Yosemite, June 2-4. 1961, conducted by Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis, Past Grand Lecturer, in the absence of Worshipful Raymond G. Taylor, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division V. at Ventura, April 21-23, 1961, conducted by Worshipful Ralph W. Collins, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division V.
Division VI, at La Jolla, March 17-19, 1961, conducted by Worshipful W. Ben Sorrells, Assistant Grand Lecturer, Division VI.
The Ritual Committee, with the Acting Grand Lecturer, attended all
conferences except as noted.
All questions arising during my absence were referred to Brother
Davis and either handled as routine or discussed with me by mail and
disposed of in harmony by the Acting Grand Lecturer. Complete agreement has characterized the conduct of ritual affairs over the years, and
since we are charged with maintaining the essential purity of the work,
the existing Ritual Committee system has resulted in uniformity not
otherwise possible.
The Grand Lecturer's duties include the Annual School for In-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

109

spectors held this year on Saturday, September 23rd. After enforced
absence from the ritual for these many months, this school became a
welcome homecoming to active Masonry.
This school again proves the efficacy of our present system of instruction. It is further proof that the instructive tongue and the attentive
ear remain the greatest teaching tools for the spoken ritual and that
seeing and doing beat a textbook any day. The Inspectors of the six
Divisions performed their assigned portions of the work in excellent
fashion and are to be congratulated on it.
Prior to the disablement of the Grand Lecturer, muoh work had
been done on an augmented system of Candidate instruction. Valuable
work has been done in educational matters over many years by committees in this field. Particular attention was given, starting two years
ago, along the line of broadened material for the advancing Candidate.
A year ago. the task of Candidate educ·a tion was placed in our hands.
Had not fortune dictated otherwise, this report would have contained
the background of our effort on constructing a workable and sensible
system. The Grand Master was understanding of the situation confronting the Committee in the disablement of the one who had correlated its efforts and granted such further time as might be required to
complete the project. Although work is now going forward, I cannot
report a finished product to you at this time. My hope is that your
patience and our perseverance will in time produce results of benefit
to the lodges.
I cannot clo~e without paying tribute to the fraternal love which has
buoyed me over the past months. Life without friendship would be
dark and dreary. The cards, notes and good wishes of my brethren did
much to add determination to desire and much of my recovery is due to
you. The ties more strongly bind when adversity strikes and our feeling
of brotherly affection could save die world from itself if only we could
spread it over all mankind.
Respectfully submitted,
DONALD G. CAMPBELL

Grand Lecturer
Referred to Committee on Distribution.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REPOR T OF TRUST EES OF THE MASON IC HOME S

GENERAL REVIEW
It would seem with over sixty years of experience behind it, the
work of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of Californ ia
would be largely routine. Such. however, is not at all the case. As in our
national and personal affairs, change seems to be the order of the day,
creating ever new problems, and of course inevitably adding new expenses to the disbursement side of our ledgers.
Our buildings in both Decoto, or Union City, and in Covina are
no longer new, nor are they as modern as we would like. They need
continual repairs and replacements to keep them in the state of perfection that you demand. The cities are building up around us. freeways
are threating encroachment, new laws and bureaucr atic decisions tend
to hamper us, labor and material costs continue to climb, all of which
presents continuing problems to your Board.
There is, however, a brighter side to the picture for which your
Board can never express enough gratitude . The Homes seem to be one
of the favorite charities of our brethren and it is always a source of
joy to report that the many bequests that we receive from the brethren
and their widows, yes, and from non-Mas ons as well, make is possible
for us to maintain our exacting standard s without undue calls for per
capita taxes. For this your Board expresse s its deep appreciation, and
urges that continue d publicity be given this importan t part of our
program .
The Board of Trustees also wants to express its thanks to the
Masonic Homes Endowm ent Board for their excellent educational work
among the co~stituent lodges. Each year surpasse s the previous year
in the voluntar y contributions from the jurisdiction, thanks to their
untiring efforts, the cooperation of the lodges and the generosi ty of the
brethren .
Our sincere apprecia tion goes also to the Investme nt Committ ee of

funds of the Masonic Homes, including of course the Endowm ent Fund,
the income from which is so indispensable to our homes program .

MASONIC HOME AT UNION CITY ( DECOTO)
Our handsom e new hospital building at Union City so much admired
by our visitors was flrst occupied on August 23, 1960, with approximately 80 patients. However , the hospital populatio n increased to approxima tely 90 in a few months and then reached a peak of 96. You
will note that the grounds around this new hospital now have been
landscap ed and a complete sprinkling system installed so that this
facility is in every sense of the word complete.
The populatio n of our Decoto home is presently the greatest in its
history. From time to time there is a short waiting period for women ap-

112

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

plicants and a slightly longer one for couples. It had been our hope
to remodel the old hospital facility to give us additional guest rooms.
The Board was advised, however, that clie buildings comprising t'he
old hospital were inadequate structurally and hazardous from a fire
protection standpoint for residents. Consequently a small amount of
funds were used to rehabilitate it for employee use on a temporary basis.
Besides housing male employees, one ward section is used for a recrea~
tion room for employees when parties are being held by them. Another
ward is used for occupational therapy.
The ground occupied by this old hospital offers an opportunity for
expansion of the residential quarters of the Masonic Home. The Board
has authorized a preliminary study toward this end. In this event the
three buildings which comprise the old hospital facility, of course, will
have to be demolished as they cannot be rebuilt adequately to conforw
with State standards.
Among the many repairs, improvements and replacements required
and made during the year to maintain and modernize our old buildings,
you will observe that new and brighter hall lights have been installed
by Home employees in all of the hallways and have proved to be a big
improvement much appreciated by our guests.
Last year a survey was made looking toward the improving of our
purchasing and receiving procedures and the handling of and prepara~
tion and serving of food. The program outlined by a firm of experts in
this line has gradually been adopted and is expected to effect material
savings as well as offer other advantages to the Home and its residents.
A program of occupational therapy for members under the super~
vision of our new Matron, Mrs. Velma Huckabee, has been introduced
and we are happy to report that it has progressed very satisfactorily.
At a recent meeting of the Board approval was given for the purchase
of materials to expand this program. Monthly excursions by bus for
those who are able to take such trips also have been inaugurated. In all,
your Masonic Home at Union City has had another rewarding and
successful year.
CHILDREN's HoMEATCovIN A

The population figures for the Children's Home in Covina reveal a
new all~time low. This in turn plays havoc with our per capita costs, as
of course it is impossible through the most careful management to reduce
expenses in the same proportion as clie population decreases.
As you know, the Grand Master in his message recommends that
authority be given the Board to broaden the base of our admissions to
our Children's Home. The Board is willing to accept this responsibility
and concurs with the thinking of the Grand Master that service to a

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

113

larger number may be rendered by so doing without materially in~
creasing our over~all costs.
T 1he urbanization of our present location in Covina has given your
Board a great deal of concern. Thinking into the future we have com~
menced a study of possible relocation and attendant modernization of
our Children's Home, with the thought in mind of a reduction of the
per capita costs. 'Dhe age and obsolescence of our buildings account in a
great measure for our high operational expenses, and your Board feels
that a change to a more rural location might be both advantageous and
desirable in the not too distant future.
Our Superintenden t's report on Covina activities will indicate a most
active and successful year.
FINANCE

The new Hospital construction, and existing building modification
program required by State authorities, has now been completed and all
~harges have been paid. This has been accomplished by tran sf ers from
reserves and sale of securities. No portion of per capita tax receipts, etc.,
has been used for this purpose.
Current operating expenses have risen along with experience in
private industry. In addition, the opening of the Hospital has added new
burdens to our payroll and related &arges. Medical and hospital serv~
ices provided by Palo Alto Clinic and Palo Alto Stanford Hospital have
also resulted in higher charges because of greater use of their facilities
occasioned by ~erious illness and hospital requirements not available
at our infirmary.
During the past five years our current operating expenses have ex~
ceeded income in substantial amount and only the profit from sale of
securities has prevented us from requiring an increase in per capita taxes.
The year just closed discloses a 1heavy deficit and the coming year will
show no improvement.
To meet recurring deficits, your Trustees have been transferring
funds from reserves to meet specific operating charges and at its next
general meeting a further study will be reviewed and action taken
thereon.
Every effort is being made to keep our expenses in line with income
and with this premise in mind a continuance of the $1.00 per capita is
requested for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1963.
CONCLUSION

The Board wishes to express heartfelt appreciation to the Super~
intendents of both of our Homes for their years of untiring, unselfish and

COVINA HOME

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is with great pleasure that I present my thirteenth report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina, for the year
ending June 30, 1961.
HOME MEMBERS HIP

As of June 30, 1961, the population of our Masonic Home Family
numbers thirty-eigh t children- twenty-fi ve boys and thirteen girls. During the fiscal year of 1960-61, four children 1have been admitted to the
Home, all boys (ages 16, 15, 11, and 11 ) . Twelve children left the
Home, five graduating from high school, and seven returning to their
families or guardians. Two of the graduates plan to continue their education through scholarships while remaining in residence at the Home.
Two plan to enter the service, and to resume their education at a later
date. One will reside locally with his mot'her, and attend Junior College.

eleven in grade school. The twenty-th ree families are here on applications from twenty-th ree Lodges.
HOME, SCHOOL, AND COMMUNI TY ACTMTIES

The past year has been outstandin g in several respects. One girl
and two boys were awarded the distinction of representing the high
school and the Home at Girls' and Boys' State in Sacramento. Linda
Williams was sponsored by American Legion Auxiliary, Victory No. 54.
Linda also won the Adolph Koshland "Good Citizenship" award for
1960. Bill Barraclough and Jim Hoard were sponsored by the Sunshine
and the F. J. Irwin Posts of the American Legion, respectively. Fred
Clinkscale won the coveted distinction of being "Boy of the Year."
Our 4-H Club, the Masonic Home Pioneers, enjoyed an extremely

119

successful year. At the 1960 Los Angeles County Fair, we received a
"first" and followed this with Senior Champion and Grand Ohampion
for our Herd Boar, Reform Ranger 3. In addition to this, Reform
Ranger 1st became Senior Reserve Champ and Reserve Grand Champion Boar. At the affair, the Home received three Firsts, one Second,
four Thirds, and two Fifth prizes, in addition to the above.
At the 4-H Fair at Pomona, the Home club "Masonic Pioneers"
took eleven "firsts," seven "seconds, " two "thirds," and one fourth
place. Climaxing this event, Georgia Cox received the First Place
Award for Showmanship. Young Steve Archinal received a trophy for
poultry. The Home placed second in the trophy for horses, and second for swine. At the Third Annual Malibu Horse Show, Georgia Cox
received a First Place in the Halter Class for her filly, "Flash Can,"
and again she was awarded a handsome trophy as the Champion in
Horse Showmanship.
Our 4-H Club, the Masonic Pioneers, numbers seven boys and one
girl. Our Home children have obtained notable achievements in competition with thousands of young people in this interesting and important phase of our American Way of Life. Mr. Smithson, our Farm
Manager, is to be complimented for 'his efforts in behalf of our Masonic
Pioneers 4-H Club.
At Charter Oak High School the Home children have attained many
honors. Officers for the Freshman Class were Fred Clinkscale, President: David Kilpatrick, Vice-Pres ident: Sharon Williams, Secretary:
and Terry Hepry, Legislator. Susan Farmer was Legislator for the
Junior Class: and Tom Henry was Program Co-ordina tor and Student
Body President, 1959 to 1960. Tom Orth, Jerry Orth, and Bob Faulk
played for the high school Band and Orchesqa . Linda Williams is a
member of Dionecian's, Girls' Honorary Service Organizat ion.
Athletic-wise, our boys have been outstandin g. Richard Farmer and
Ken Wylie played on the outstandin g Championship Varsity Football
Team which went up to the very last contest in the CIF Playoffs. Richard Farmer was chosen as Left End on the Honorary All-Star High
School Eleven, and Player of the Week. Ken Wylie was also outstanding in wrestling competition - he won twenty-th ree straight contests.
Twelve of our boys won many honors in track competition, and several
competed on the baseball and gymnastic teams.
All the children are encourage d to participat e along broad horizons.
Several of the Junior Girls are Brownie or regular Girl Scouts. Many
children regularly receive piano lessons from an accomplished concert
pianist. Three of the boys belong to the De Molay group. When the
children reach the acceptable age, they are encourage d to take Behind
the Wheel and Drivers' Training Courses, and are carefully instructed

VISITATIONS

Visitations by the various Masonic Lodges, which come out to picnic
on the beautiful grounds and tour the buildings, continue to be very
popular. For most months, the quota is filled almost a year in advance,
and there is always a gay, exciting aura about these third Sundays of
every month. The children are as happy and inspired to meet and guide
the Lodge members and guests as the visitors seem to be to make the
acquaintance of their "Brothers' Children." The result is invaria~ly a
pleasant day for all. These visits seem to perpetuate and keep ahve a
warm interest in the children of the Covina Home Family.

HEALTH

Every possible effort is made to keep the young residents in topnotch condition. The Magan Clinic, founded by Dr. W. P. Magan, Sr.,
supervises the health of the children. Here they are sent for regular
physicals and any supplementary care, either medical or surgical, which

THE ALUMNI

The Alumni contact is maintained on a vital and constant basis, both
through the medium of personal visits at the various Alumni Reunions
and visits to the Home at Covina, but particularly through the medium
of the Newsletter. The 1961 edition is one of the largest ever published,
and contains about three times as many contributions from the Alumni
as the one published in 1%0. Copies of the 1961 Newsletter were mailed
to all active Alumni who had contributed, all those who responded to a
subsequent questionnaire, Masonic Lodges sponsoring children in the
Home, Grand Lodge officers, and members of the Board of Trustees and
the Endowment Board.
There were three official gatherings of Alumni groups during the last
year: a Sacramento Picnic on the first Saturday in June 1961: the Covina
Reunion on the second Sunday in September: and the Reunion Dinner
in San Francisco on the Saturday preceding Grand Lodge. All were
well-attended ... and enojyed. Another heartening feature is the way in
which our Alumni come "Home" with any problem, thus revealing that
this is their Home in the truest sense of the word. Various Alumni spend
a portion of their leave from the Military Service or Weekend Liberties
with their Brothers and Sisters of our Home Family. At the present
time, two members of the Alumni are resident here while taking classes
at a local Junior College, and in all probability, three others will be living
here for the same purpose in the near future.
This "electric" contact with the Alumni, Lodge members, the Staff,
and the friends of the Covina Home is an invaluable inspiration which
gives a special meaning and substance to life. It is a privilege to be
placed in this unique position of being able to "give and receive," and
I wish at this time to express my sincere appreciation for having been
given this opportunity with its perennially rewarding relationships.

Respectfully submitted,
ROBERT M. HENRY,Superintend ent

ANNUAL REPORT OF
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

special listing of those Lodges which average $3 or more per member,
listed according to average, and to be as high on that list as possible.
To these Lodges we give our special thanks and congratulations. Last

follows:

The Masonic Homes Endowment Board hereby submits its 29th
Annual Report covering the fiscal year of July 1, 1960 through June 30,
1961. A thoughtful study of this report will reveal an ever-increasing
interest and support of this great Masonic project.
CASH CONTRIBUTIONS

Individual contributions in the sum of $6451453.76 were received
through the Lodges this year, for a net increase of $94,303.42 over last
year. These figures do not include bequests, memorials, special gifts,
etc .• which are shown elsewhere in this report.
Each year there is an increase in the number of larger amounts.
Many contribute $100 to $1000 and this year one brother gave $2500
and another brother gave $5,000. The $5.000 contribution was given in
tribute to M. W. Alfred F . Breslauer, Grand Master, and the donor
insisted that his name not be given.
These larger gifts demonstrate the wisdom of this Board in no longer
suggesting any specified amount for a contribution, and certainly not
$2 as was first suggested in 1934. Times and money values have changed
since then, and so have the costs of maintaining the Homes. We now
simply suggest that each brother determine for himself, the amount he
shall contribute each year, according to his financial situation, his own
conscience, his fraternal concern for his less fortunate brethren and
their families, the dignity of "caring for our own," and his desire to
"insure the continuance of loving care."
INCOME PROM THE ENDOWMENT FUND

The income from the Endowment Fund this year amounted to
$445,000.00 and this amount was applied to the operating costs of
both Homes. This demonstrates that the Endowment Fund benefits the
present, as well as the future.
HONOR ROLL LoDGES

Honor Roll Status was attained this year by 573 Lodges averaging
$2 or more per member, as compared to 502 last year, for a net gain of 71
Honor Roll Lodges. Fifty Lodges made the Honor Roll this year for the
first time since the Honor Roll system was inaugurated in 1934. Eightyone per cent of the Lodges are on the Honor Roll this year. This Board
believes that the Honor Roll should be considered a minimum amount
but not the maximum goal. It should be considered as a stepping-stone
or mile-post along the way to an ultimate achievement.

PERCENTAGE OF PARTICIPATION

Forty..five per cent of the members of the jurisdiction made a contribution this year, as compared to 41.4% last year. This year 109,733
brethren made individual contributions, for a net increase of 9,513 over
last year. The number of contributors and percentage of participation
have been steadily increasing each year, but the above figures show that
more than 130,000 members (55%) did not contribute to the Homes
Endowment this year. To reach that otlher 55% is one of our chief
concerns.

125

WILLS AND BEQUESTS

$144,165.62 in bequests were received into the Endowment Fund
during the past year, representing final and lasting tribute to this great
work of "caring for our own." A bequest to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund is a permanent gift because the principal remains intact
and continues to earn income for the Homes for generations to come.
It is truly leaving "footprints in the sands of time" and becomes a
living memorial. Only the income from the Endowment Fund is used
in maintaining the Homes.
PRINTED ITEMS

During the past year the Lodges have ordered 1,227,000 printed
items for mailing to members as follows:
Pamphlets ................................................614,000
Contribution Envelopes ..........................279,000
Grand Master's Proclamations ................ 218,000
Stop-Think-Consolidate Cards .............. 116,000
(To enclose with dues notices)
T'hese printed items were all prepared and furnished by this Homes
Endowment Board. In addition, this Board caused to be printed and
mailed to Lodge Officers, 25,000 items of promotion such as Information
Manuals, Annual Reports, Sample Letters, Sample Contribution Envelopes, Sample Pamphlets, etc. Therefore the total printed items distributed by this Board was 1,252,500. This, of course, does not include
countless thousands of letters and other printed items prepared by the
Lodges and mailed to members.

.

ENDOWMENT BOARD PERSONNEL

At the 1960 session of Grand Lodge a resolution was passed providing for an increase in the number of Members for this Board from
15 to 21. In addition, one member, Melvin A. Pixley, asked not to be
reappointed. Therefore, seven new members were appointed to the
Board by Most Worshipful Alfred F. Breslauer, Grand Master, to
serve in the general area surrounding their city of residence as follows:
Arthur A. Anderson .................... Dinuba
James B. Baker.............................La Mirada
Fred F. Elliott.............................. Bell
Glen Gladson ...............................North Hollywood
Charles F. Minetti... ....................Santa Rosa
Charles R. Ratkovich.................. Berkeley
Kent 0. Seymour......................... Mill Valley
Edward H. Siems, Grand Secretary, was elected by this Board to
serve as its Secretary, and Arthur M. Warren, Grand Treasurer, as
Treasurer of the Board.
Our sincere thanks go to Melvin A. Pixley who worked diligently

126

on this Board for three years and was responsible for many thousands
of dollars being received into the Homes Endowment Fund.
Also, our special thanks go to Lloyd E. Wilson, P.G.M., Assistant
to the Grand Master, who was Secretary of this Board for nearly 20
years, while- he was Grand Secretary, and devoted much time and
effort to this Masonic endeavor.
OUR THANKS TO ALL
Mere words cannot begin to express our heartfelt thanks and
gratitude to all who had a part in establishing this year's record of
achievement, nor is it possible to give individual credit to the hundreds
of brethren who devoted time and effort in addition to their cash contributions. Our Grand Master, M. W. Alfred F. Breslauer, has been
of great assistance by the publicity he has given to the Homes Endowment and the encouragement and help he has given to the members of
the Endowment Board. Our Grand Secretary, Edward H. Siems, and
Assistant Grand Secretary, Henry D. Oliphant, and their entire staff
have given the very finest of assistance and cooperation. The devoted
assistance of Don G. Campbell and his Assistant Grand Lecturers and
Inspectors have been extremely valuable in establishing this high
accomplishment.
Our thanks and appreciation go to the Masters and other Officers,
and the Homes Endowment Committeemen of the Lodges who really
make possible the success of the Homes Endowment program. The
Master, who is anxious to make his year the greatest for the Homes
Endowment, and the Endowment Committeemen upon whom he places
the responsibility, are in a position to do a great job and in most cases
the record of achievement for the Endowment reflects their devoted
work. In many Lodges, "if the Secretary does not do it, it is not done."
Without the wock and cooperation of the Lodge Secretary, it would be
difficult for a Lodge to make an outstanding record. As a group the
Lodge Secretaries should, and do, receive a very large portion of the
credit for outstanding accomplishments as shown in this report.
Last, but certainly not least, our sincere thanks go to the 110,000
brethren who made cash contributions to the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund this year. Their gifts have materially helped to "insure the
continuance of loving care" to those in our two Masonic Homes.
We respectfully request the usual appropriation of $14,000.00 for the
current ·fiscal year.
Respectfully submitted,
THE MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
JOHN M. GORDON, Chairman
KERMIT A. JACOBSON, Vice-Chairman (South)
BYRON COLEMAN, Vice-Chairman (North)
ARTHUR M. WARREN, P.G.M., Treasurer
EDWARD H. SIEMS, P .G.M., Secretary

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshi pful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
The Board of Control herewit h submits its annual report covering
the most pertinen t data on the activities of our Boards of Relief and
their Employ ment Bureaus.
We are pleased to report that the work being carried on by our
Executi ve Secretaries and employees continues to reflect creditab ly
upon our beloved Fratern ity. These devoted brethre n and co~workers
continu e to go far and away beyond tlhe call of duty in carrying out
their work. The Board of Control appreciates, as we are certain this
Grand Lodge does, their continu ed dedication and devotion to their
duties. Their richest compen sation can only be their knowledge of the
service they are renderin g to our brethre n and our fellow men.
There are in our Jurisdiction nineteen Boards of Relief, five of
which operate Employ ment Bureaus. Our newest Board in Orange
County has developed into a thriving and dynami c part of our great
service effort for Califor nia Masons .
The Board of Control is charged by Grand Lodge with the super~
vision of our Boards of Relief. Uniform standar ds have been estab~
lished for their operations, reportin g and auditing, by which we are
able to keep a watchfu l eye on all of the operatio ns for whi-ch we are
responsible.
The Board of Control holds at least three meetings each year at
which times we meet with our Board of Relief Secreta ries in order that
we may have a more persona l contact with them and they with each
other, and that we may all have a better underst anding of our respec~
tive problems and responsibilities.
After having analyze d the audited reports which have been submitt ed
by our Boards of Relief. we ask your brief indulgence in the following
conden sed statistics covering their operations during the Masoni c Year
ended June 30, 1961 :
Advanc ed for Relief.................................... $35,343.69
Funeral s conducted...................................... 1,032
Total calls made.......................................... 30,052
Ca11s on the sick.......................................... 7,994
Investigations conducted............................ 2,974
Relief calls made.......................................... 8,880
Miscellaneous calls made............................ 10,204

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

149

It goes without saying that these activities require untiring dedica~
tion and devotion to Masonr y. Our brethre n w'ho carry on this work
deserve the undying gratitud e of the entire Craft. Their compen sations
are modest, except for the knowledge in their hearts of the service they
are renderin g to Masonr y and to their fell ow men.
BLOOD BANKS

Many of our Boards of Relief operate Masoni c Blood Banks, and
those which do not usually have some other arrange ment for providin g
blood for Masons or their depend ents when required. The following
figures indicate the extent of our blood donatio n activities during the
past year:
Units of blood donated ........................................ 3,876
Units of blood wit1hdrawn .................................... 3,l 97
You will note that a substan tial reserve of blood has been built up
during the Year. The actual cost, in savings to our Masoni c family, by
this service during the Year just dosed, was $78,935.
EMPLOY MENT BUREAU S

As stated above, we have Employ ment Bureaus within five of our
Boards of Relief. Their purpose, of course, is to assist our Masoni c
family to obtain gainful employment. Althoug h there has been increasing
competition in this field from public placement agencies, Unions and
others, we still feel that even the limited accomplishments are worth
our efforts in .the relief of distress to even a comparatively fow of our
Masoni c family. The following figures briefly tell of the operatio ns of
our Employ ment Bureau s during the past Masoni c Year:
Registe red for employment ..................................6,290
Positions actually secured.................................... 862
Of course, our Employ ment Bureaus operate without any charge,
either to employer or applican t. Had fees been charged for our services
on the basis of rates fixed for commercial agencies, such employment
opportu nities would have cost our Masoni c family $80,062.30. In other
words, the Fratern ity has actually saved over $80,000.00 by using these
facilities of ours.
APPROP RIATION S

For many years it has been a custom of this Grand Lodge to assist
financially our Employ ment Bureaus, when deemed, and to the extent
deemed expedient. The Board of Control has carefull y analyze d the
request s of the various Boards for appropr iations in tlhis regard and
makes the following recommendations aggrega ting $11,800.00 for this
Masoni c Year:

We have referred the matter of these appropri ations to the Chair~
man of the Finance Committee as required by Section 265 of the Cali~

REIMBUR SEMENTS TO MASONIC BOARDS OF RELIEF

EXPIRAT ION OF PRESENT TERM OF OFFICE OF
BOARD OF CONTRO L MEMBER S:

150

It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that no worthy
brother sojournin g in our Jurisdiction, or his immediate family, shall
suffer for f:lhe necessities of life, or have other than a decent burial upon
their demise, regardles s of the ability or willingness of the brother's
own Lodge to reimburse us. Our Grand Lodge undertak es to reimburse
any Board of Relief for any such unrecoverable advances . During the
Masonic Year recently closed our Boards of Relief advance d more than
$35,000.00 to sojourne rs and their depende nts. All such advances were
carefully scrutinized by one of our Executive Secretari es and efforts were
made to obtain reimbursement. lt is gratifyin g to report that out of
$35,343.69 so advance d during the year, only $513.05 was not repaid, in
accordan ce with the following requests to Grand Lodge for reimburse~
ment:
1

REIMBUR SEMENT TO THE SAN FRANCISC O BOARD OF RELIEF

The San Francisc o Board of Relief has requeste d $488.05 for a case
which has continued over many years. This involves a very worthy
brother from Scotland , and his wife, for whom the Grand Lodge of
Scotland makes some provision, but not sufficient for their essential
needs. This is a most deserving case.
REIMBUR SEMENT TO THE SAN DIEGO BOARD OF RELIEF

The San Diego Board of Relief has requeste d reimbursement in the
amount of $25.00 which represen ts relief extended to a brother from a
mid~western state. We have carefully reviewed the correspo ndence
with the brother's Lodge and the St. Louis Board of Relief and are
satisfied that the San Diego Secretar y displaye d good judgmen t and
Masonic Charity in this matter and is to be commended for his handling
of the case.
The Board of Control has recommended that the Finance Com~
mittee approve these reimbursements totaling $513.05.
The Board of Control has received the most helpful cooperat ion
during this past year from the Most Worship ful Grand Master, the
new Grand Secretar y and the Assistan t Grand Secretar y, as well as

MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE CORPORATION
This is the Seventh Annual Report issued by the Board of Trustees
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The Board of Trustees met following the close of the 1960 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, as is required by the By-Laws, for
the purpose of organization. The election of Brother Guy B. Mize,
Deputy Grand Master: Brother Ira W. Coburn, Senior Grand Warden: and Brother Elmer W. Heald, Junior Grand Warden, was formally reported to the Board, and on motion duly made, seconded and
carried, they were elected members of the Board of Trustees. Appointed
to the Board by the Grand Master were Brother Ralph W. Head and
Brother Samuel I. Jacobs. The Board elected the following officers: Ira
W. Coburn, President: Frank Harwell, Jr., Vice-President: Paul A.
Pflueger, Treasurer, and Edward H. Siems, Secretary.
As a part of this report, we are submitting the reports of Lybrand,
Ross Brothers & Montgomery, Certified Public Accountants, and
Brother Alvin A. Horwege, Building Manager.
The Board of Trustees has, as a continuing concern, the increase
of rentals from the auditorium and the convention area. These facilities
have now been in public use for a period in excess of three years. Experience suggests that certain changes (some brought to our attention
by users of the auditorium) would make an already attractive facility
more acceptable for certain types of performances. To this end a detailed study ·has been made.
In considering the problem, the Board recognized that the auditorium was built primarily for Grand Lodge purposes, and that nothing
should be done to impair this use. It was felt that in the event that any
alterations or additions were made, the appearance and architectural
effect of the auditorium would remain the same as originally designed.
It was also the consensus that if the stage were raised, it should be
done by the ·Creation of a portable stage-capable of easy installation
and removal so that the present level would be maintained for Grand
Lodge purposes.
After many conferences and sub-committee meetings with recognized experts in the various fields, namely: structural design: acoustics:
sound system: lighting, the Board selected Brother Harold M. Engle
as the structural engineer charged with doing the following: ( 1 ) Design
a stage 3'7,Vi" above the auditorium floor-which stage may be easily
removed and stored - the design to include provision for portable backdrop and wings. ( 2) Make recommendations for the installation of

153

The design of the stage proposed by Brother Engle was accepted,
and f?llowing the submission of bids, the William Horstmeyer Construction Company was awarded the work. This part of the project
should be completed by October 15, 1%1.
Upon the recommendation of Brother Engle, the Board selected
Dr. Vern Knudsen of UCLA (one of the world's recognized authorities on acoustics) to make a complete re-survey of the acoustics and
sound system of the auditorium, and to submit recommendations to
the ~oard. Action will be taken as soon as Dr. Knudsen's report is
received, and action will also be taken on Brother Engle's recommendations for improved lighting.
The operation of the garage for the past year has shown an increase in revenue, but with greater use of the auditorium (as a result
of the changes outlined above), the number of stalls rented should materially increase.
A study of the curtailment of expenses and procedures was madeas a result of which, fees paid to the Certified Public Accountants were
appreciably decreased. This was brought about by having the office
staff assume cettain accounting work heretofore done by outside accountants. fo addition, maintenance costs of the elevator system were
reduced.
There is one part of the Accountant's report which the Board wishes
to bring to your attention: "The General Contractor of the Temple filed
a suit against the Temple on August 4, 1958. The architect, general
counsel, and the trustees contend that this action is without merit. The
Temple has flied an answer and crosscomplaint. Additional related
issues also have been raised-which matters may be resolved by compromise, or settled by trial. The interests of the Temple will be vigorously prosecuted by its counsel."
The Board feels that all applications for the use of our facilities
should be carefully screened so that our building will not be physically
damaged by unreliable lessees. In order, however, to avoid any unfavorable publicity in regard to its action in this connection, the Board has
adopted the policy that all bookings will be confirmed and agreed upon
by the President, Secretary. and the Building Manager.
The Most Worshipful Alfred F. Breslauer, Grand Master, requested

REPO RT OF BUILD ING MANA GER
To the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple:
Brethren:
In present ing this, my third annual report as Manage r of the California Masoni c Memor ial Temple , may I call your attentio n to a comparison of the operatin g experience during the year 1959-60 and the
year 1960-61.
During the 1959-60 year we had 58 days of occupan cy by ten conventions plus 37 days of occupan cy by concert s and shows using the
auditorium. During the 1960-61 year there were 32 days of occupan cy
by four conventions plus 45 days of use of the auditorium for concert s
and shows.
As pointed out in the report submitted last year, the sharp drop in
the use of the exhibit space is account ed for by the addition al space
for similar purposes which has become available in the hotels. The
encouraging increase in auditorium occupan cy is a start toward building up this alternat ive source of revenue.

have not been answered. We regret to report that out of the seven
hundred working Lodges, we have received to date reports from only
11 7 Lodges, containing a full report of their outstanding events during
the past ten years: 134 reports from Lodges are but partially in response
to the request and must be returned for amplifkation: Hi Lodges have
not responded at all. The committee well realizes that everyone is not
historically minded, nor are many of us able to see much of what some
day may become historically important in most of the events in which
we take part. For these reasons it is forgivable that so many Lodges
have not responded to assist in the compilation of unusual contemporary
events. Unusual events are those which do not recur very often, whether
they be big or little events. Some unusual events which should be recorded in the archives are: cornerstone layings: dedication of Lodges;
institution of Lodges, including the first officers: dedication of schools
or public buildings: unusual and/or interesting local Lodge eventsperhaps in connection with Public Schools Week or Constitution
Month Observance; visits to the local Lodge by important persons,
such as the Grand Master or others. The committee would like the
Lodge Historian to advise us of any event he deems unusual whether
it seems important to him or not. From such material submitted, the
committee will make its choice for the archives. As an example of
what is important and which in this instance has been overlooked, we
cite the following: Several years ago, the Grand Master of the Philippines was visiting the United States. While in San Francisco, he informed some friends that he would like to visit a California Lodge.
Among those present was a former Inspector of the Philippines who
said he would artange the visit. Accordingly, at the forthcoming stated
meeting of a Bay Area Lodge, the Grand Master of the Philippines
presented himself and was received with grand honors and seated in
the East. At the close of a brief business session he was invited to
address the Lodge which he obligingly did, giving a most informative
and inspirational address. This was the only Lodge in California that
was so honored and should certainly be classified as an unusual event
and one which ought to be recorded, especially since this Grand Master
is today one of the leaders in the Philippine Gove.mment.

Along with outstanding events, the committee is interested in human
interest stories-stories about rank and flle members that can be substantiated and which of themselves are of interest to others: such as a
Brother who confers a degree on his son and also on his grandson: or
on three sons in one evening, as has occurred: or where some Brother
has gone out of his way, over and beyond his obligations to assist a
Brother; or where a Brother, in his daily practice of Masonry carries
on a continuing campaign to aid and assist the distressed and needy,
wherever he may find them, without remuneration from the Lodge or
even reporting to the Lodge his many acts of kindness and charity. The

164

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

instances that can be reported upon are legion and they occur almost
everywhere. It can be said that there is not a Lodge in California, large
or small. but has had one or more unusual happenings during the past
ten years. History is nothing more than the recorded acts of people. It
is these acts which we recite here, together with many others, that make
history.
On May 6, 1961, it was our privilege to participate in the celebration
of the centennial of Lassen Lodge No. 149, at Susanville. California.
This centennial was most unusual because our Grand Master opened
t,he Grand Lodge there in special communication in order to receive
the Grand Masters of Nevada and Oregon. Grand Master Stanley D.
Sundeen of Nevada and Grand Master Julius M. Swanson of Oregon
were invited by our Grand Master to be present in commemoration of
the part citizens of Nevada and Oregon played in the founding of
Susanville and Lassen County. Each Grand Master made appropriate
remarks. In the afternoon our Grand Master officiated at the dedication of a bronze plaque, set in native granite in front of Roop' s Fort,
an historical monument in Susanville. Tihe plaque was dedicated in
memory of Brothers Isaac N. Roop. founder of Susanville. and John
S. Ward, the first Master of Lassen Lodge. Brother Roop was one of
the great, hardy pioneer Masons of California, as was Brother Ward.
Also, Brother Ward was Senior Grand Warden of the Grand Lodge
of California in 1869 but passed on before he could serve as Grand
Master. During the ceremony of dedication of the plaque, Brother M.
R. Arnold, a grandson of Isaac Roop and member of Lassen Lodge.
presented to the Lodge his grandfather's Masonic apron, which was
suitably framed behind glass and now ihangs on the walls of Lassen
Lodge. Lassen Lodge called upon the History Committee for assistance
in preparing their centennial. and Brother 0. J. Wohlgemuth responded
with an impressive and well-received history.
On Saturday, May 13, 1961, the Grand Master opened the Grand
Lodge of California in special communication, in the Masonic Temple,
12th and JStreets in Sacramento for the purpose of re-laying the cornerstone of the State Capitol Building, on tihe occasion of the one hundredth
anniversary of the original cornerstone by the Grand Lodge. the Worshipful N. Green Curtis, Grand Master on May 15, 1861. A full account of the original ceremonies and the banquet which followed may
be found on pages 231-239 of the Proceedings for 1861. The chief
architect of the building was Brother Reuben Clark, a member of
Mount Moriah Lodge No. 44 at the time. As in 1861, after the opening
of the Grand Lodge, Grand Master Breslauer led a public procession, in
regalia, from the Masonic Temple to jjhe northeast corner of the capitol
building. It is estimated that over 1000 Masons in white aprons took
part in the procession, including the Shrine Band of Ben Ali Temple of
Sacramento. Acting as an escort, was the Sacramento Commandery

No. 2, Knights Templar; Master Masons; Blue Lodge Officers: York
and Scottish Rite Officers: Masters of Lodges: City, County and State
Officials and Grand Lodge Officers. Edmund G. Brown, Governor of
California, not a member of the fraternity, met the procession at the
Capitol building and extended his greetings and remarks. The cornerstone ceremony was performed by the Most Worshipful Grand Master,
Alfred F. Breslauer, assisted by the Grand Officers. Grand Lodge was
opened at 1 :30 P.M. and the ceremony commenced at 2:30 P.M. At
7:30 P.M. the Brethren met in tihe banquet room of the Elk's Club for
the commemorative banquet where the Most Worshipful Leslie E.
Wood, Past Grand Master, presided as Master of Ceremonies.
Several members of this committee appeared at various times
throughout the year as speakers before Lodges or in conjunction witih
other speakers at District meetings. One member of the committee
lectured on Masonic History at five of the seven education conferences
sponsored by the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Education. Two
other members continued to lecture and show the colored slides on old
pioneer Lodge Halls in California, titled, "SOME CAME BY LAND
AND SOME CAME BY SEA," which has been given before many
Lodges and districts during the past three years. This lecture and showing is still available. Applications should be made to the Chairman of
~he History Committee. There is no charge except a nominal one for
expense~ of the lecturer when he is put to expense in coming to your
community.

to present historical lectures to the Lodges when requested. As, in the

committee members to engage personally in assisting the Lodges, considerable expense may be involved. We therefore request that the sum
of $3000.00 be appropriated for the use of this committee for the ensuing year.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism is indeed pleased to advise that
reported violations of our law, rules and regulations continue to lessen
in scope, number and seriousness.
Most noticeably it has been found that the constituent Lodges and
the appendant organizations are asking to secure clearance before acting. Because of this, a number of proposals which could have resulted
in violations were dropped when the applicable sections of our code
were made known.

In a few instances, constituent groups of appendant organizations
have not proceeded on the above basis. Such situations, wherever
possible, were called to the attention of the responsible Grand Officers
of the appendant organizations who proved most cooperative by taking
prompt and positive corrective action.
There have been a few instances where it has been necessary to caution individual members of the craft, who, either through lack of knowledge or inadvertance have committed violations. In all such situations
coming to our attention, through the cooperation of the Inspectors and
Masters of the Lodge, corrections were effected by "whispering good
counsel."
Additionally, attempts at sales solicitation, originating in other
Grand Jurisdictions, have been made, on the basis of Masonry, principally to appendant organizations. Again, when such actvities were
called to appendant Grand Officer's attention, prompt corrective action
was taken within the group.
As Shown above, the Grand appendant organizations are most
anxious to cooperate by "cleaning their own house" when questionable
matters are called to their attention, which is as it should be.
Our greatest problem has been with privately published so-called
Masonic magazines originating in other Grand Jurisdictions. Their
salesmen usually use the long distance telephone and high pressure sales
tactics in their endeavor to sell advertising. In each instance coming
to our attention, such action is taken as is felt right and proper to protect our name and symbols. Through the efforts of our Grand 1M aster
and with the cooperation of the Grand Master of Oregon, we have been
given assurance that one such magazine, published in Portland, will
cease solicitation of advertising in this Grand Jurisdiction.
Last year in our report, we referred to correspondence with the
Grand Master of New York in regard to an author, member of a New
York Lodge, whose activities we felt should be brought to a halt. As a
matter of interest, under date of March 23, this year, the Grand Master

By Ordinance , under Section 246 ( formerly 86) with respect to
investment of Grand Lodge funds, and Section 403 (formerly 152.1 )
respecting investments by Constitue nt Lodges, the following provisions
prevailed as of June 30, 1961:
GROUP I. At least 20% of the funds available for investment must
be in:
A) Cash and/or bank accounts.
B) Obligations of the United States.
C) Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions.
D) Such other securities as are legal investments for savings
banks in California or Hawaii (as amended 1959).
GROUP II. Up to 20% maybe invested in:
A) Other evidences of indebtedness, which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an Exchange registered with the
Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange , except that this listing requirement shall not
include railroad equipment trust issues ( 1955).
B) Preferred stocks. which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange , except that full listing and registration of preferred stock shall
not be required whenever the common stock of the corporation issuing such preferred stock is fully listed and registered
on such an exchange, provided that such preferred stock is
traded on such an exchange ( 1956).
GROUP III. Upto60% maybeinv estedin:
A) Common stocks, which must be fully listed and registered on
an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange , except that
this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance stocks.
B) Shares of Investmen t Trusts.
C) Shares and/or certifkate s of insured Federal or State Savings and Loan Associations ( 1957 and 1959). The amount

invested in any one Association shall not exceed the amount
covered by insurance.
(THIS AMEND MENT APPLIES ONLY TO CONSTITUE NT LODGES AND DOES NOT APPLY TO
THE INVEST MENT OF GRAND LODGE FUNDS. )
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and III, the
Ordinance s read as follows: "No such investments, however, shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market value
of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent
(or sixty per cent) of the total market value of all the cash. bank accounts and securities held," - the controlling point being that there
cannot be more than 20% or 60% invested in Groups II and III. at the
time of purchase.
SHOULD A LODGE ELECT TO INVEST ITS FUNDS
UNDER THE PROVIS IONS OF GROUP II OR III HEREOF . IT
SHALL CONFER AND COUNSE L AS TO ANY SUCH PROPOSED OR CONTEM PLATED INVEST MENTS WITH THE
PROFES SIONAL INVEST MENT ADVISO R USED BY GRAND
LODGE, WHOSE FEES WILL BE PAID BY GRAND LODGE.
At the 1959 Communication certain amendments were passed with
respect to the percentag es which could be invested in Groups I and III.
Group I was reduced to 20% and Group III was increased to 60%. In
this connection, it is very important to call attention to the following,
which is contained in the Reports of the Committe e on Jurisprudence
and the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
"Your Co~mittee on Jurisprudence respectfully calls attention to
the fact that this proposed amendment is permissive only and is not a
directive. Great care should be exercised in making investments under
the authority granted by this proposed amendme nt.''
"Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends the
adoption of Resolution D-7 but with this admonition to the Lodges:
"A) The authority granted is permissive only and is not suggested
as an investment guide under present economic conditions.
"B) That in making investments in Group III the Lodge be most
circumspect in taking advantage of this additional authority.
"C) And that they strictly comply with the provisions of the last
paragraph of Section 403-3B of our ordinances, consult with and heed
the advice of the professional investment advisors used by Grand Lodge,
and made available to the Constitue nt Lodges without charge to the
individual Lodge."
The above comments are included in the reports of the Committees
as they appear on page 282 of the 1959 Proceedings.

to $645,453 for the year ending June 30. 1961. Other gifts and bequests
for the Masonic Homes amounted to $948,672. The Masonic Homes
Board of Trustees determines how these gifts and bequests shall be
allocated - these allocations are made in accordance with specific
bequests, or in the absence of such, at the direction of the Trustees. The
Endowment Fund contributions remain in that Fund, and only the income is used.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It is with pleasure and satisfaction that the Committee on Lodge
Financing submits a report of its activities during the past year. The
pleasure being in having the privilege of serving the Gra~d Lodge a~d
the Lodges and Temple Associations operating Masonic Temples m
the California jurisdiction: the satisfaction lies in seeing the continued
improvement each year in the construction and operati~n of Temple
properties. Each year indicates improved management m Lodge and
Temple affairs, and the Committee on Lodge Financing . is proud to
have a part in the continuing successful programs. Durmg t~e pa~t
year fewer Lodges and Temple Association~ have shown~ l~ss m their
operations and these losses are. in most instances, negligible. More
and more Lodges indicate by their financial statements that they ~re
operating in the black and are establishing cash r~serves and depre~1a­
tion accounts which will be so important to them in the future. During
the past year more than 235 Temple Associatio~s and Lodges have su~­
mitted financial statements as required by Section 200 of the Masonic
Code. These statements indicate total assets of Lodge properties of
approximately $25,000,000.00, an increase of about four and one~half
million dollars over the previous year.
At the time that this report was compiled, on August 10, 1961, ap~
proximately 60 Lodges and Temple Associations had su~mitted ap~
plications to tlhe Committee for its consent and approval in the purchase of property, the construction, repairs and other financial matters
related to the operation of their facilities. The Committee granted
consent to approximately 40 requests to transfer funds from Lodges to
Temple Associations to be used in various matters concerning the
Temple operations: 8 requests to start construction of new Masonic
Temples: 11 requests for expenditure of funds for capital improvements:
12 requests to form nonprofit Temple Associations and 21 requests to
purchase property for the eventual construction of their own Masonic
home. This, together with other miscellaneous items. required the ac~
tion of the Committee on more than 80 transactions.
The volume of correspondence has been exceedingly heavy and on
very many occasions the members of the Committee have met with ~e
brethren of various Lodges and discussed with them the problems being
confronted in their Temple construction and financial programs. The
results of these meetings have been most successful and in each instance 1all difficulties and problems have been resolved. It is the in~
tention of the Committee to always meet with and advise various Lodges
and Temple Associations relative to tlheir building and financial mat~

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

177

ters, and to particularly point out the benefit to Lodges in incorporating
as nonprofit corporations to carry on their Temple affairs.
It has been most rewarding to the Committee to be a part of such
activtity and to enjoy the complete willingness and cooperation of each
Lodge and Temple Association in an endeavor to satisfactorily pursue
their programs and desires. The Committee, during the past year, has
worked together in unity and harmony, each member thereof contributing his efforts readily and completely. During the past year the
Committee has received many letters of commendation and sincere appreciation from Lodges expressing tlheir thanks to the Committee for
its help and assistance. These letters are gratefully acknowledged. In
a few instances criticism has been directed at the Committee; however,
those who were most critical either by neglect or lack of courage failed
to make themselves known. Nevertheless the criticism is also acknowledged because when properly given it tends to strengthen not only the
proceedings.
The yearly activities of the Committee are set forth in detail in the
following pages of diis report and will be included in the published
Committee but the fraternity.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The success of the 42nd Annual Observance of PSW in California
is evidenced by ~he fact that your Committee was able to effectively
bring home to the Public School Teachers that they are the "Builders of
Tomorrow's Leaders."
Reports of this committee during the past twenty years or so (which
I have reviewed in preparation for this report) contain a running account
of the progress made over the years. This report is made primarily to
record and acknowledge the splendid work accomplished by the con~
stituent Lodges and Districts during the 42nd Observance.
"T'he Year of the Master Mason" has been the theme of our Grand
Master's general program. His program has been geared to the dues~
paying member, the brother on the side~lines, the person for whom we,
as officers, perform our work. He carried this general idea into his theme
for the 1961 PSW Observance by directing that the TEACHER the person on the firing line - be recognized and honored.
Through the cooperation of the San Francisco Unified Sdhool
District, the assignment was given to the journalism students of the
seven SF high schools to complete the slogan: "The Public School
Teacher
"
Hundreds of slogans were submitted. Our Grand Master, without
knowing the identity of the student, selected the one submitted by
Shirley Cooper, a student of San Francisco's Lowell High School. who
completed the slogan: "The Public School Teacher - Builder of
Tomorrow's Leaders."
This meaningful phrase at once identifies those charged with the
task of pereptuating the freedoms we enjoy, and is descriptive of what
the teachers are doing: Building Tomorrow's Leaders.
So this slogan was sent on its way throughout our great jurisdiction
where it met with enthusiastic acceptance of everyone connected with
our PSW program. This slogan, we are sure, was particularly appreci~
ated by the 130,000 public school teachers in our jurisdiction.
At the April 18th meeting of the San Francisco Board of Education,
the winner, Shirley Cooper, was presented with a little gift of apprecia~
tion from the PSW Committee. This gift was presented to her by our
revered Past Grand Master and Founder of PSW, Charles Albert
Adams.
Seven thousand copies of the "Guide for Planning" were printed.
These were distributed to PS officials, the Lodges, and to the concordant
Bodies, who, in a spirit of splendid cooperation, issued Proclamations
to their members, similar to the Proclamation of our Grand Master.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

185

We must here express appreciation to the California Teachers As~
sociation for its assistance and cooperation. The CT A ran our Grand
~od~e e~velopes through its addressograph equipment, and a copy of the

REPORT OF
SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON DE MOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A growing awareness of the Order of De Malay is quite obvious in
all Masonic circles. This is due in a great part to the Proclamation of
De Malay Week by our Grand Master, an action which was very
favorably received.by the Masons of California and which this committee
heartily recommends to succeeding Grand Masters.
Another factor which 1has contributed to this ·awareness is the attention being focused on youth by tlhe various agencies dedicated to
the fight against the growth of Communism in this Country. During
the recent Anti-Communist School conducted in Los Angeles, a great
deal of time was spent in exposing the Communist efforts to infiltrate
and influence youth ·groups. Dr. Schwartz, the man responsible for the
School's success, stated in one of his stirring addresses that the Communist effort had infiltrated a great many youth groups. He stated ~hat
one of the few groups that was completely free of the Communist
influence was the Masonic De Malay movement. This factor alone
should inspire every serious Mason to be proud of the De Malay movement. It should emp'hasize the need for a growing support of the Order
of De Malay by the Masons of California.
Your Committee has received no reports during the past year of any
actions by De Malay Chapters which were contrary to the policies of
the Grand Lodge. 'Dhere appears to be a complete and unequivocal
acceptance of the commercialism principles of this Grand Body.

188

PROCEED INGS OF THE

Your Committee has accepted every invitation to meet with Masonic
and De Mo lay groups. We have been most pleased by the attention
given to us and the interest shown in our discussions.
Activities such as the Californ ia State and Jurisdictional Conventions, De Molay activities at the State and County Fairs, the De Molay
Week Observa nce held by the San Diego Masonic Officers Association,
and increasing number of outstand ing ritual, athletic and social events
were critically observed. We are happy to report that these activities
were conducte d in a most creditabl e manner. The Masonic fraternit y
can be justly proud of its association with these functions.
One disturbing trend was observed. This was the tendency on the
part of several Masonic Temple Associations to expect the Masonic
youth groups to shoulder unreason able rent burdens. Some De Molay
Chapter s are practical ly being priced out of existence by the rents that
they are expected to pay. An examination of the financial structure of
the average De Molay Chapter indicates that rents of 20 to 25 dollars
per month can be met without undue hardship . With this in mind, you
can readily see what rents ranging up to 80 dollars a month, plus as
much as 40 dollars for a special night for installati on of officers, are
doing to the chapters concerned. We believe that this problem merits
the attention of this Grand Lodge.
It is our sincere recommendation that this Committ ee be continue d
and that the sum of $750 be appropri ated to cover its necessar y expenses.
This Committee wishes to express its apprecia tion to our Most W orshipful Grand Master Alf red F. Breslauer for his generous support and
encourag ement during this past year.
In closing, we wish to remind you that "as a twig is bent, so grows
the tree." Let us turn our attention to the young men represen ted by
the Order of De Molay so that they will grow tall and straight in the
shadow of Masonry .
Respectf ully submitted,
