REPOR T OF COMM ITTEE ON
RECOG NITION OF FOREIG N GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Your Committ ee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges has had
under consideration several requests for recognition as well as other information from foreign Grand Lodges and submits the following report
and recommendations:
BELGIUM

As mentioned in our report at the last Communication, a new Grand
Lodge of Belgium was formed in 1960. As of February of this year,
this Grand Lodge had eleven regular Lodges under its jurisdiction, eight
of which were formerly constituents of the Grand Orient of Belgium.
Three of these are over 150 years old. There are several other regular
Lodges still affiliated with the Grand Orient of Belgium, which we do
not recognize, but it is hoped that they, too, will join the new Grand
Lodge. The Grand Lodge of Belgium fulfills all of the conditions of
regularit y demande d by us and your Committ ee recommends that the
Grand Lodge of Californ ia extend fraternal recognition to the new
Grand Lodge of Belgium, its official address being 5, Rue Du Chene,
Brussels 1, Rene Neirinck x, Secretar y.
CUBA

Under present conditions in Cuba, the situation of Masonry is, of
course, very confused. In February of 1959 two of our Past Grand
Masters, M. W. lienry C. Clausen and M. W. Lloyd E. Wilson, visited
the Grand Lodge of Cuba. This was after the time of the taking over
of the governm ent by the Castro regime. Our represen tatives were assured then that there would be no interfere nce with Masonry under the
new regime. Later, however, the records, parapher nalia, membership
lists, and other records and property of the Grand Lodge of Cuba,
including the Grand Lodge Temple, were seized and confiscated by the
dictators hip. The Grand Master of Masons in Cuba, for the preserva tion
of his life and safety, was compelled to flee to the United States of
America after declaring the constitue nt Lodges in recess and is presently
residing at Miami. The Grand Master of Masons in Florida has granted
full permission to the Grand Master of Masons in Cuba to reside, in his
official capacity as Grand Master of Masons in Cuba, within the Grand
Jurisdiction of Florida and the Grand Lodge of Cuba has been granted
permission to have its official residence and home within the boundari es
of Florida and to take such official and fraternal action in Masonic
affiairs as may be appropri ate under the circumstances, to the same
extent and in full measure as it would or could do within the boundari es
of Cuba. Since the promulg ation of this order we have received further
informat ion that a Grand Lodge is trying to function within the ter-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

ritory of Cuba, although other information is not encouraging because
the remaining officers appear to be completely under the domination of
Castro.
Under ~he circumstances, your Committee recommends no action
at this time, awaiting fucther developments.

it is n.ow entirely regular, we recommend that the question of recognition
by this Grand lodge be held under study for another year.

FRANCE

Your Committee has reported at several prior communications on
the situation within the Grand Lodge of France. We presently recognize
this Grand Lodge and also the Grand Lodge National of France. Both
of these Grand Lodges are officially regular, though the question has
been that the Grand Lodge of France, the larger body of the two. may
not always have been successful in enforcing its regulations within its
own organization of constituent Lodges. We are happy to report,
however, that recent information we have received, including personal
visits by the Chairman of this Committee with the responsible officers
of the Grand Lodge of France and others well informed on the situation. indicates that substantial progress has been made in the last year
toward achieving full compliance with the official requirements of the
Grand lodge of France. One Lodge was suspended for non compliance and other disciplinary action taken.
In view of the progress which is undoubtedly being made, we recommend that no action be taken now toward discontinuing recognition of
the Grand Lodge of France, but that the situation be kept under review
and if conditions within that Grand Lodge should warrant, further
recommendation will be made by your Committee.
ITALY

During 1960 the Grand Orient of Italy, which we recognize, accomplished union with the National Grand Lodge of Italy, heretofore
not recognized by us. We have received a request from the expanded
Grand lodge for continued recognition. The Grand Orient of Italy,
with its 300 Lodges, added some fifteen which comprised the former
National Grand Lodge. and the expanded Grand Lodge will continue
to be known as the Grand Orient of Italy, its address being Via
Giustiniani 5, Rome. We recommend continued recognition of the Grand
Orient of Italy. as expanded by the merger referred to above.
LUXEMBOURG

The Grand Lodge of Luxembourg. which has been in existence since
1849 but not heretofore recognized by us, has now applied for our
recognition. This request is based primarily on ~he fact that the Grand
Lodge of Luxembourg has recently severed relations with the Grand
Orient of France and the Grand Orient of Belgium, neither of which
bodies is recognized by the Grand Lodge of California. While information furnished us by the Grand Lodge of Luxembourg indicates that

be held over for further study.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E
ON CONSTITU TION OBSERVAN CE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In its 1960 report to this Grand lodge, the Constitution Observance
Comn:ittee vo.iced its .concern over the ever-mounting evidence that
~m~r~ca was m the midst of a frightening moral slump. Further, that
its citizens were most apathetic in their efforts to prevent the onslaught
of transgressions \vhich are being made in the rights and privileges
guaranteed by the Constitution.
. That report proposed that the Constitution Observance program of
this Grand Lodge must have for its purpose: First, that we must recapture the "Spirit of '76." Second, that we must recapture the courage
of our forefathers. And ~ird, we must recapture the American challenge.
These purposes we strongly reaffirm and believe it to be self-evident
if this nation is to survive. We must implement these purposes with a
c~n~tructive working program that each and every Mason in this jurisdiction can and must take an active part.
.. The Preamble to our Constitution begins with these famous words
We the people of the United States." They proclaim to the world that
our government BELONGS to the people, is RUN by the people, and
EXISTS for the good of ~he people. We the people, then, must make
sure that our government truly belongs to, is run by, and exists for
the American people.
In keeping with these purposes and with the responsibilities imposed
by the Preamble, we propose that the Constitution Observance Com-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The original plan was administered by a Pension Committee composed of the entire Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes of California.
The amended Plan covering all employees of Grand Lodge is now
governed by a Committee, three of whom are selected by the Homes
Board and two by tihe Grand Master.
The current members are:
L. HAROLD ANDERSON, P.G.l\'.L ...... .....•............... 346
REGINALD M. MILLS............. ................................. 61
JAMES LEO HALLEY................................. ............... 375
LEO SIEVERT.. ................................. ......................... 685
ARTHUR M. WARREN, P.G.M ... ........... ............... 481
This Committee is charged with the full responsibility of administering the Plan in accordance with its written terms.
Among its responsibilities are the following:
1. Approval of requests for early retirement.
2. Approval of requests for disability retirement.
3. Approval of optional retirement requests.
4. Approval of requests for continuance of employment
after retirement date has been readied and establishment of conditions of such employment.
To sustain the plan, the Pension Committee is required to determine
from time to time, with actuarial assistance, the amount of money essential to keep the plan solvent and to meet its liability both for current
and accrued service.
This sum, togetiher with a 3% contribution by member employees is
deposited with the Trustee, Wells Fargo Bank American Trust Company of San Francisco. The Trustee cooperated 100% with the Committee and has adopted for its guidance the Grand Lodge "Prudent Man
Rule" for investing these funds. In addition, ·all contemplated investments are referred to and cleared with the Grand Lodge Committee on
Investments.
The Masonic Homes of California paid over to the Trustee from its
reserve sufficient funds to fully cover all past service credits and has
discharged its liability in that respect. In addition, it has paid annually
all charges for current service.
When the Plan was amended to include Grand Lodge employees,
no cash payment was made to the Trustee for past service liability insofar as these employees were concerned. As of January 1, 1961 this
liability has been computed to be $127,898. Current service contributions only have been paid.
Because of this situation, Grand Lodge is required ·annually to pay
to the Trustee in addition to the current service contribution, interest
which would have been earned were it fully funded. This has the

effect of making our annual payment supported by per capita tax larger
than necessary if the Plan had been fully funded.
It is the recommendation of this Committee that Grand Lodge fully
discharge its liability to tihese covered employees by paying from its
reserves the sum of $127,898, plus interest to date, thereby completing
its contract.
Authorization for this payment is contained in the resolution of
1956 and sufficient funds are in the Grand Lodge Treasury.

196

When this payment is made the Plan would then be completely
funded and the ~ension Committee would be relieved of this phase of
superv·ision. The only annual payment required thereafter would be
for earned current service and would be reduced as the Plan seasoned
and as demands on reserves are reduced by virtue of natural mortality
affecting pensioned employees.
Respectfully submitted,
ARTHUR M. WARREN
L. HAROLD ANDERSON
}AMES LEO HALLEY

Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren:
It is wonderful to have this opportunity to express to the Grand
Lodge and to our Most Worshipful Grand Master my deep appreciation for the privilege of serving in this station throughout the past year.
This has been a glorious year in California Masonry! The inspired
leadership of our Grand Master and the enthusiastic support given him
by all the brethren have been superb. His warm and fri~dly. manne~,
the wisdom, strength and beauty of harmony of all his actions, his
understanding of the role of the Master Mason, 'his love for all the
brethren, have brought new distinction to the craft. To have been of
some small service to him and to the Grand Lodge has been a joy,
which I shall treasure always.
You have given explicit instructions to him who occupies the station
in which I now stand. By tradition, you have made it his duty to
address the Grand Lodge upon matters appertaining to the Craft.
Implicit is the obvious injunction that the matters spoken shall be of
maximum import. In the discharge of this duty, your help and your
assistance are necessary, for this is a mutual endeavor in which we
search togetlher for new and further light in Masonry.
In a little European mountain village, a traveler noticed in the late
afternoon that the people of the village left it to walk up a path on the
mountain side. Each carried a lamp. He followed and found that they
were going to a small church.
In the church, there were no light fixtures. It was lighted only by
the lamps the people brought with them. At first, when only a fe"'.' had
arrived, the traveler dimly saw the outline of the pews and pulpit. It
seemed quiet and peaceful, and he bowed his head in a moment of
prayer. When he looked up, the room was becoming brighter and
brighter as people came in. With the increased light, it became more
beautiful.
The traveler learned that the pioneers who built t<he church wanted
every person in the village to come to the..church for worship t~ere. So
they gave each person a lamp and said, Some corner of God s house
will be dark and lonely, unless all his sons and daughters come to

What, t1hen, is our most important Masonic concern, upon which to
focus all the light we now have? Could it not he said that these are
reflective moments-a pause in the day's occupation, as it were-to ask
ourselves:
. .. whence came we?:
... where are we?; and,
... whither are we traveling?
When we ask ourselves these questions, we realize that our concern
is not the means hut the ends of life. The president of a great university
ask~d a .~tudent why he w~s att~nding the school. The young man
replied: To b~ome an engineer. This, the ~fofessor said, was very
commendable. But why are you really here? , he insisted. Puzzled,
the student answered: "To obtain further knowledge." "That, too, is to
~e admired," responded the professor, "But what is your goal in life?"
Oh! I see what you mean. My purpose in life is to learn the will of
God for my l{fe and do everything within my ability for the good of
mankind."
. . So it is in 1Mason~. Important as is the business of making a
hvmg-the means of hfe--our great concern is ~he ends of life. This
is the objective of Masonry: to help us achieve the ends of life. All of
our symbolism, all of Masonry's lessons are pointed in that direction.
How may we he certain that, in our day, we achieve the ends of life?
. Our concern is not for ourselves alone. We needs must keep faith
with our brethren of other years who have long since joined the Great
Grand Lodge on High, whose sacrifice and devotion have made life
possible for us today, and wit1h our children and our children's children,
the character of whose lives will he determined by our own sacrifice
and devotion.
How like a great relay race life is for us! What a thrill it is to witness
the relay at a great track meet or in the modern Olympics. Each runner
on the team carries the baton for a measured distance, then passes it on
to a teammate who runs awhile until he, too, hands the baton on to

We did not begin the race of life alone. Others preceded us. They

For our generation, these are days of tremendous challenge. We
live in the greatest age of all time. Within our lifetime, more has
happened-more is happening-than in any previous period in the
history of the world. Think how the world has changed since we were
born!
Distances have become insignificant. The ·h orse and buggy have
given way to the automobile and the airplane. And now the space age
is upon us. With the turn of a dial, we telephone 'round the world. By
television, we see events as they transpire across the country. The
world grows smaller.

. Herein is the paradox: dazzling progress in technology and materialism on the one 1hand and confused retrogression in satisfying the deepest
needs of the human spirit on the other. This we recognize as evidence
of a grave disorder in man's relation to his God and with his fellow man.
The great English historian, Arnold Toynbee, tells us that, actually,
we are engaged in three kinds of war:
... a physical war:
... an ideological war: and
... a spiritual war.
On a worldwide basis, two opposing philosophies struggle for control
over the minds and hearts and consciences of men:
• .. corporate despotism vs.

Creature comforts have increased. Modern industry produces for
us limitless conveniences unknown to kings at the turn of the century.

. .. tyranny

Life spans have lengthened. Newly discovered medicines, surgical
techniques and the science of nutrition extend the lives of men.
Leisure time has been expanded. New methods of production,
automation, make machines do more work for us.
Power beyond imagination has become ours. In a 15 pound package,
a child could carry enough fissionable material to produce all the power
required in the United States for an entire year. Mankind now has
the power to provide all its necessities. The atomic age is here.
Man's inventive genius has created a new world for men to live in,
and has us poised at the threshhold of still other worlds about to be
explored.
But, in the midst of all this scientific progress, we are sobered by
the realization that comparable progress has not been made in moral
and spiritual matters.
Man's inhumanity to man has surpassed all Biblical records! Two
World Wars have been fought, and now we are engaged in a cold
war, the horrors of which, if it becomes a hot war, make every thinking
man shudder in advance. The human race now has within its possession

"the right to life, liberty and

The gravity of events in the life of our world is such ~hat none of
us can afford just to "do business as usual." Our society, our whole
way of life, everything in which we believe, are being challenged by a
powerful atheistic attack that endangers every privilege we have--even
our very right to be Freemasons.
"For such a time as this," we are confronted by the question: "What
shall we do?"
In the language of numbers, much spoken of by Masons, there are
three things that we individually can do:
I.

Obtain all the knowledge that we can about the alien philosophy which is so diametrically opposed to our beliefs.

II.

Replenish the springs of our faith in our principles and ideals.

III. Sustain the institutions so essential to our freedom.

I. Consider the first category: to obtain knowledge. Let all of us
make it our duty to study and acquaint ourselves with the dangers

202

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

w:hich lurk in the alien and counterfei t philosoph y which threatens all
free men. Espoused by Marx and given the name of dialectical materialism, it now goes by the name of communism. Its theory is that
economic and materialistic forces determine the events of history; that
there is no place for individual motive, spiritual inspiration, moral
discipline or ethical law; and that the human personalit y must be
subservien t to the interests of the state.
It says to us: God is dead! There is no divine creator. Life just
happened. There is no wisdom over all.
It establishes its own morality by the dictates of a dominant minority.
It defines truth as anything that serves its purpose.
It waives human freedom aside as nothing.
It masquerad es as an economic and political concept, when in fact it
is philosophical.
It worships itself-ma terialism -as a God, while denying that there
is a God. As such, it is idolatry and violates God's first commandment:
"Thou shalt have no other gods before me!"
It purports to be utopia and in less than half a century has imposed
itself upon nearly half of mankind.
It seeks to dominate the world through the destructio n of all free
institutions and the will to resist.

It uses physical force and intellectual subversion to attain its purposes. It employs the most subtle methods to discredit and ridicule
western civilization and instill fear.
It knows that apathy, indifference and inaction are its allies.
Standing squarely in opposition to this ideology is the spiritual
concept of western civilization: that man is a cllild of God and therefore
of supreme worth; that the highest value to be attained by man is the
development of his human personality; that man's rights come from
God and man forms his governme nt to protect those rights.
When the two philosophies are thus contrasted , we realize more
clearly why no Mason may accept ~he dogma of dialectical materialism
and. as individuals, each must put himself against the creeping paralysis
of the counterfei t ideology which threatens to engulf the free world.
So, as a first step. to avoid being deceived by it, let us obtain all
the knowledg e we can about the gigantic evil.
II. Consider the second thing that we must do: replenish our faith
in all of our principles and ideals.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNI A

203

To be against an insidious movement is well, but it is not enough.
We must be "for" the principles in which we believe. We must remember
~hat no doctrine, truth or knowledg e can live in the intellect if it does
not renew itself in experience. If our beliefs do not renew themselves in
our experience, they become just words.
So if we are to make certain whither we are traveling, we must reexamine and re-evaluat e the principles by which we live, and dedicate
and devote ourselves anew to our faith.
We believe in God and the immortality of the soul. In our application and throughou t the degrees we have testified to that repeatedly ,
for no atheist may pass our tiled door. Shall we each not ask: How
deeply do I believe in God? Is God at the center of my life, where He
has a right to be? Is He my constant companion, nearer to me than the
breath I breathe, or is He a pocket God, to be consulted only at my
convenience?
Emerson wisely said that a man is what he thinks about all day. T 1h at
which dominates his thinking tends to find expression in his life. What
is the pattern of our thoughts? Do we think about God and thus give
Him a place in our lives? To truly believe in God. let us let God occupy
our thoug·h ts and thus guide our lives.
The great Jewish physician and philosoph er of the twelfth century,
Maimonedes, has some wise advice for us. In his view, there are four
states of perfection :
(a) A material. level in which men seek happiness through goods
and property;
( b) A physical level based upon the development of bodily strength;
( c) A moral level developed by adhering to the laws of righteousness and virtue; and
( d) A spiritual level founded upon faith in God.
"The knowledge of God," he said, "is the only perfection we should
seek."
Daniel Webster once was asked what was the greatest thought that
had ever entered his massive mind. Reflecting a moment, he answered:
"The greatness of God and my accountability to Him!"
We read in the rule and guide to our faith, open upon our altar:
"The earth is the Lord's and the Fullness thereof; ~e world and they
that dwell therein."
God is the giver of life, the creator and owner of all things on earth

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

and in the heavens. Everything we have and are, we hold in trust for
Him. We have the deed to nothing. We are leaseholders from God who
holds the title to all. As trustees under God, every power and every
attribute should be used, not for selfish or ignoble objectives, but for
the glory of God and the loftiest development of individual personality.

Justice: There is yet so much injustice in the world that, with new
resolve, we must exemplify this virtue.

204

So it is with the great tenets of Masonry: brotherly love, relief and
truth. Never before have we needed so much to devote ourselves to
these great principles.

If we have accountability, how are we accountable? We have an
accountability for the right use of our time, our talents and our pas~
sessions.
Time is a deposit in the bank of God. No one of us knows how
much of a balance any of us has. In the sigiht of God, we are trustees
of the hours, the days and the years.
The Great Architect endowed us all with the talents we possess.
To use them to the exclusion of his purposes is to frustrate the end for
which they were given.

Sometimes, we have difficulty with the word "love." "Love thy
enemies" is the Biblical message. How can we love those who would
destroy us? The problem is one of definition in translation of the Bible
from the Greek. The Greek language has three words for love, each
with a different meaning: Eros; philia; agape.

Because the Kingdom of God deals with lhuman beings in their
earthly relationships it must employ earthly institutions . and instru~
ments. For the wise and earnest use of those possessions we are
accountable to God.

Agape love does not depend upon lovableness of the other person
or shared interests. It arises from recognition of the need of the other
person for fellowship. It is a consuming concern for the welfare of
others.

Harry Emerson Fosdick puts it this way: "It is a good .thing to
check up once in awhile and make sure you have not lost the thmgs th.at
money cannot buy.... Everything that money can buy depends for its
ultimate worth, for the purpose it serves, for its final effect on human
life, upon the things that money cannot buy."

This is the need of the hour: agape love, a consuming conrcern.

We believed in immortality. Too easily, it can be assumed that this
is a state of being that occurs when we die. But, if we are immortal ever,
we are immortal here and now. Let us resolve, then, to live our immor~
tality now, by living every waking moment as though we do expect to
live forever.
We believe in the cardinal virtues: temperance, fortitude, prudence
and justice. Consider their application today.

Temperance: We shall need to be especially temperate i~ our atti~
tudes toward the underprivileged of the world who, to obtam enough
to eat, fall victims to the alien philosophy.
Fortitude: Nothing undermines so completely as fear. Fear is every~
where in the world. Fear alone can overwhelm our will to resist. The
only antidote is the shield of faith.
Prudence: How heavily we must draw upon this virtue, on an inter~
national basis, lest, by accident, a thoughtless act precipitate a halo~
caust.

Eros is the love of husband for wife: attraction to another because
of the other's attractiveness.
Philia is the love of parents for child: attraction because of mutual
concern.

We believe in the spiritual graces: faith, hope and charity. How
greatly the world is in need of their message today!
Joseph Fort Newton tells us that: "Belief is a truth held in the
mind. Faith 'is a fire in the heart." Think of it! To have such a con~
viction about our beliefs that our hearts are on fire. It is the virtue by
which we are united to God.
Hope is the "anchor of the soul," the source of that energy, courage
and endurance without which spiritual progress would be impossible.
Nothing great, Emerson admonished us, is ever accomplished with~
out enthusiasm. My brethren, as never before, let us from this day
henceforth be enthusiastic about our principles and ideals, that we may
achieve true perfection.
III. And now a very brief comment concerning our third thing to
do: sustain our free institutions.
Today we enjoy life in a free country because of a document con~
taining approximately 4,000 words and 89 paragraphs-our Constitu~
tion. It assures us of government by law. It is a priceless heritage. Let
us here resolve to support and sustain it with greater earnestness than
ever before.

Likewise, let us strengthen our support of our public schools, the
institution through which man obtains the education necessary to govern
himself.
And lastly shall we not encourage one another to support more
faithfully the church or synagogue of our faith?
Masonry, we so well know, is religious but it is not a religion.
Masonry supplements and undergirds the work of synagogue and
church, but never was intended to take their place in our moral and
spiritual development. Let us emulate the example of our Grand Master
who, for more than 30 years, has been active in the religious school of
his faith-most of the time as Superintenden t of his Temple School.

For such a day as this, these then are the things we can do, my
brethren, to help resolve the paradox of our generation: Obtain knowledge of the evil that confronts us that we may avoid it; replenish our
faith in our beliefs; and sustain our free institutions.
We live at a great time-the wind is blowing-the trees are bending
-the earth is shaking, but these are great days in which to be alive.
Life was not made to be taken easy. Life is an uphill climb all the
way. But, with Luther, "If God be for us who can be against us?"
In the long war between the evil and the good, our faith in God will
see us through, for, in the words of Patience Strong:

"If you stand very still in the heart
of a wood - you will 'hear many wonderful things - The snap of a twig and the
wind in the trees and the whirr of
invisible wings .... If you stand very
still in the turmoil of life - and you wait
for the voice from within -you'll be led
down the quiet ways of wisdom and peace in a mad world of chaos and din ....
If you stand very still and you hold to
your faith - you will get all the ·help
you ask - You will draw from the Silence
the things that you need - Hope and
courage, and strength for your task."

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1960 Communicatio n the dispensation of Yucca Valley Lodge
U. D. was continued for an additional year. During the current Masonic
year six more Lodges have been instituted. Six of t'he seven Lodges
under dispensation have applied for charters.
All of the Lodges have submitted their records and have sent
deleg'ates to appear before the Committee on Charters. In some cases
there were minor errors or omissions in their records but these were
of a nature that could be easily corrected. All of the Lodges are in
sound financial condition.
One of the continuing pleasures enjoyed by members of the Committee on Charters is the contacts they have with the enthusiasm and
zeal of those who work to form new Lodges. Examples of this devotion
to Masonry are so commonplace in the formation of new Lodges that
they are seldom recorded in the reports of this Committee. However, it
might be of interest to this Grand Lodge to have an example which
typifies this spirit.
The Masons of Yucca Valley, a fast growing community situated
in t'he high desert area between Palm Springs and Twentynine Palms
in Southern California, have long desired a Masonic Lodge of their
own. A Masonic group was formed and, as there was no meeting place
in the area, they constructed a building suitable for Masonic and other
community ll).eetings. A group of the brethren then organized for the
formation of a Lodge and Yucca Valley Lodge was instituted June 11,
1960, and the dispensation was continued at the last Communicatio n.
On April 3rd of this year a fire broke out in the Lodge Room,
destroying the furnishings and doing major damage to the building.
Courageous efforts by brethren present saved the records in the Lodge
and some of the smaller pieces of paraphernalia. On the following day
the Worshipful Master, Louis L. Cunningham, organized a committee to
deal with the emergency. A member of the Lodge donated the use of
a market building without charge; a carpenter member and others put
up partitions, where needed, rugs and drapes were brought in from
surrounding homes, and by April 6th, three days after the fire, the Lodge
held its regular Stated Meeting in a suitably tiled, comfortable, and
adequate temporary Lodge Room. This is only one example of the
spirit shown of overcoming obstacles during the formation of new
Lodges and should serve as an example to all of our Lodges.
The •Committee on Charters unanimously recommends that charters
be granted and numbers assigned to the six petitioning Lodges as follows:

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your committee has completed the publication of volume 8 of California Freemason and has culled the proceedings and publications of
sister Grand Lodges for information of interest to California Masons.
The format of a 48-page lithographed 6-inch by 9-inch magazine
with the flrst eight pages and last eight pages in two colors has been
continued. There is a liberal use of pictures.
The California Freemason is an official publication but its articles
do not necessarily present the opinion of Grand Lodge. It is attempted to
maintain sound Masonic standards and to give our readers Masonic
information and inspiration. Articles which are educational. informative, stimulating and sometimes provocative are presented.
Nearly everyone connected with California Masonry agrees that
our publication should be in the hands of every member in the state.
The advantage of such a plan would be that members not in close touch
of filieir lodges would be exposed to Freemasonry. The only thing
which prevents our Grand Lodge joining the company of New York,
Virginia, Oklahoma and other states which have 'a "house organ" for
their membership is the cost, which would be less than 50 cents a
member.
This is a question for Grand Lodge and not one for your committee. It will be noted, however, in the financial report which follows
that over one...third of our expenses is the recurring of and renewing
subscriptions.
If and when Grand Lodge decides to grasp the opportunity of
reaching all of its members the committee should be given a reasonable
time to make the change~over. For example, if the present session of
Grand Lodge should make such a decision it would be well to start the
operation of the plan for volume 10 for the year 1963. The committee
as individuals have presented a resolution to this effect.
The number of forward looking Lodges which send the magazines
to their entire membership have increased. This arrangement is that if
a Lodge adopts a resolution so to do, each member, will be mailed the
quarterly and, in January of each year, Grand Lodge will bill the Lodge
at the rate of not to exceed 60 cents for the number of members shown
on its last annual return. Changes in membership during the year do
not affect this charge.

Your special committee on Masonic Education reports as follows:
First, the committee wishes to pay tribute to our Grand Master, the
Most Worshipful Alfred F. Breslauer, for his inspiration, his unfailing
assistance, his guidance and leadership during the past year, without
which this committee could not have accomplished its desired goals.
Each one of us is grateful to him for our appointment to the Education
Committee and the opportunity to serve this Grand Lodge and the
Masons of California.
As was indicated in the last Report, a seminar on Masonic Education was held in this Memorial Temple on the Tuesday evening of the
1960 Grand Lodge communication. The Report, submitted prior to the
seminar, could not include any statistics. For the record, we include
them here although it was a function of the previous committee. From
the standpoint of attendance, and as could be interpreted, interest,
the seminar was the best attended of any such event to date. Twelve
hundred and fifty-nine brothers registered for the classroom session
and attended the second half, general session. These were augmented
by an estimated additional three hundred for the general session who
had not registered but who apparently participated only in that portion
of the evening's program. The Education Committee believes that so
much interest in Masonic education has been generated by the six seminars held to date as to warrant scheduling such as an evening for each
forthcoming communication and we so recommend.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Since January of this year, the committee, together with the four
Research Lodges has been planning for the seminar to be held in this
building on this Tuesday, September 26, starting at 7 o'clock P.M.
Two 45~minute classroom sessions will be held, in meeting rooms,
in the main auditorium and the exhibition hall, below. featuring five
timely subjects. Two subjects, following one another, will be presented
in the main auditorium. These will not be repeated. The three others,
held in the smaller rooms, will be repeated at 7:45 P.M., so as to accom·
modate those attending other classes during the previous period. The
general session will commence at 8:30 P.M., in the main auditorium.
During the general session no other classes will be held. Our speakers
for the general session will be the Very Worshipful Elbert W. Davis,
Past Grand Lecturer, speaking on the subject, "What May I Tell My
Non-Masonic Friends About Masonry?" and the Worshipful Ted
Meriam, Past Grand Orator, who will present a subject with which
he is very familiar, "The Local Lodge and Public Relations." Subjects
and personnel for the classroom session may be found in the seminar
programs distributed in the registration area.
This year the committee did not publish the booklets or papers
formerly called "Research Notes," because we felt that interest in
them was not sufficient to warrant the expense involved. If the Lodges
would like to see material of this type distributed, either on a monthly
or an occasional basis, we suggest that you convey your ideas on the
matter to the incoming Chairman of the Education Committee. He will
appreciate your guidance •a nd quite probably be able to help in ob~
taining the kind of material you seek.
The major work of the committee this year was the publication in
February of the booklet entitled, "A Brochure Comprising Three Plans
for Masonic Education." Most of the work in gathering material and
proving it as workable for Masonic Lodges, was done by the previous
committee during 1960, but it could not be finished in time for publication prior to the last Grand Lodge communication. The booklet is in·
tended to be a helpful guide in the institution and conduct of educational programs within the Lodges, it being the committee's conviction that most of the effort on Masonic education will have to come
from within the respective Lodges, by their own will and pleasure,
using outside help, including speakers and lecturers, only on special
occasions. By this time it is well recognized throughout the Masonic
world that there is a great deal more to Freemasonry than meets the
eye or can be conveyed during the receiving of a degree. Since everyone agrees to this as fact then it is but a step further to put some plan of
Masonic education into action at the local Lodge level. We believe it
is safe to say that our survival as a craft, as we know it today, depends
on this. We most 'heartily urge Senior and Junior Wardens to make
plans now for a regular course of Masonic education in your Lodge,

if you have not already undertaken this step, or to continue and attempt to improve upon it in the event you have already started. It should
be re~ognized that while one program given once during the year is a
step m the right direction it is not nor should it be the entire effort in
this most important area of Lodge work. For some ideas on this subject,
we recommend that you consult the "Brochure Comprising Three Plans
for Masonic Education." If you do not have a copy, you may obtain
one or more by writing the Grand Secretary's office.
We are again glad to report that the activities of the four Research
Lodges, as in previous years since their inception, continues to inform
to instruct, to stimulate our brethren into seeking the truth. Each
Lodge performs in its own way in a creditable manner. We wish that
time permitted us to detail some phase of the work of each one. California Masonry may indeed be proud of the many consecrated, dedicated brethren who voluntarily contribute time, talents and their personal funds towards the enlightenment of their brethren. As each year
passes, the work done by the brethren of the four Lodges once again
demonstrates the wisdom of this Grand Lodge in bringing them into
existence. The officers of each Lodge have repeatedly shown an interest and a desire to assist the local Lodges by presenting speakers or
panels on a variety of Masonic subjects, or to provide worth-while
papers which the local Lodge Education Chairman may present to his
Lodge.. We once again :emind you that the services of these Lodges
are available for the askmg. When constructing your education program for the coming year, may we suggest that you take advantage of
the services of .one or more of the many talented brothers from the
Research Lodge nearest you or of some interesting papers which a
Lodge may obtain on request. You will find a warm, ready response
and an interest in your education problems.
By way of experiment, the committee this year engaged in a series
of education programs in areas not easily nor comfortably served by
one of the Research Lodges. We wish to comment that without the
kin~ly and generous help and support of the Inspectors, and of the
Assistant Grand Lecturers for each division where we appeared, the
programs could not have been held; in addition to whk:h the efforts of
these brothers greatly contributed towards the success of these "conferences," as we called them. Meetings were held at Santa Maria,
Eureka, Chico, Jackson, Redding, Georgetown and Auburn. Speakers
were provided by the committee and the speakers panel consisted mainly
of committee members wit'h the help of several others, all active and
well known students of Masonry in their own right. All of our speakers
were members of a Research Lodge. The committee itself did nothing
by :Vay of promoting or publicizing the conferences, leaving such promotion to the local Lodges. Those of us who participated unanimously

215

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

feel that this experiment was quite successful. judging by the interest,
enthusiasm and generally good attendance at each conference as well
as unsolicited. laudatory letters in the committee's files. We therefore
recommend to the incoming committee that an education conference of
this nature be repeated in each of the places above mentioned and in
so many other places throughout the jurisdiction as the committee has
time to undertake.
In conclusion, we unanimously recommend to the incoming Grand

continued and request that the sum of $2500 be appropriated for its
expense during the coming year.

REPORT OF
SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON SCHOLARSIIlPS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
When Most Worshipful Henry C. Clausen was Grand Master in
1955 he recommended the creation of a Scholarship Fund whereby two
annual awards of $1,000.00 each would be made by the Grand Master.
one in the North and one in the Sout'h, for the best thesis and dissertation on the subject of Public Schools by graduate students working for
doctoral degrees in the field of education, and he stated tihat among
other benefits this would provide fruitful source material for use in
curricular and comparative studies.
The program was initiated during the year 1956, in which Most
Worshipful Edgar V. Stewart, Jr., was Grand Master, and during that
year announcement of the Scholarship Program was made at the University of California, Stanford University, and the College of the Pacific
in Northern California, and the University of California at Los Angeles,
University of Southern California and The Claremont Graduate Sdhool
in Southern California. Candidates were to submit an essay to the
Public Schools Committee of Grand Lodge on the subject, "The Origin,
Development and Purpose of our Public Schools." During that year
two $1,000.00 Scholarships were awarded.

Most Worshipful Leo E. Anderson reported in his message as
Grand Master that "it seemed to be the general feeling that the Scholarship Program was not accomplishing what was intended and it seemed
best to hold up any further scholarship awards" until a study was completed. He also stated in a letter to the Grand Secretary that from his
o:"'n experience with the Scholarship Program for over a two year period, he had the feeling that the Fraternity was not getting out of the
program the results originally hoped for and that none of the papers presented during that period came within shooting distance of the subject
which was presented as tihe basis for the applicant's research. He concluded that no papers Should be asked for during his year as Grand
Master, and that time should be taken to study and evaluate the program and determine whether or not the Fraternity was on the right
course or whether the funds should be used to do the job originally intended in another way. He also requested that Southern California
Research Lodge undertake research into various subjects concerning
the Public School System, both in America and in California, and to
prepare papers on the history, and development of the Public Schools
in America and in California, on what the Public School System has
contributed to the American way of life and on the contributions of the
Masonic Fraternity and its members to the Public School System in
California.
•
Your Committee :has had several meetings, has studied the various
submissions of applicants during the years the program was in operation, 1has had correspondence and conversations with the Dean of the
School of Education at Stanford University and has had a conference
with Dean William A. 1Brownell of the School of Education of the
University of California.
Your Committee finds that the Fraternity has not received from the
program any of the results originally hoped for and also finds that the
program as originally set up did not have the cooperation of the Universities having Graduate Schools in Education. Your Committe also
finds that the various submissions of applicants during the years that
the program was in operation were in general unsatisfactory and left
much to be desired. Your Committee believes that one of the reasons
for the poor submissions while the program was in operation was the
requirement that the applicant had to write a thesis or dissertation on
a subject selected by the Fraternity. Applicants were already engaged in
writing theses for their doctorate degrees involving an original study

216

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

approved by the Dean. Independent theses on a subject selected by the
Fraternity would by their very nature be inadequate because they would
be extracurricular. The Committee therefore believes that the program
should not be used to obtain source material.
The Committee also agrees with Dean William A. Brownell of the
School of Education at the University of California that the .Pr.ogram
should be more limited and the field of applicants should be limited to
candidates for a doctorate degree who are specializing in School Administration and Curriculum Development. Your Committee has assurances that the Schools of Education at Stanford University and the
University of California would cooperate with this type of program.
Aside from financially assisting t'hose who will some day be leade~s
in the teaching profession, the Committee believes that one of the primary objects of the Program should be to disclose to.those persons :Who
will some day be School Administrators and Curriculum Supervisors
the interest of the Fraternity in the Public School System .. Once t~ey
are convinced of the merit of the true philosophy of public education
they can be most effective in achieving the goals ultimately to be re~ched
by such a philosophy. The very nature of their positions should influence the teaching profession as a whole.
your Committee therefore concludes that the program can be made
to serve a useful purpose and that the Fraternity can make a definite
contribution to t'he Public School System by continuing the program.
With this in mind, your Committee makes the following specific recommendations:
1. The field of applicants should be limited to candidates ~o~ a d~c­
tor' s degree who are specializing in the field of School Adm1mstrabon
or Curriculum Development.
2. Applicants must be enrolled in. the ~raduate. Sch~ol~ of Education at Stanford University or the University of Cahforma m Northe~
California or the University of California at Los Angeles or the Uruversity of Southern California in Southern Califo~nia .(note: Clar~­
mont College would also be eligible in Southe~ C~hfor~a, but there is
no third university or college in Northern Cabforma ihavm~ a school ~f
education concentrating on awarding doctorates in education). Applicants must pursue a full-time program of doctoral study as defined and
approved by the School of Education attended.
All academic qualifications must be certified by the Dean of the
School of Education of the particular university.
3 Proper publicity should be circulated in the aforementioned
Scho~ls of Education so that graduate students who are qualified may
have ample opportunity to be apprised of the Program.
4. An application form should be printed and made availabl~ to
the aforementioned Schools of Education. A single-spaced, typewritten

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

statement on the topic "Public Schools in a Democracy-Their Place
in American Society" should be included as part of the application.
The application should be substantially in the form attached to the report of this Committee as presented to the 1960 Annual Communication
and marked Exhibit B.
5. .Each applicant shall cause to be submitted to the Grand Lodge
Committee on Scholarships letters of recommendation from three ( 3 )
individuals having personal knowledge of his ability and character, with
emphasis on the potentialities of the applicant in the field of education.
. 6. Emphasis should be placed on a personal interview of the applicants. Assurances have been given by Dean Brownell of the School
of Education at the University of California that the Dean's office would
assist in screening the list so that it could be narrowed to five or six.
Similar assistance could be obtained from the Deans of the other Schools
of Education involved in the Program.
7. The Grand Master should appoint a Committee to administer
the program, consisting of educators and laymen. There are in the
Fraternity many prominent members of the teaching profession whose
services would be valuable on such a Committee. The Committee
should be divided into two subcommittees, one whose members are
from Northern California and the other whose members are from
Southern California. The Committee would give publicity to the Program, forward the application forms to the various Schools of Education, personally interview a selected field of applicants on a given day
and recommend to the Grand Master the granting of two awards of
$1,000.00 each, one from the Northern Schools of Education and one
from the Southern Schools of Education. It is suggested that in the
personal interview the applicant be interrogated on a variety of subjects and that each applicant be told of the interest of the Fraternity in
the Public School System.
Although financial need should not play a primary part in making
the award, it should be considered by the Committee and may be used
as one factor among others to enable the Committee to make its choice.
8. Announcements of the scholarships should be made not later
than December 1: applications should be on file with Grand Lodge,
F. & A. M. of California, 1111 California Street, San Francisco, California, not later than February 1: awards should be announced on or
about April 15.
9. After the awards are announced the Committee should see that
proper publicity is given to the making of the awards toward the end
that the public may know of our efforts in making a concrete contribution toward the future of our Public School System.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The year of 1960 has been ·a somewhat frustrating year for the
Committee on Masonic Cemeteries due to the fact that we didn't have
any laws or legislation to support our recommendations or studies.
Nevertheless, we felt that in order to justify our existence we should
continue to do a good job of public relations for the Grand Lodge in
continuing our investigations wit'h regard to upkeep and maintenance
of our cemeteries, so they will reflect credit to the Masonic fraternity.
During this period we had the pleasure of meeting with our Grand
Master, Most Worshipful Alfred F. Breslauer, who was kind enough to
give me generously of his busy and valuable schedule. He suggested
that although no legislation existed to support our activities, we could
proceed under Section 204 of the Masonic Code which states in part,
"It shall be the duty of said committee to investigate and report to the
Grand Master t'he status and condition of Masonic Cemeteries and
Masonic plots in cemeteries in this jurisdi:ction, and to perform such
other duties relating to the subject as the Grand Master may direct."
Therefore. while our efforts are not authorized by formal legislation,
we have authority through the office of the Grand Master and Section
204, consequently our activities have been pursued at the pleasure of
the Grand Master.
Throughout the year it has been interesting to note that we have
been contacted by several corporations who are attempting to establish
new cemeteries containing Masonic plots. In making recommendations
to these organizations, we have endeavored to ·advise them of the requirements and procedures we would like to have observed in our State
with regard to upkeep and appearance and advocating at all times perpetual care. We also endeavor to see that the ·commercial aspect is
retained at a minimum. With reference to this commercialism, we have
advised corporations attempting to capitalize on the Masonic fraternity
in their cemetery operation that we would not tolerate this attitude.

Harold Anderson, after viewing the deplorable condition of this cemetery, this Committee was formed to remedy this and similar situations.
After investigation we recommend the following:
(a) Enclose section with strong chain link fence with iron posts
and gate.
( b ) Clean and restore headstones.
( c) Trim out superfluous brush and shrubs.
For the above, we request the sum of $500.

condition is a disgrace to the Fraternity, and should be corrected im·
mediately.
As is well known, the old town of Columbia is now a State Park,
and several buildings, including the schoolhouse, have been restored.
The Grand Lodge of California, at the cost of many t:housands of dollars, has rebuilt the old Masonic Temple in Columbia to its original
condition, and it is being frequently used by California Lodges on
visitations for the conferring of degrees. It would seem only reasonable
that the Grand Lodge should likewise restore the Masonic Cemetery to
a presentable condition. After investigation, we recommend the expenditure of $3000 to be used as follows:
(a) Surround Masonic section with a wood rail fence similar to
the original. or use a strong link fence with proper gates.
(b) Clean and restore head stones.
( c) Fill in sunken graves.
( d) Repair curbing around graves.

( g) Remove one old oak tree completely and generally trim all
ot!her trees.
('h) Straighten up leaning head stones and set them in cement.
These recommendations have nothing to do with future upkeep, but
should put these properties into condition so that future maintainence
should be comparatively easy. We also would appreciate the continuance of our present appropriation of $275 for the general use of the
Committee.

REPORT OF LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
With the approval by Grand Lodge of the necessary funds this
year, your library was born. The space on the second floor of the
Masonic Memorial Temple in San Francisco, which had been set aside
for a library and museum, now has one complete wall of shelving filled
with more than 2000 Masonic volumes. A .filing cabinet and an exhibit
case contain many valuable and historical items for the museum.
The library has been extremely fortunate this year in having as its
first librarian Brother William McMaster, a member of Corvallis Lodge,
Corvallis, Ore~on, who has given freely of his services in cataloging and
placing on the shelves the several hundred Masonic books received by
the library this year. Brother McMaster has enabled the Library Commission to keep your Grand Lodge library and museum open every
Wednesday from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. It is our sincere hope that with
additional support this coming year, the library may be kept open at
least five days a week. The indexing and cataloging of the books would
have been an almost insurmountable task, had it not been for the
scholarly assistance of Brother Paul Kruse, a member of Revelation
Lodge No. 180, Denver, Colorado, and presently librarian of Golden
Gate College. San Francisco.
It was the earnest wish of our Grand Master M.W. Alfred F.
Breslauer that our California Grand Lodge Library perform two functions which would make the library invaluable to Masons throughout our
jurisdiction. The first injunction from the Grand Master was to gather
all possible Masonic Californiana. Your commission wishes to express
its gratitude to the many lodges which provided histories. valuable documents. centennial volumes, and other materials which shall be preserved
in the Grand Lodge Library and when added to the P.G.M. Whitsell

222

collection of Californ ia Masoni c history documents will provide scholars
and student s with an extraord inarily fine foundation. The second in~
junction given by the Grand Master was t'hat a circulating library be
established, which would provide reading lists and books, to be mailed
to Master .Masons anywhe re in California, at no charge to them other
than the few cents return postage . Your Commission assembled and
had printed cards for book request s and stickers for book-mailing, and
mailing 1envelopes. We are indebte d to Brother Wende ll Walker , Librarian of the Grand Lodge of New York, and to the Librarians of the

reading. Things learned by word of mouth alone tend to be th~n and
transitory. No, the spoken word is a fleeting shadow. It will not
stay put to be mastered. Sound has the habit of floating in one ear
and out the other without so much as dropping anchor for a short
stay. Only the written word gives students, and others, the solid back~
ground that underlies all real culture. So it is in Freemasonry. The
written word provides the genuine basis upon which we may under~
stand the spoken word of the ceremony and will lead the solid reader
on the road to practical brotherhood.
The deeper and more abiding rewards of literature are hard to co~e
by. Reading is work. Even in its lightest form it demands s~me dis~
cipline and investment of self. But it is this self~investment which. over
the long haul. pays off in dividends to the mind.
Before making a beeline to the bookstore or to the shelves of your
Masonic library, let us be sure that we fully understand what we mean
by "reading."
You can get helpful assistance, if that is what you need, by com~
municating with your Grand Lodge Library.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC INFORMATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Before one passes through the sculptured bronze and aluminum
grille gates from the foyer of the magnificent California Masonic
Memorial Temple and enters the carpeted conicourse which leads to
the beautiful 3,200 seat auditorium he reads:
"CALIFORNIA FREEMASONS HONORING THEIR HEROIC DEAD
ERECT THIS TEMPLE
DEDICATED TO FREEMASONRY, VIRTUE, AND UNIVERSAL BENEVOLENCE
THAT THE CAUSE OF FREEDOM FOR WHICH THEY DIED
SHALL EVER BE THEREIN THE SACRED TRUST OF THEIR BRETHREN
AND OF FREEMASONS YET UNBORN"
The foregoing expresses a noble and sincere sentiment. It is consistent with the lofty traditions and majestic philosophy of Freemasonry ·w hich has contributed to public welfare and the progress
of human institutions. Carved in marble are words expressing the belief
of Masons in the dignity and rights of the individual and the firm
conviction of Masons in the brotherhood of man and the fatherhood
of God. The perpetuation of these exalted precepts to "Freemasons yet
unborn," however, requires more than passivity. It demands that the
public know that Masons are not immersed in ritualistic work and not
smug in the belief that the Masonry established by their forbears will
continue in high esteem, but, on the contrary, Masons are actively
contributing their efforts for the betterment of man. It is hoped that
our Fraternity will be joined by millions of "Freemasons yet unborn."
But today there are living millions of eligible persons who would seek
membership if they were aware that Masons do something more than
go to meetings at Lodge Halls and indulge in ceremonies of a ritualistic
or symbolic nature.
Masonry in many parts of the United States, including California,
is concerned about membership in the Craft falling behind the pace

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

235

in the growth of population because of lack of interest. It is true that
our ·i nterest is principally in the quality of members rather than quantity
but members are important in any endeavor. Perhaps one of the reasons
many fine prospective members do not petition for degrees is their
absolute lack of knowledge about the teachings and objectives of
Freemasonry. In the effort to conform strictly to one of the precepts of
our Order that we should not solicit members, we fail in the altruistic
purpose of making known the character of Freemasons and the fundamental philosophy of the Craft in the promotion of the rights and
dignity of all men and the preservation of the institutions of our American form of democratic government.
In the Bible, the book of our faith, we find the following: ". . . for
whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Galatians, ch. 6,
v. 7). If we have failed heretofore in sowing, we should now spread
publicly the seeds of our good works so that men "of moral conduct"
may have a sound basis for petitioning for membership. There are many
examples of men who hesitate to join Freemasonry because they lack
information about our activities but once learning of our purposes,
teachings and objectives they join with eagerness. A favorable impression or image of Masonry is essential in the encouragement of a
prospective member. This impression ofttimes may be given by individual Masons such as illustrated in the article entitled "Impressions
of a New Mason" published in the Winter 1961 issue of California
Freemason (Vol. 8, No. 1). p. 21:

"It was because of the fine character of the two or three
Masons I mave known with some degree of intimacy, and the
high esteem that I have for them that I first sought to become
a Mason. These are men whom I respect immensely, men whose
lives in the communities in which they lived seemed to me to be
highly exemplary. They are modest men; they are men of vision
and foresight who stand out forcefully in the communities in
which they serve; they are men of great and tireless energy. Most
important, they are men with ideals and the courage to move
forward toward the fulfillment of their ideals."
The foregoing presents a good example of the influence of men of
character but through widespread knowledge of the good works of
Masons the beneficent power and attractive virtues of the Fraternity may
receive greater propagation. The dissemination of knowledge in this
manner is commonly a part of a program of "public relations" or "public information." A fair definition of such a program is the translation
with good sense and good taste of the actions and aims of an
individual or organization into terms found understandable and sympathetic to other groups, or the public at large. The way to good
public relations has been summed up simply in the words, ( 1 ) do good,

tribution to the public as well as to Masons which may reflect credit

in 1959 and 1960 are "Our Public Schools" and "The Road to

CONCLUSION

Of foremost importance in the development of any program of public information is the relationship between Masons and others in the
community. That relationship must be one of friendship and respect.
The words and acts of Masons in daily life must be entirely consistent
with the high precepts learned in the lodgeroom. We should remember
that we convey thoughts with our every word and deed. The communication of our activities through public media such as press, radio
and television merely is our implementation of our relationship in the
community. Our activities, if praiseworth y and for the public good,
should receive favorable comment reflecting honor on our Fraternity.
We learn in our teachings that we seek always the truth. As
American citizens abiding by that principle we can perform a great
service. The public should know generally of our evercontinuing effort
to seek the truth to make men free. This search for truth has a close
relationship with the idealogical battle now raging the world over.
Americans must not come to the disillusioning and disheartening condition expressed by the late Boris Pasternak when he said:
I am lost like a beast in an enclosure,
Somewhere are people, freedom and light.
Behind me is the noise of pursuit,
And there is no way out.
Dark forests by the shore of the lake,
Stump of fallen fir tree,
Here I am cut off from everything,
Whatever shall be is the same to me.
1

But what wicked thing have I done,
I, the murderer and villain?
I, who forced the whole world to cry
Over the beauty of my land.
But, in any case, I am near my grave,
And I believe the time will come
When the spirit of good will conquer
Wickedness and infamy.
Pasternak's hope that truth will prevail shines through his words.
What greater service ,can be performed than in the honest effort to
seek the truth. America must be encouraged to lay hold of the truth

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

239

wherever it may be found so that there will not be in America such a
calamity as pictured by Pasternak.
In our effort to seek the truth others may be encouraged to do
likewise. In this manner we may gain strength that may be our hope
of the future.
Respectfully submitted,
GERALD LEVIN
WILLIAM H. ADAMS
THEODORE MERIAM
WILMER G. BRILL

REPORT OF COMMIT TEE ON
MASONIC 1-IlSTORICAL MONUME NTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Your special committee on Masonic Historical Monuments reports
as follows:
At the 1960 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, Harmony
Lodge No. 164 requested that it be made a Masonic Historical Monument. Grand Lodge adopted the recommendation of the Policy and
General Purposes Committee, that a special committee be appointed
to study and recommend to Grand Lodge means and procedures by
which Grand Lodge may aid our early California Lodges, when aid
is needed, in the preservation, safekeeping and security of the invaluable Masonic possessions, to the end that they may not be destroyed
or lost and that they may be made available for the enlightenme nt
and benefit of Masons in California for generations to come.
During the year your Committee held meetings with eight of our
early Lodges, located principally in the Mother Lode area, to determine the needs of each particular Lodge, in carrying out the directives
of Grand Lodge.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

We found that many of the records and items of Masonic historical
interest were being kept in an unsafe manner, and that in the event of
fire they would be lost. After a complete study by >:our co.mmittee, it
determin ed that the need is not so much for financial assistanc e but
for technical advice in providing a safe deposito ry for these invaluable
records to be preserve d for all time to come.
It is therefor the recommendation of this committee that the Grand
Lodge off er its assistanc e in furnishing designs for the installation of
fire proof safes or vaults, to be construc ted by the members of the
Lodges, of sufficient size to contain these records.
It was clearly indicated to your committee that these Lodges are
asking for technical advice and are not soliciting financial aid from
Grand Lodge.
Respectf ully submitted,

To the Most Worship ful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Columbia Temple Committ ee wishes to report that:
Seventee n events were held in the Columbi a Temple during the 19601961 fiscal year and that the events consisted mostly of visiting Lodges
conferring the third degree on their own candidat es which they brought
with them. One event was a visit of Grand Lodge Officers when the
Columbia School was re-dedic ated in the Columbia State Park by
Grand Lodge Officers.
Other items of interest to the brethren were:
The entire inte~or, and the outside wood-wo rk of the Temple
received new paint. Even the basemen t which had never been painted
was given a coat of white paint.
The window shades on the windows have been replaced with
interior wooden shutters, in keeping with the old time atmosphere.
An entire new roof has been put on the Temple.
Signs have been installed on the south side and the west end of
the Temple. These signs read "MASO NIC HALL" since the original
Temple was so designat ed in the old days.
The records consisting of bound volumes and microfilm are in
perfect shape in the vault.
The local members of the committee were saddene d by the death
of Brother Bert Bullock on July 31st. Brother Bullock was the custodian of the Temple for the past two years. He was also a Past Master
of Tuolumn e Lodge No. 8 and a past Inspecto r.
Mr. Buck Nelson, who lives in Columbia, has been appointe d to
replace Brother Bullock as Custodia n of the Temple. At present he is
the Junior Warden of Tuolumn e Lodge No. 8.
Your committee sincerely hopes that the Lodges will continue to
make use of the Columbia Temple in the future. The committee will
endeavo r to make their visit a pleasant one.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
MASONIC CLUB
UNIVERSIT Y OF CALIFORNI A, BERKELEY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Board of Directors is pleased to submit its Annual Report
for the fiscal year ending July 31, 1961.
Efforts have been redoubled this past year to promote increased
use of the Clubhouse. A special Board Committee, headed by Bro.
Gordon F. Black, maintains regular liaison with the Student Council
and works with a student committee formed to develop student suggestions and recommendations for expanded use of the Clubhouse.
Also, the President of the Student Council, and an officer of his choosing, have been invited to sit in with the Board and discuss with the
members of the Board their problems and suggestions for improvements. Results included a program of regular notices and advertising
for special events in the Daily California newspaper, as well as
weekly activities, and posters displayed in the lighted Bulletin Board
in front of the Clubhouse. In addition, letters went out to all Northern California area DeMolay, Jobs Daughters and Rainbow Girls
groups.
A series of Thursday night open Seminars on current events by
University lecturers was developed. An Opinion Poll on Club activities helped formulate the students' social calendar and the 1960
Fall Semester Open House dance gained nearly one hundred new
members to start the year.
Pledge projects, dances and socials, the U.C.L.A. weekend visit,
the Home Coming with the Grand Master's visit, snow trips, picnics
and the regular use of the Clubhouse, including daily snackbar luncheons, entertainment with the TV and Hi Fi set and numerous other
Club facilities all brought stimulating enjoyment and scores of students in spite of the heavily increasing competition for the students'
time and support of other campus organizations and activities.
The Personnel Committee, Bro. John L. Wixon, Ch., interviewed
prospective candidates for the position of Resident Hostess for the
Club during the past two years, since Mrs. Esther Mainwaring had
expressed the wish to retire. It was not until the late 1961 Spring term
that choice settled on two ladies to perform the heavy duties formerly
carried on by Mrs. Mainwaring. Mrs. Janaice Kohl was employed as
Resident Hostess and Mrs. Stuart Kierulff was hired as Social Hostess.
A vote of thanks and sincere appreciation was recorded by the
Board of Directors to the retiring Hostess, Mrs. Esther Mainwaring.
for her years of devoted interest and service "beyond the call of duty"
on behalf of the students and the Masonic Clubhouse. Slie .will be

fondly remembered by Board members and the many students who
profited by her gracious help and advice on their Club and personal
problems.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON INSURANC E
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Recently, a survey of the insurance program of Grand Lodge was
made by the Insurance Committee.
The coverage has been checked against records previously set up by
us and we accounted for all the policies except Fire Insurance, Workmen's Compensation in the State of Hawaii, and Comprehensive Public
Liability coverage.
Protection for these risks are in the form of Binders which are
being watched carefully and policies should be issued very soon.
Our survey finds the insurance being maintained in good order
and fully covering any foreseeable risks of Grand Lodge.
The assistance of your staff in making this review was excellent.
Respectfully submitted.

T. J. CARLILE

POLITICAL ACTIVITY OF LODGES
(22)
Report of Special Committee:
At the last regular Communication of Grand Lodge our venerable
Past Grand ·M aster, Charles Albert Adams, presented an important
resolution respecting the activities of Grand Lodge and the constituent
Lodges. This matter was referred to a special committee for study and
recommendation. Your committee has carefully considered the resolution
and its implications and finds itseJf generaJly in accord with Brother
Adams' expressions. Before submitting our redraft, however, it might
be well to discuss briefly the problem which the Adams resolution is
attempting to solve.
Masonry, unlike many other organizations and lodges. has never
tried to dictate to its members in the realm of religion or polit:Iics. We
recognize that any attempt to do so would ineviitably lead to bitter
disharmony and would be fatal to our ultimate goal to inspire men in
all walks of life to nobility of thought and conduct. Freedom of polit:Iical
action, freedom of religion, freedom of expression, freedom to explore
the unknown and to develop new and even daring ideas are necessary
characteristics of a dynamic society. Thus Masonry concerns itseJf with
liberty of thought and action. The demands of Masonry on the conscience of man are but few and are fundamental. The ·M ason must
believe in God and in the immortality of the soul. But there is no
dictation as to his religious preference; indeed we invite men of all
religious convictions. '!'here is no dictation as to political preference;

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

249

indeed we embrace people of all true political parties. The Mason is
not told. on penalty .of expul~io~, what he •shall not read or say or how
he must vo_te ~n a given public issue. He is not prohibited from joining
aniy organizations save those dedicated to subversion or violence or
other forms of lawlessness.
Howe~er, while we all recognize harmony and freedom of thought
and ~onsc1ence. a.s essential characteristics of ·Masonry, we are equally
~ogmzant ~hat it is essential in the sensitive and dynamic era in which we
live ~o ~chieve the greatest possible degree of enlig'h tenment on the great
public 1ss~es of ~he day. It is unrealistic and dangerous for us. as Maso.ns, to hide. our heads in the sand, and concern ourselves exclusively
with our ~ncient rites and rituals. In the past, our cautious attitude and
f~ar of disharmony may have led us into unjustified timidity and consi.derab~e confusion as to what we could safely permit by way of free
discussion on the floor of our Lodges. It is to the clarification of this
matter that Brother Adams' resolution addresses itself.
Thus the Adams resolution recognizes the propriety and desirability
of free and ~pen discuss.ion within a Lodge of matters concerning the
general public .wel~are. including the subject of pending local, state,
and federal l~gislation. This ~ould lead to the more intelligent exercise
of the franchise and a keener interest in our duties as citizens.
~~e. resolution, .however, provides certain safeguards against the
pos.s1bdity of embroilme.nt in the arena of local, state or federal politics,
which has been so detnmental to Masonry in some of the countries of
the Old World. It recognizes the very real danger of the depletion of
Lod~e funds for political purposes. and of the public endorsement
or disapproval of candidates or legislation where t'he existence of the
Lodge i~ ~ot i'?1mediately endangered or imperiled. It recognizes that
~uch ~c~1vity w11J re~ult in disha~m~ny, public discredit and an attempted
imposition of the wiJI of the maJority on the conscience of the minority
As pointed out by Brother Adams such activity would impose .. a~
ex_press or implied duty" on the part of Masons to vote dn accordance
with the action taken. This is abhorrent to free men and would result in
what might be termed "dnstitutionalized thinking."
~ e, o~ the committee, feel that the proposed resolution is another
manifestation of the wisdom, keen intellect, and foresight of Charles
Alb~rt Adams, and we respectfully recommend adoption in the following redrafted form:
RESOLUTION

hereafter be ~ermitted ~n Gr~nd Lodge, and in the constituent Lodges,

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON NECROLOGY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The report of the Committee on Necrology tends to promote serious
and melancholy reflections. Death is an occasion of sadness. No matter
how strong our faith in the immortality of the soul. we all know we
shall see our departed no more in the flesh. and the fellowship we have
had remains only as a precious memory. We all come to this Service
with a certain heaviness of spirit because we have known some of those
who have passed from our midst. We miss their warm greetings at
Grand Lodge and the companionship we 'h ave had with them. It is not
possible that any of us knew all who have gone on and only at this
time do we get the full picture of the total loss of this body.
As we might expect from an organization that is constantly increasing in numbers, the death roll is also increasing. For several years
there has been a slight increase each year. This year again the number
has grown. During the past Masonic year three hundred ninety-one
members of this Grand Lodge have welcomed death. "as a kind messenger sent to translate them from this imperfect to that all perfect.
glorious, and Celestial Lodge above, where the Supreme Grand Master
of the Universe forever presides." Losses have been sustained by two
hundred seventy-one lodges scattered throughout the State. One hundred seventy-nine lodges each lost one of its Past Masters; sixty-nine
lodges lost two; eighteen lodges lost three; and five lodges lost four.
Many of those on the roll had been Masons and served in their
lodges for many years. We find at least fifty-two had been Masons for
over Jlfty years. Four were Masons for over sixty years, and one who
will be mentioned later was raised on August 1, 1889 and at the time
of his death was a Mason of over seventy-one years standing. The
name of Past Grand Master Samuel E. Burke is on the roll. A suitable
eulogy will be presented by Brother Ralph H. Head. Also the names
of Brother Ralph E. Hoyt, a member of the Grievances Committee,
Ralph M. Foote, former Assistant Grand Lecturer, and several former
inspectors.
