JAMES ANDREW LYNCH

On October 28, 1960 death took from our midst James Andrew
Lynch of Long Beach. Brother Lynch was born in Brooklyn, New
York on May 13, 1880. He saw service in the Spanish-American war.
In 1902 he came to Long Beach, where he worked for the Pacific Telephone and Telegraph Company for twenty years. He then went to
work for Sou~hern Cali_forn~a Edison Company and, after twenty-seven
years of service, he retired m 1947 as Assistant Manager.
James A. Lynch was raised a Master Mason in West Lake Lodge
No. 392 in Los Angeles on May 21, 1921 and later affiliated with Palos
Verdes Lodge No. 389 in Long Beach. He became Charter Senior
Deacon in Service Lodge No. 594, Long Beach and served as Master of
that Lodge in 1927. In 1928 he was appointed Inspector of the 98th Masonic District and served as such until 1935. He was a member of the
Order of Sciots and served as top officer, both in his own Pyramid in
Lon~ Beach and i~ the Supreme Pyramid. For many years he was
Chairman of the Sciot Foundation Fund which administers aid to needy
children of all races and creeds. He also was a member of both York
and Sc~ttish Rite Bodies and a Charter Member of El Bekal Temple of
the Shrine. A member of the First Baptist Church of Long Beach for
many years, he served on the official Board and as an usher in that
Church. Over a long life, he was always active in good work and was
a blessing to his fellowmen. We are confident Brother Jim Lynch has
heard his Master's "Come, ye blessed of my Father, enter into the Kingdom prepared for you."

GEORGE HoWE BUTTRICK

The man who was probably t'he oldest member of this Grand Lodge
was removed from our midst when death came to George H. Buttrick of
Stockton.
Brother George was born on October 24, 1862 and died May 6,
1961, having thus reached the age of ninety-eight years and seven
months. He was raised a Master Mason in Morning Star Lodge No. 68
on August 1, 1889, thus having been a Mason for nearly seventy-two
years at the time of his death. He has been a member of this Grand
Lodge for at least fifty-six years since he was Master of Morning Star
Lodge in 1905.
While the length of time Brother George lived and was a Mason was
truly remarkable and must constitute something of a record, the truly
significant thing about him was the full measure of service he crowded
into those years. Always active, since his retirement from the position
of Chief Engineer at the Stockton State Hospital in 1939 after fortyt'hree years service, he had devoted himself largely to Masonic Service.
At the time of his death 1he was serving his forty-ninth consecutive year
as Secretary of Morning Star Lodge.
He received his 32nd degree in San Francisco Consistory in September, 1919 and became a Charter Member of Stockton Consistory
when it was organized in 1922. He served as Secretary of all Scottish

Rite Bodies from 1922, and, in honor of his valued services, was made
Secretary Emeritus in February, 1955. He was coronated 33rd degree
on December 16, 1939. George was a sincere and loyal Master Mason,
and today we respectful ly thank Almighty God that he was given such
a long life to labor so abundantl y for his brother man.
RALPH EDWIN HoYT

Death came suddenly to Ralph E. Hoyt. when he died of a heart attack in his Oakland home on Saturday, July 29, 1961. He was sixtyseven years of age.
Ralph Hoyt had a distinguis hed career as a member of ~he Califo~a
Bar and was a long time associate and close personal friend of Ch.ief
Justice Earl Warren, P.G.M. Born in San Diego County, he studied
at the University of California and received his law degree in 1917. He
was admitted to the Bar in that year and in 1919 he became a member
of Alameda County District Attorney' s Staff. He served as Chief As-sistant to District Attorney Earl Warren from 1926 to 1939, and. when
Earl Warren became California Attorney General. he was made Dis-trict Attorney in his place. In 1947 Governor Warren appointed Ralph
Hoyt to the Superior Court Bench, describing him as "a fine, courageous,
public servant." He has served in that position with g~eat ~istinction
and last year was President of the Conferenc e of California J~dg~s.
He spent the last five months of his life on assignmen t to the Distnct
Court of Appeals.
Ralph E. Hoyt was made a Mason in Durant Lodge No. 268 on
Septembe r 18. 1916, while still a student at U. C. He was Master of
Durant Lodge in 1928. He was appointed a member of the Grievance s
Committee in 1949 and was serving on that Committee at the time of
his death. He was a member of Scottish Rite Bodies and was coronated
33rd degree. He was also a member of Aahmes Temple of the Shrine.
He is survived by his wife of forty-four years, a son, Ralph B.
Hoyt of Oakland, daughter. Mrs. J. D. Sanderson of Orinda, and six
grandchildren.
Ralph Hoyt was a courteous, courageous gentleman and Califor~ia
lost a revered Jurist and this Grand Lodge a beloved hard working
member when he passed. We hoped he might have been spared for
more years of service but
"God has led our brother on,

HENRY KOBER

At the time of his death on March 30, 1961 Henry Kober had been
a Mason for aliftost sixty-six years. He was a member and Past Master
of North East Lodge No. 266 in Fort Bidwell. We do not know how
often Henry served his lodge as Master, but we understan d he did so
on more than one year. He also served as Secretary . A storekeepe r in
a small town in an isolated area, he was one of those devoted characters
Who help to keep Masonry alive where numbers are small and outside
fellowship somewhat remote.
Henry was Grand Bible Bearer in 1953 and won a warm place in
the hearts of the Grand Lodge Officers of that year. He attended a
number of Grand Lodge meetings during the year. In order to get to
the meeting, Henry drove from his home at Fort Bidwell. in the Northeast corner of California , to Reno, a distance, over mountains, of about
235 miles. From Reno he flew to San Francisco from where he proceeded with some of the rest of us to wherever Grand Lodge was meeting. He was at the time about eighty years of age. This kind of effort
was indicative of the fidelity of this brother over many years.
Many of the officers of 1953, as well as others who knew him, will
be saddened to learn that gentle, kindly, faithful Henry Kober has left
us and will feel like saying, "Goodbye , Henry, till we meet again."

FRED A. KELSEY

EULOGY

On September 2, 1961 a very widely known man, an~ popular
member of the Fraternity left us when Fred A. Kelsey died at the
Motion Picture Country Home and Hospital in Woodland Hills, at
the age of 77 years.
Fred was one of Hollywood's busiest character actors and was one
of the first to take such roles in talking pictures. He began his film
career in 1909 and came to Hollywood witlh the late D. W. Griffith
during World War 1. He won wide recognition in ?ot~ silen~: and
later in sound films. He appeared with Rudolph Valentino m the Four
Horesmen of the Apocalypse" in which he portayed four different Ger#
man officers.
A very popular member of Mount Olive Lodge No. ~06, he served
his lodge as Master in 1936, and as Secretary from Apnl 20, 1942, to
December 31, 1958. He was also a well known member of this Grand
Lodge, which he served as Grand Sword Bearer from October, 1937 to
October, 1939.
Fred has gone but he lingers on as an enlivening influence in. the
memory of the many who knew him.
We cannot even call tihe names of all on the roll. A complete list
is attached and made a part of this report. They gave long years of
service to their Lodges and their fellowmen. Many served on City
Councils and on School Boards. Masonry does not promote projects,
but it has sent out men of 1high principles to serve in every field of
human endeavor. They have labored mightily. but God has decreed that
their work is done. We mourn their loss, but we are not among those
"Who, hopeless, lay tfheir dead away," but rather among those who
believe:
"That Life is ever Lord of Death,
And Love can never lose its own."
ADAM B. MORTEN

SAMUEL EDGERTON BURKE

By Ralph H. Head
The proceedings of the seventy#third annual Communication of
Grand Lodge contain in part a biographical record of the then presiding
Grand Master, the beloved Samuel Edgerton Burke. After properly
extolling his virtues and his accomplishments, the report concludes.
"May he live to a green old age.''
Our venerable Past Grand Master took this wish -seriously. Who#
ever summarily concluded that the "good die young" did not take Sam
Burke into account. He died one day after his noinety#ehird birthday
and the good he did is not interred with his bones. It will live on and
on for many, many years.
Propriety requires that the recordation of this eulogy include the
Masonic statisticoS of this great and kind man. It would be my prefer#
ence to use this time and space in a plea that Ms exemplary life be a
constant inspiration to every Mason in California.
Samuel Edgerton Burke was born in the Province of Ontario,
Canada, on February 13, 1868. He graduated from Lake Forest
University, Illinois, with a Degree in Dental Surgery. He was made a
Master Mason •in Sunset Lodge No. 352 in 1903 and became its
Master in 1906. He iserved Grand Lodge faithfully as an Inspector
for mine years. HioS devotion continued in 1911 with his appointment
as Grand Chaplain, Grand Bible Bearer in 1912, one of the most
affluent of all Grand Orators in 1915, Junior Warden in 1918, and
was elected to California Freemasonry's highest honor as Grand Master
in 1921.
Dr. Burke's Masonic life was well rounded, for he not only joined
but took an active part in the affairs of other affiliated Masonic orders.
He was Grand MaoSter of the Grand Council of California in the Y erk
Rite and received his honorary 33rd degree &om the Los Angeles
Bodies of the Scottish Rite.
He is survived by his loving and devoted son, Frazee, a member
of his own Lodge.
Sam Burke enjoyed everything he did in Freemasonry. He did
everything well and with the highest of fotegrity, but if he could have
been made to account for his most enjoyable years it would have been his

260

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

long, faithful, and valuable tenure as a Trustee of the Masonic Homes
of California.
A1s he closed his address to Grand Lodge on October 10, 1922. in
his typical graciousness he thanked his officers without whose help,
he stated, he would have been "a very small bark on a mighty sea."
Those who knew Sam Burke will forever disagree. Here was a
Mason who so Hved his life that he was always "a mighty big bark on
a great sea of friends."
The Masonic poet, Douglas Malloch, wrote words which should
convince us that the loss of Samuel Edgerton Burke is but another
reminder of the immortality of the soul.
I would not hold our loss too lightly,
God knows, and he, 'how deep the pain:
But friends, I see still shining brightly
The brightest link in all our Chain
That links us with a new domain.
For friendship binds the world together,
World over there, world over here.
F,rom earth to heaven is the tether
That brings the earth and 'heaven near
And makes them both a bit more dear.
W 'h atever vales we may yet wander,
What sorrow come, what tempest blow,
We have a friend, a friend out yonder,
To greet us when we have to go-Out yonder someone that we know.
To all eternity he binds us;
He links the planet and the star;
He rides ahead, the trail 'he finds us,
And where he is and where we are
Will never seem agafa so far.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Grievances reports as follows:
The Committee has considered 60 trial records, of which 37 will be
covered by this report. The remainder will be subjects of special reports.
There are a few matters which we wish to stress.
A copy of charges should always be sent to the Grand Secretary
as required by Section 691 of the Masonic Code. It would be ~ell to
notify the Grand Secretary of commencing the procedure calle? .automatic expulsion" under Section 732 of the Code, although this is not
specifically required. Section 732 should be used whenever an accused
Mason ·h as been convicted of a crime classed as a felony and has served
any time pursuant thereof. This means time served in a prison or in a
county jail, road camp, or state hospital as a sexual psychopath (an~
not as mentally ill) so long as the crime was one "classed as a f~o~y.
However, if a person is given straight probation on a felony conviction,
without any imprisonment as a part of it, Section 732 may not be used.
In these and all other matters affecting our disciplinary procedure,
a careful reading of the Code and of the trial guide is recommended.

TRIAL RECORDS NOS. 1594, 1596, 1597, and 1607
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In each of these records the accused was expelled after proper proceedings, the charge being a violation of the edict of the Grand Master
concerning the Royal Order of Caritas, etc. The edict has since been
repealed. This, of itself, does not justify the offense for w'hic'h each of
these accused Masons was charged. It was the violation of the edict
while it was in force and effect that constituted the offense. However,
there was no real moral turpitude in any of these cases. Each of these
expelled men has now asked for restoration, and the record indicates
that each is ,a moral man and a good citizen, repentant of his offense.
We feel that restoration of each would be proper.
'rhe accused in 1594 was a member of a North Carolina Lodge,
expelled by Argonaut Lodge No. 461.
The accused in 1596 and 1597 were both members of Alcatraz Lodge
No. 244.
The accused in 1607 was a member of Fellowship Lodge No. 480.
We therefore offer the following resolution:
RESOLVE D, that each of the accused in Trial Records Nos. 1594,
1596, 1597, and 1607 be restored to all the rights and privileges of
Masonry.
Adopted.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1660
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
There is a petition for restoration in this case. The accused was expelled over two years ago by Torrance Lodge No. 447, the charge
being falsification of his petition for the degrees in that he did not disclose that he had been elected by a lodge in West Virginia some years
before and had received the first degree but had been stopped from
advancemen t by that lodge.
1
At this time, the accused seems to be of good repute in his community
and his petition for restoration has much supporting data.
However, it is our opinion that tlhis accused cannot legally be restored in this jurisdiction. As an Entered Apprentice he is still within
the perpetual jurisdiction of West Virginia. Inquiry from that grand
jurisdiction indicates that he has never been suspended nor expelled
there and is still an Entered Apprentice of his lodge, although not in
good standing.
Grand Master Perine rendered a decision reported in the 1908
Proceedings of Grand Lodge at page 39 in which he said in part, "The
Grand Lodge of California recognizes perpetual jurisdiction only when

277

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

an applicant has been elected and initiated by ~he lodge to which he
applied."
According to Landmark Sixteenth. no lodge can give degrees to
brethren who are members of other lodges.
Torrance Lodge had no right to elect this accused and give him the
degrees, and would not have done so if he had not concealed the fact
that he was already an Entered Apprentice elsewhere. Having been
expelled, the accused is in the same position he was before petitioning
Torrance Lodge. His only recourse is to ask for advancement in the
lodge in West Virginia.
For these reasons we must recommend denial of the petition, and
we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the petition for restoration of the accused in
Trial Record No. 1660 be denied.
Adopted.

The petition for restoration is accompanied by several letters of
recommendation and your Committee also heard remarks in behalf of
the petitioner by members of this Grand Lodge.
While your Committee recognizes the rehabilitation of the petitioner
up to this time, it cannot overlook the fact that petitioner is still under
probation of the court which does not expire until December 8, 1962 and
feels that petitioner should wait until all the terms and conditions of his
probation be completed to the satisfaction of the Court.
THEREFORE, be it resolved that the petition for restoration to all
the rights and privileges of Masonry be denied.
Adopted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Grievances to whom was referred the petition
for restoration to all rights ,a nd privileges of Masonry of a former member of Garvanza Lodge No. 492 has carefully considered the same and
reports as follows:
Petitioner, a pharmacist. was convicted in the Superior Court of
Los Angeles County of violation of Section No. 11715, Health and
Safety Code of California. The judgment of the court was that petitioner be sentenced to one year in jail. suspended for three years and
given three ( 3) years probation. The judgment was rendered on December 8, 1959 and probation expires on December 8, 1962 if petitioner
conducts himself in a manner satisfactory to the court.
Petitioner also received 'five years probation from die State Board
of Pharmacy of the State of California but was permitted to continue
with a valid license while on probation.
Petitioner was charged with Masonic offenses and petitioner entered
no plea and upon investigation by the Worshipful Master of Garvanza
Lodge No. 492, was found guilty of all five specifications and ordered
the penalty to be a reprimand.
Your Committee on Grievances at the 1960 Annual Communication
investigated this case in detail and carefully considered all evidence
presented to it orally at the time and recommended the penalty be raised
to suspension, which finding was affirmed by this Grand Lodge.
After this judgment was affirmed and petitioner notified, he made
certain threats against officers and members of his former lodge as well
as members of this Committee of Grand Lodge. Your Committee is
willing to overlook this as a reaction of bitterness which it considers
understandable in view of the fact that petitioner now indicates his
regret over his attitude at that time.

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1699
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In this trial record El Cerrito Lodge No. 705 took action under 732
Masonic Code to expel a member who had been convicted of two
felonies in New Mexico. However the judgment in die state court
showed that accused was not imprisoned as a result of his conviction,
but that sentence had been suspended and that he had been turned
over to the State of Texas for trial for similar felony charges there.
The proceedings based on the New Mexico conviction are therefore
improper under 732 Masonic Code, and we must reverse the same.
(However, we are informed that die accused was later convicted in
Texas and sentenced to prison and proper proceedings in the lodge are
now taking place to expel him. If the accused is expelled because of
the Texas conviction, no further action on the New Mexico conviction
wiU be needed:)
We offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the expulsion of the accused in Trial Record
No. 1699 by El Cerrito Lodge No. 705 be reversed and remanded to
the lodge for further procedure, if necessary.
Adopted.

TRIAL MANUAL
(29)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Resolution No. 29 concerning the appointment of a special committee to prepare a trial form book has been referred to both the Policy
and General Purposes Committee and the Committee on Grievances.
The latter Committee, while having great respect for the author of the
resolution as an outstanding member of this Grand Lodge, has doubt of
the necessity of a new trial form book. The little Trial Outline which

280

~RAND

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

was originally prepared by our present Grand Master, and which has
been kept up to date from year to year, seems .to state the procedure
for trials in simple language and reference is made throughout t~ the
proper sections of the Masonic Code. The Grand Secretary furnishes
forms to Lodges requesting them which cover almost all procedure.
Most of these forms are set out verbatim in t!he Masonic Code.
A special committee would entail some expense, and the publication
of a form book would cost a considerable sum at best. If Masters or
Trial Masters do not read the present Trial Outline and the pertinent
Code Sections carefully, they would do no better with a new form book.
We move the adoption of t'he resolution and recommend a no vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes indicated their
concurre~ce in the recommendation.
Adopted.

Lodge, dies while serving as Master, may by resolution of his Lodge

The resolution was adopted by a 5/6 vote.

We believe that the report of the Special Committee on Visual Aids
which was adopted by Grand Lodge in 1959 adequately covered the
objects sought by this resolution.
First, it recommended no change in the presentation and lectures
of the three degrees, which means that no use can be made of visual
aids in the conferring of the three degrees, other than those Which are
now an integral part of our ritual.
Second, it suggested that there was a place in the Lodge building
for appropriate physical representations, but that these should not be
a part of any ritual.
Third, it suggested that Masonic education programs were possible
to be built around visual representations of the degrees, but that these
likewise should not be a part of the ritual and should be designed to
supplement the degree experiences even as the Seminars conducted by
the Research Lodges.
Thus, the use of visual aids has been outlined by the 1959 report, and
the Master is fully authorized to make use of so-called visual aids in
an educational program which would be supplemental to the degrees,
but not as part of the ritual.
The means of carrying out the recommendations and suggestions of
the Special Committee are already within the grasp of the Master of the
Lodge, and all that is required of him is a little work and planning and
ingenuity on his part in preparing and presenting such a program. If
he needs any assistance, he can readily secure it from any of the Research Lodges or from the Committee on Masonic Education, which
exist for the purpose of rendering such assistance, and which are freely
offering their services to the Lodges.
It is therefore our opinion that a new committee is wholly unnecessary, and accordingly we recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
We move the adoption of the resolution, but the committee recommends a no vote
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated their concurrence in the
recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

TfilRD DEGREE PROFICIENCY
(6)
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred Resolution No. 6 by the Master and Wardens of Lemon Grove
Lodge No. 736, requesting that the incoming Grand Master appoint
a special committee to work out details, procedures and feasibility of
mandatory proficiency in the third degree, have considered this resolution.
The proposal to compel proficiency in the candidate's lecture of the
third degree has been before this Grand Lodge on several occasions
since the adoption of that lecture a little more than fifty years ago. The
proposal has been rejected each time it was presented.

286

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The candidate who has received his third degree and signed the
by-laws is a member and we do not believe t!here are any feasible means
of compulsory enforcement of proficiency. The proponents of this resolution have suggested none.
Grand Lodge has provided certificates of proficiency for presentation to those members who learn the work and pass a satisfactory
examination. We believe that the Master, Officers and Coaches of our
Lodges can induce voluntary compliance if they follow the matter up
promptly after conferring of the third degree. Proficiency :is now a
requirement of receiving any degree or being initiated in any Lodge or
organization the prerequisite of membership in which is that a person
be a Master Mason. These Should be sufficient inducements or incentives to learning the necessary work to acquire proficiency.
A<:cordingly, while we are wholly sympathetic with the purposes of
the resolution, we recommend that it be not adopted.
We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

PUBLIC SCHOOIS WEEK OBSERVANCE
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred
to it Resolution No. 19 which would restrict a Mason residing in California from attending the meetings (during Public Schools Week) of
any organrization which requires Masonic affiliation or relationship as
a prerequisite to membership.
Your Committee feels that Public Schools Week is an important
and necessary function of the Fraternity and is so recognized not only
in California but in other jurisdictions as well and deserves the wholehearted support of all Masons.
We agree with the statement in the resolution, that so called affiliated
organizations are in sympathy with the aims and purposes of Public
Schools Week, but for the most part have not adopted legislation
concerning it; but to place the restriction that no Mason can attend
meetings of these organizations would not. in our opinion. cause more
of them to attend Public Schools Week meetings. No man appreciates
being told what he must do. We feel that the proper and reasonable
solution to this problem is for the Grand Master, early in his term, to
address a communication to the heads of these organizations requesting
that no meetings be held by their respective groups or Lodges and that
they urge upon their members the importance of supporting Public

RECOMMENDATION V
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes to which was
referred the Grand Master's recommendation No. V, reports as follows:
The Grand Master recommends that Annotation 199-i be repealed.
That Annotation summarizes a 1959 ruling made by Grand Master Phil
N. Myers and approved by Grand Lodge that "the sale of alcoholic
liquor in Mason<ic Temple property is prohibited under any circumstances, and a department store leasing ground floor space may not be
permitted to maintain a package liquor department."
Grand Master Breslauer states that various Temple Associations
and Lodges owning real property are handicapped b~. the rul!~g. just
quoted and he reasons that since the operator of an off-sale liquor
store is eligible for Masonic membership, it is inconsistent to forbid
the sale of packaged liquor by a store tenant of a Masonic Temple
Association.
It seems to this Committee that the reasons stated are insufficient
to justify the reversal of the action taken by Grand Lodge in 1959.
For many years it has been the consistent policy of Grand Lodge to
avoid bringing the Craft into disrepute and to avoid criticism of the
Fraternity by reason of any action which might appear to associate the
Fraternity directly or indirectly with the traffic in alcoholic be~erages.
In our opinion, the ruling made by Grand Master Myers m 1959
was a necessary and desirable implementation of that policy. We are
not informed that any considerable number of Lodges or Temple Associations have been or are handicapped by reason of the ruling, and we
believe the ruling should stand.

the Grand Master be not approved.

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
(7 and 8)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, to which was
referred Resolutions numbered 7 and 8 proposing elimination of the
requirements of physical qualification, have carefully considered these
proposals.

PROCEEDING S OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The physical requirement s for qualification of candidates for the
degrees of Masonry are probably as old as .Masonry itself. These requirements are a survival of operative Masonry and are peculiar to the
Masonic institution. One of the Ancient Landmarks stated by Dr.
Mackey is the "qualification of candidates for initiation."
A natural sympathy for those unfortunate people who have suffered
severe physical injuries has caused numerous proposals to change the
old requirements and these have been presented throughout the history
of our Grand Lodge. They have been rejected except for the compromise
which resulted in the adoption of our present regulation many years
ago, now contained in Sections 51 ,1 and 512 of the California Masonic
Code: "having no maim or defect in his body that may render him
incapable of learning the art, and physically able to conform substantially to what the several degrees respectively require of him." Under
this regulation, the question as to physical sufficiency of the applicant
is left to the sound discretion of the Lodge, and it is determined by the
ritual.
Since the rule of physical qualification has existed for so long that
it is regarded as one of the ancient landmarks, it should not be changed
without some change in all conditions which would compel it. We may
properly inquire what change has occurred in the conditions of the
Craft which would now require a dhange in the ancient regulation. We
know of none.
If these proposals were adopted, it would require a different ritual
for each case of physical defect, depending upon the nature of the particular deformity. This would completely destroy any uniformity in
the ritual. Under our law the conferring of a degree in merely a symbolic
manner is out of the question. ( C.M.C., Sec. 512-j)
The most appalling thing about the elimination of physical requirements would be that it would subject a man who may have suffered a
repulsive physical injury to the required unanimous ballot with _the
great probability that some one or more of the members would reJect
him. The resulting damage to an already damaged personality would
be incalculable and irreparable. It would be far kinder to reject such
candidates on purely legal grounds.
In our opinion, this Grand Lodge has already gone as far in meeting physical insufficiency as it can reasonably go, making it depend
upon the applicant's ability to conform substantiall y to what the ritual
may require of him.
We recommend that the resolutions be not adopted, and in view
of the fact that they would repeal Sections 511 and 512 of the Ordinances, we suggest that a 5/6ths vote would be required to adopt.
We move the adoption of the resolutions, but your Committee
recommends a no vote.

The Committee on furisprudence:
We present the following:
Resolutions Nos. 7 and 8 should be defeated, for the following
reasons:
1. Both infringe Landmark Eighteenth ( C.M.C. p. 343).
2. Grand Lodge itself is limited by a strict adherence to the Ancient
Landmarks of our Order (Sec. 17 C.M.C. - Constitution ).
3. "A candidate must be without blemish and have the full and
proper use of his limbs: for a maimed man can do the Craft no good."
(Old York Constitution of 926, Article 5 C.M.C. p. 344)
4. "That no person shall hereafter be accepted a Freemason but
suc'h as are of able body, .. ," (Regulation s of 1663 Sec. 2 - C.M.C.
.
p. 346.)
5. "And that the Apprentice be freeborn, and of limbs whole as a
man ought to ·be, ... (Ancient Charges at Makings. Sec. 2 - C.M.C.
p. 348.)
6. Items 3, 4 and 5 above constitute a part of our Written Law
of Masonry and can be changed by Grand Lodge but the landmark
under Item 1 above a part of our unwritten law, being unrepealable,
must ever remain in force. (C.M.C. p. 364.)
7. The present law of Grand Lodge is as follows: " (an applicant)
having no maim or defect in his body that may render him incapable
of learning the art, and physically able to conform substantially to what
the several degrees respectively require of him." ( C.M.C. p. 511.)
"The question as to the physical sufficiency of the applicant shall
be left to the sound discretion of the Lodge. When the applicant is
unable to comply literally with the physical requirement, the Master
shall state the nature and extent of his disabilities to the Lodge before
ballot is taken." ( C.M.C. p. 512.)
We conclude that said resolutions infringe a landmark, and
We move that Resolutions 7 and 8 be adopted and recommend a
no vote.
The Committee on Ritual indicated their concurrence in the recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolutions.

MINIMUM DUES
( 1O)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The resolution offered by Brother Ralph W. Collins, increasing the
minimum dues from $12.00 per year to $15.00 per year, has been referred
to and has had the consideration of your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes. To remove all doubt about the position of the Committee, we will say at the outset that it is unanimously opposed to the
change.

295

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The increase in the annual amount of dues is taking place volunt:arily
and the Committee feels that at this point it ~ould not be mandatory.
Five years ago 320 Lodges had $12.00 dues and today that has been
reduced to 121 Lodges by their own voluntary action. One Lodge has
$14.00 dues so that the number of Lodges which would be affected is
121 out of 700. Five years ago the average dues were $13.96 and now
the average dues are $15.56, which is beyond the amount recommended
in ·the resolution. Your Committee feels that, in the light of this voluntary
raising of dues, any further mandatory action is not necessary.
While there may be some Lodges which, due to possible reactionary
tactics of a few, cannot raise their dues, it should also be born in mind
that there are many Lodges which can support themselves on $12.00
per year. Many are relatively small, own their own Temples without
debt, and pay relatively light taxes. In these Lodges the wives of members still bake the cakes and prepare the sandwiches, and there is little
expense for refreshments. There are also in many of these Lodges
pensioners on whom an increase could conceivably work a hardship and
the necessary remission of dues might even offset any possible gain.
Your Committee therefore recommends that at this time there be
no change in the minimum dues required.

RESEARCH LODGE OFFICERS
(12)

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred
to it Resolution No. 12 entitled "Research Lodge Officers."
This resolution would rescind Paragraph 18 of Section 355 of the
California ·M asonic Code enacted at the 1960 Annual Communication
~f this Grand Lodge. This section, as last amended, provides that
None but a Past Master of a California Lodge is eligible for eledion
as a Master, Senior or Junior Warden of a Research Lodge."
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is of the opinion
that the work and activities of our Research Lodges are beneficial
to the craft and ;ohould be encouraged. We find, however, that by reason of the present limitations in the California Masonic Code our Research Lodges are hard pressed to find Past Masters who are willing
to s~rve as their senior officers. Further, we find that they are thus
deprived of the services and abilities of many members of the craft
who are otherwise well qualified to preside over and administer the
activities of a Research Lodge.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes that
the administrative duties and obligations of the Master and Senior
Officers of a Research Lodge differ in many respects from the administrative duties and ritualistic obligations of the Officers of a Symbolic
Lodge. T1his fact, coupled with the fact that the existing provisions of
the California Masonic Code clearly provide that "No Officer or Past
Master of a Research Lodge shall, by that reason alone, be a member
of Grand Lodge, causes your Committee to seriously question the
wisdom of the e::idsting limitation in the Code.
We recommend a yes vote.

STUDY OF SUBVERSIVE TECHNIQUES
( 16)
The Committee on Masonic Education:
The Committee on Masonic Education, to whom the Grand Master
referred Resolution No. 16, titled, "Subversive Techndques," reports
as follows:
The members of tlhis committee are deeply sympathetic and in complete accord with the philosophy behind the resolution and the objectives
which the sponsors seek to attain even though we unanimously oppose
the resolution.
From time immemorial, even to the days when our Lodges were
operative, it has been customary and traditional that discussions of
politics and religion, in the Lodge room, not be permitted. Furcihermore,
in this jurisdiction, it has been a matter of Constitutional Law since
1875, (Article Ill, Sec. 16-j, CMC) that no discussions may be held
on either of these two subjects in the Lodge room.
This committee opposes this resolution because:
1. As a fraternity and as a philosophy of life we were not organized
to be political in nature but rather to promote the well-being of each
other. The requirements of this resolution are not properly the function
of a Masonic Lodge.
2. It is our opinion ~t the adoption of this resolution would tend
to create dissension within the Lodge and friction between the fraternity
and non-Masons on the outside.
3. For many reasons, apparent to everyone, Masonic Lodges should
not be public information bodies, as this resolution proposes.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

299

In view of the foregoing, we oppose the resolution and urge a no
vote on it.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes indicated their
concurrence in the recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

MEMBERSHIP IN SUBVERSIVE ORGANIZATION
( 17)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has had referred
to it a resolution entitled "Membership in Subversive 0J:"ganizations."
The resolution recommends that the following question be added to our
Application for Degrees. "Would you be willing to take an oath that you
never were, or are, or ever will be, knowingly affiliated with any subversive group or organization inimical to the Government of the United
States of America?"
The proposers of this legislation undoubtedly have in mind, as their
preamble states, the protection of our fraternity from infiltration by
subversives under any name. No Mason can take issue with such
motives, as the aim ds indeed a most commendable one.
Remembering, however, that to subversives an oath is meaningless,
that they are in general a God-denying group wholly unacquainted with
the meaning of trujjh as we know it, we fail to see how the addition of
this query to our application form would serve anry useful purpose.
More careful and complete investigation of candidates, using all of
the many means available, we feel is the ,answer to the problem of keeping our organization free from undesirables, and this cannot be stressed
too strongly. We commend the intent of the makers of the motion in
the interest of Freemasonry but feel that we cannot recommend the
adoption of the resolution.
We recommend a no vote.

(18)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Polky and General Purposes has had referred
to it a resolution entitled "Subversive Activity" signed by 34 members
of Grand Lodge in the San Fernando Valley area. It recommends that
"Constituent Lodges become active in alerting its members, their family
and friends, to the meaning and dangers of Communism," etc.
Again your Committee is in full sympathy with the intended effect
of the proposed legislation but feels that Masonry as an organization
must, in defense ·to its age-old character, refrain from attempting to
legislate against ·any ideology. regardless of how unsavory it may be.
If Masonry teaches anything, it teaches the importance of the individual and that its strength lies in individual action. When Masonry
enters the political arena it becomes a target for all !its enemies.
Communism and all other subversive activities must be curbed and
they will be but only by right thinking and fearless men acting as
individuals and not by Masonry as a pressure group.

Mason to uphold the principles of freedom whidh have made this
country great, but that the institution of Masonry as such should
devote itself to imbuing that spirit of devotedness and patriotism within
the individual which will lead him to proper civi"ic: activity within the
appropriate sphere.

EXPENSES OF MEMBERS
(24)
The Committ ee on Finance:
There has been referred to this Committ ee the resolution introduc ed
by Grand Secretar y Siems which would amend Section 174 of the Code,
to change the method of computing compensation for transpor tation of
represen tatives to and from the annual Grand Lodge Commun ication
from railroad fare to a mileage basis, the rate per mile to be fixed by
the Committee on Finance.
We have discussed this proposal at length with Brother Siems. The
reason for the change is to correct some inequities which exist under
the present method of compensation, mainly relating to the dividing
line between Pullman fare compensation. For example, a delegate from
Livingston receives $11.82 while a delegate from Merced, in the same
area, receives $25.82 which includes Pullman. Under the mileage system,
the delegate from Livingston would receive $15.96, and the delegate
from Merced $17.92.
Based on estimate s compiled by the Grand Secretar y this change
should increase the over-all cost to Grand Lodge less than $200.00 per
year.
We favor the adoption of the resolution and recommend that the
rate per mile be set at seven ( 7) cents, which is the rate currently
allowed for Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors, and otlhers when traveling
on official Grand Lodge business.

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON RITUAL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

CIPHER RITUAL CODE
(2)
The 'Ritual Committee, to Which has been referred the resolution
calling for the adoption in this jurisdiction of a cipher ritual, reports
as follows:
The premise upon which this resolution is based is false. The living
Past Grand Lecturers can testify that during their ritualistic experience
of better than thirty years, there have been no changes in the ritual
except those directed by the Grand Lodge in 1942, t'he effect of which
was merely to make uniform a certain few words. The statement that
there have been repeated changes is patently without foundation in
fact.
There are, however, implications in this resolution which none of
us who have knelt at the altar of Masonry can view without a feeling
of shock.
We are, by this resolution, asked to violate our obligations, to
wipe out one of t'he landmarks of Masonry, and to engage in a practice
which is repugnant to the ideal of Masonry as practiced in this great
jurisdiction.
Each Master and Past Master here representing his Lodge has
signified his assent to those ancient charges and regulations, including
the following:
"XI. You admit that it is not in the power of any man or body of
men to make innovations in the body of Masonry.
"You are further enjoined that our awards and resolutions must in
every case be consistent with the Constitutions of the Order and that

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

305

no Edict of the Grand Lodge may be subversive of the principles and
groundwork of Masonry."
Section 16 of the Constitution strictly limits the Power and Authority
of the Grand Lodge by a strict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks
of the order and by the provisions of its own Constitution and Regulations.
Landmark Twenty-third. The secrecy of the Institution.
Under such hallowed precepts we have labored for better than a
century. During that time the subject of cipher rituals has been before
this Grand Lodge. In 1908 (Sec. 554 d) Grand Lodge condemned the
purchase, sale or use of cipher rituals and reaffirmed that the secrets
of the ritual should be ever concealed and never revealed: that they
are communicated only by the instructive tongue to the attentive ear;
that the writing, printing or marking of the same whereby they may
become legible or intelligible to any person is forbidden; that no human
power can authorize a Mason to write, print or mark them and that
the secrets are ancient and cannot be changed. In 1911, 1918 and 1955,
there was repeated condemnation of cipher rituals and their possession
or use as a violation of Masonic law.
The Ritual Committee, as constituted, is charged by Section 159 of
the Ordinances to be the custodian of the esoteric work. No member
of this Committee has the authority to prepare a cipher ritual. nor do
we believe that this Grand Lodge has the power to direct the Grand
Lecturer or this Committee to do that which our solemn obligations,
the Landmarks of Masonry, and the Constitutions and Ordinances
prohibit. As a matter of deep personal conviction, the present Grand
Lecturer would be obligated by his own vows to refuse the commission
of the task alloted to him under this resolution and would refuse the
office if it entailed such a Oagrant abuse of the principles and groundwork of Masonry.
We believe that this Grand Lodge should refuse to entertain this
resolution, declaring it to be repugnant to and inconsistent with the
Constitution and Ordinances and that, as such, it shall not be adopted
as it is in violation of the Ancient Landmarks as cherished by this Grand
Lodge.
We move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a no vote.
Respectfully submitted,
DONALD G. CAMPBELL
CLARE B. CAMPBELL
HAROLD N. RICHARDS
KAHN
ARTHUR
COLLINS
RALPH

SHORTENING THE RITUAL

view of the duties of a Mason as exemplified in these few minutes.
Many members may miss degree work and only have the contact at
stated meetings with the ritual. Are we to slight these members in our
work?
There is no dead wood in the ritual of Masonry. Each word is
fraught with significance. The lectures, the charges, the degrees can
only be of significance if they are transmitted from mouth to ear.
In order to conform to the required procedure, we move the adoption

(3)

The Ritual Committee to which has been referred the resolution
entitled "Shortening the Ritual" reports as follows:
The resolution directs the incoming Grand Master to appoint a
special committee with the end of proposing changes in the ritual by
eliminating portions of the work, including the opening and closing
ceremonies, the floor work of the degrees, and the lectures.
Section 555 of the Ordinances states as follows:
Sec. 555. Change of ritual. The Grand Lodge alone has power to
authorize any changes in the Ritual for the purpose of having it remain
as it was handed down from time immemorial.
Unless it can be shown that a form of ritual embodying short forms
of opening and closing, curtailed floor work and abbreviated lectures
has in the past been the practice of this Grand Lodge, the resolution
would first require the amendment of Sec. 555 by striking out the
phrase "for the purpose of having it remain as it was handed down from
time immemorial."
From the standpoint of our law we therefore do not believe the
resolution to be in order.
From the standpoint of the health and well-being of the Lodges,
we mention the following points to consider.
1. The applicant is the person to be considered as far as the degrees
are concerned. The lessons of Masonry are too important to be slighted
by mere reference to printed materials. The beauty and wisdom of
Masonry is not something to be handed the candidate like a library
card. It must be lived to be felt. We have as an institution deplored the
degree-mill type of operation and prided ourselves that while our
imitators may engage in the practice, we believe that our candidates
put trust in us for something better.
2. Masters can heighten the interest of the members in many ways.
The first might well be to limit the number of candidates to one in any
evening. With this limitation, the members will be home in good season.
The promotion of sideline teams, not limited to the third degree, will
offer opportunity for members to participate. Those who thus participate
will not, we believe, complain of late hours. A high standard of excellence demanded of every participant in ritualistic work will bring
meaning to the sideline observers as well as the candidate. Above all,
the work of the Master in the lectures, whether he merely recites as a
machine or breathes life into the words, will determine, in the end, the
feeling of his listeners as to whether the evening is long or short.
3. With regard to stated meetings, we are all familiar with the
Master who can arrange an interesting program, facilitate the business
of the Lodge, and close Lodge before ten o'clock. The time used in
opening and closing represents to his members a period for quick re-

OFFICERS' APRONS
(4)
The Ritual Committee, to which was referred a resolution to permit
wearing of aprons bearing the insignia of the officer's rank or station
either by the installed officer or at the option of the Lodge by the
member temporarily oc,cupying the station, reports as follows:
This is essentially the same resolution as that introduced in 1957.
We report in the same language used at that time.
The praotice adopted and taught by the Grand Lecturer and Ritual
Committee is that an officer vacating his station or place shall surrender
to the person occupying it, not only the jewel, but the apron, if it bears
insigne indicating the office.
Several years ago, the Ritual Committee became aware that two
differing practjces prevailed in this jurisdiction with respect to this
matter, and the practice adopted was to make uniform one practice
throughout the jurisdiotion. The Committee was unanimous that the
correct practice was the one it adopted and that it was taught in the
greater number of areas in the State. Furthermore, it conforms to the
practice of the Grand Lodge officers at Grand Lodge ceremonies, at
which the man filling the office customarily wears both jewel and apron
indicating the office.
We have pointed out on prior occasions that there is no authority in
our law or regulations for so-called officers' aprons, and no regulation governing color, design or insignia to be placed on them. They
exist in contradiction of the instruction given to candidates to the effect
that the white lambskin apron is the badge of a Mason. H we are
to adopt an amendment to section 554 to prescribe the practice with
respect to aprons, we should first adopt a regulation specifying the
color, design and insignia to be placed thereon.
There is neither law nor precedent for the contention that the apron
belongs to the installed officer. It is merely part of the equipment belonging to the Lodge, just as is the jewel with which the officer is formally
invested at installation.

308

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The officer who is selected to act in any station or place is selected
by the installed Master. but, nevertheless, for the purposes of degree,
he is the officer of the Lodge which has been convened to confer the
degree. The Junior Warden, acting as Master in a Lodge of Entered
Apprentice Masons, is for all purposes the Master of that Lodge. He
must be addressed as Worshipful Master. He wears the Master's jewel.
He wears t'he Master's hat and he wields the Master's gavel, which
is the distinct emblem of the Master's authority. These are all surrendered to him without question. So also, we think, must the apron
be surrendered, if it designates the office.
If the installed Master is to sit on the sidelines with the Master's
apron, then by the same token, he should retain the hat and the gavel.
It requires very little reference to our ritual to demonstrate that the
officer occupying the station or place is the officer of the Lodge as thus
convened for the degree. These references obviously cannot be written
in this report.
If the rule suggested in this resolution were adopted, the result
would be confusion because half the officers conferring the degree
might be clothed in officers' aprons and half of them clothed in white
aprons.
Since our law requires, under section 554, that each degree conferred must be in conformity with the ritual now taught by the Grand
Lecturer and recognized by the Grand Lodge, and, further, since this
resolution would destroy the uniformity required by this section, we
suggest that it purports to amend this section and would require a
five-sixths vote of Grand Lodge.
In order to conform to the required procedure, we move the adoption of the resolution and recommend a no vote.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes indicated their concurrence in the recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

SALARIES

At the last Annual Communication Grand Lodge, by a 5/6ths vote,
adopted a resolution employing Most Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilson as
Assistant to the Grand Master at the same annual salary of $20,000.00
which he was receiving as Grand Secretary, with such duties as would
be assigned to him by the Grand Master.
This action was taken for two reasons. First, Brother Wilson requested that he be relieved of the strenuous duties of Grand Secretary
because of the ill health which he has suffered for the last several years;
and, secondly, because Grand ·Lodge could retain the services of this
able Grand Lodge Officer in a muchly needed position where the duties
would be less exacting of time and energy.
The Grand Master, if he wishes, may report on the work which has
been successfully carried out by Brother Wilson in the past year.
With the above as background, we now report to you that Brother
Wilson has voluntarily chosen to retire under the physical disability
provision of our Retirement Income Plan effective January 1, 1962.
The pension which he will receive under Disability Retirement is
$254.05 per month. In order to bring this up to an adequate amount,
we propose and recommend that Grand Lodge make a supplemental
pension payment of $746.00 per month. This Grand Lodge cannot, of
course, make future commitments, but we recommend, and so record
herewith, that this supplemental pension payment be a continuing program for Brodrer Wilson.
May we call your attention to the fact that the net result of this
action, insofar as expense is concerned, is an annual saving to Grand
Lodge from now on of $11,000.00 as compared to the present salary
paid Brother Wilson by resolution of Grand Lodge.
It hardly seems necessary to recount that, after his year as Grand
Master, Lloyd Wilson began an unbroken term of twenty years as
Grand Secretary, during which the administration of the aff·airs of the
Grand Lodge Office reached a peak of efficiency, and in a period when
membership in the Lodges almost doubled.
There is much more that we could say, but we feel that you know
what his service 1has meant to California Masonry. Now that ill health
has forced his early retirement, we also feel that you will give hearty
approval to this measure of support and appreciation for a true and
faithful servant.

.316

The estimated deficit of $9,286.00 results from increased operating
costs beyond our control in such fields as Social Security and Unem~
ployment Taxes, telephone and telegraph, travel expense, insurance
costs, and Pension Plan expense. In this last item we may expect some
reduction in the 1962~1963 fiscal year as a result of funding Past
Service Credits, and in future years as employee retirement plans mature.
All other items in the budget have been set at minimum figures con~
sistent with sound operation, but in spite of the most careful scrutiny,
we must face the fact that, based on our estimates, we will be in the
red for this fiscal year on the present per capita.
Your Committee feels that deficits are just as unsound fiscal policy
for this Grand Lodge as t'hey are for national governments and that to
avoid this, t'he per capita should be increased by the small amount of
five ( 5) cents.
We therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED that for the purpose of paying the expenses of
Grand Lodge, a per capita aggregating $3.30 be levied for the
fiscal year ending June 30, 1962, divided as follows:
Constitutional per capita for

323

for

LLOYD EARL WILSON
by
HENRY C. CLAUSEN

Brothers and Friends:
We who survive - we who ourselves are
"only waiting 'til the shadows are a little longer grown"
pay now a last tribute of that respect and affection we feel for Lloyd
Earl Wilson. The Great Architect of the Universe summoned him from
our midst on November 2, 1961. Thus there came to ·a peaceful close
a distinguished ca·reer.
His was a powerful influence upon the fraternal and social fabric
of his times. We need not here record his virtues. They are engraved
upon the heart·s of those who knew him best. Gifted with extraordinary
natural abilities, directed by unswerving fideli.ty to his convictions,
matured by reflection and experience, he devoted almost a lifetime to
the cause of humanity. Called by his brethren to the highest offices in
their gift to bestow, he will be ranked for his achievements among the
immortals of Masonry. An orator with ability to stir and inspire, a
champion and defender of freedom, a gifted leader of the good fight,
a master of the "retort courteous," a wit and lover of life, his was a
powerful per•sonality and a luminous mind. He has left a lasting mark
for good upon 'the men and events of his time.
And so, by his passing we are all diminished.
"And man's death diminishes me .. .
"And therefore never send to know for whom the bell
tolls;
It .tolls for thee."
His early years and school days were spent among the greens and
the waters of Oregon. Born in Portland, August 16, 1895, he there
attended the public schooJ.s and then Drake University at Des Moines,
Iowa. 'f.ypical of his patriotic zeal, he enlisted at the outbreak of .the
First World War. Serving with his units of the Fourth Division, he was
in the thick of combat through five major campaigns in France. His
heroic devotion to duty and acts of bravery on the battelfield in the
face of mortal danger bear eloquent testimony to his courageous and
commanding character. It foretold the man who in the future would
"move toward the sound of the guns" and would ·speak out strongly for
what he thought best for his community, state and country.
On his return from France in 1919 there commenced an active
business career at San Francisco and then at San Diego. But his true

324

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

call was to help his fellow man. And so, from 1922 to 1940 he was with
the Young Men's Christian Association of San Francisco a·s Membership Sec•r etary, as Director of Promotion, and as Director of Public
Relations.

Our eminent brother added to his honors by allied activities. He
was one of .those rare Masons, members of the Scotti·sh Rite, elected
to receive the 33° as its last and highest degree. He was a Red Cross
of Constantine member of the Yark Rite. He had been honored with
awards by sister Grand Lodges, including Israel and Cuba, with the
Henry Price Award by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts, and as an
honorary member of the Grand Lodge of France. He was on the
Executive Board of the George Washington Na!ional Masonic
Memoflial.

He was happily married on September 7, 1933, to ever charming
Elsie McElaney. Her pleasing personality, her womanly attainments,
and her loving devotion beyond the call of duty, ideally complemented
his dedicated work. This marriage was blessed with a most delightful
daughter. Helen Janet, further to brighten their lives. With nearby
friends and relatives, including especially Helen and Donald Messer,
the Wilson home was a pleasant scene of fortunate and happy companionships.
Our beloved brother commenced his rise to commanding Masonic
height·s by being made a Mason in 1917. At the organization of
Ingleside Lodge No. 630 in San Francisco he became a charter member
and its first Senior Deacon. He was a Past Master and remained a
member of that Lodge. His unusual ritualistic and dramatic ability was
recos:inized and rewarded by appointment as Inspector and then Assistant Grand Lecturer. Elected to the Grand Lodge line he was elevated
to the office of Grand Master on October 11, 1940. The following
October he was elected Grand Secretary. This was the office he filled
with such outstanding honor to himself and advantage to his brethren,
until ·a ppointed Assistant to the Grand Master in September, 1960.
He served in that capacity unNl illness forced him to announce arrangements for his retirement.
Thus, for two decades our brother labored for Grand Lodge as Grand
Secretary. His title itself denoted little of his real stature. He combined
with the daily routine affairs unusual executive ability and a clear vision
of the higher reaches toward which we aspire as Masons. Few are gifted
with ·such insight. The work of his staff under his direction was creative,
dignified and dynamic. This impetus toward those things we hold dear,
our members, Lodges, charities, homes and ·r elated activities, will long
continue.
Among the achievements he helped inspire and guide to success was
this magnificent Grand Lodge Temple in which we have assembled
today. This monumental structure - the present home of Grand Lodge
- was erected as a memorial to those wartime Masons who gave their
lives in battle that we might live in freedom. But it also shall stand as
a symbol of determination by those who worked to build the Temple.
And thus it reflects in part his genius.

325

He was a dynamic force in his community and state. He gave of
his talents freely to the civic life of his city as a member of the San
Francisco Grand Jury, the Public Welfare Commission, the Recreation and the Park Commission and the Housing Authorit•y . He was
active in many groups, including the Rotary Club, the American
Legion, the Council of Churches, the Sojourners, the San Francisco
Young Men's Christian Association and the San Francisco Golf Club.
But lest these words of mine be thought oversweet, let me say that
most assuredly our brother's virtues were not of the sanctimonious
cloi·ster. His feet were firmly upon the g·round. He abhorred domination by medieval creeds and wasted no time on empty ceremonial p•iety.
His goodness found expression in the ready and firm handclasp of
greeting. In the ear of one to whom the burdened heart could pour
out its sorrow. In the voice of cheer to a discouraged brother. In the
picture of a strong and hearty manhood. As an inspiring man among
men. As an orator of power and melodious voice, always ready with
the wiNcism, epigram or adage to express the sentiments of the occasion.
As a companion at the Lodge, the dinner table, the golf links, the trout
stream or the camp fire. As a friend with a smile of congenial fellowship.
He has made his last brave fight and no one may venture to say that
his place ever can be filled. But we can say with Browning that he was
"One who never turned his back but marched breast forward,
Never doubted clouds would break,
Never dreamed tho' right were worsted, wrong would
triumph,
Held we fall to rise, are baffled to fight better,
Sleep to wake."
Sadness and •s orrow, weeping and wonder, of course attend his
passing from us into eternal rest. With the utmost sincerity, we express
our deep and Masonic sympathy to his loved ones, those whose affec-

326

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

tion he valued above all else in this world. It is hard to see the tall trees
go down, one by one. In this case there trut.y is an empty place against
the sky!
But we can console ourselves with our faith; and with the observa~
tion that even though our brother has been called to leave the watch
towers of this world, nevertheless, through the vast serene, like the
deep melody of an angel',s song, Heaven's approving voice shall be
heard:
"Servant of God, well done!
Thy glorious warfare's past, the
battle's fought, the victory's won.
And thou are crowned at last."
And our instinct seems to tell us:
"So he passed over, and all the
trumpets sounded for him on the
other side."

GRAND LODGE, F. & A. M. OF CALIFORNIA
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

337

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

JUNE 30, 1961

Note 1 - Basis of Accounting
The financial statements are prepared on the cash basis
of accounting. Current operating expense bills
applicable to the year ended June 30, 1961 and unpaid
as at that date were of nominal amount.
Note 2 - Furniture and Fixtures
Grand Lodge at the 1957 Communication approved the
capitalization of amounts expended for furnishings
and equipment after that date • . Additions during the
year ended June 30, 1961 amounted to $3,256.48 as
compared with the budget of $4,425.00.
Note 3 . - Insurance Premiums Advanced for Lodges
Comprehensive public liability insurance is purchased
by Grand Lodge on a three-year basis to cover the
Lodges not otherwise covered by su~h insurance.
P;remiums are collected from the covered Lodges on an
annual premium basis. At June 30, 1961, $578.02 was
advanced and due from the Lodges.
Note 4 - George Washington Masonic National Memorial
During the current year contributions totaling $7 1 086.00
were remitted to the Endowment Fund of the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, in
accordance with the Ordinances, leaving a balance of
contributions on hand at June 30, 1961 of $5,21~.oo.
This balance will be remitted to the Endowment Fund
during the year ended June 30, 1962.
Note 5 - Retirement Income Plan
The 1955 Communication approved the inclusion of the
employees of Grand Lodge under the Masonic Homes of
California Retirement Income Plan. On October 3, 1958
the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes of California
approved and adopted an amended plan to extend
coverage of the plan to the employees of Grand Lodge
effective on January 1, 1956, and to the employees of
Masonic Clubhouses, Boards of Relief, and Employment
Bureaus effective on January 1, 1959. The plan, as
amended, has been approved by the Internal Revenue
Service as a qualified trust under Section 4ol(a) and
exempt from income tax under the provisions of Section
50l(a) of the Internal Revenue Code.

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

JUNE 30, 1961

Note 5 - Retirement Income Plan (Continued)
For the fiscal year ended June 30, 1961, the current
service cost amounted to $12 1 033.96 for the participating employees of Grand Lodge and $13,415.19 for
such employees of Grand Lodge agencies.
The total past service cost for the participating
employees of Grand Lodge and its agencies amounted to
approximately $128,000 as at January 1, 1961, according
to the actuary. This amount has not been funded. In
lieu thereof minimum annual payments of 2-1/2 percent
on the past service cost have been paid to June 30
1961. Such payments for the fiscal year ended Jun~ 30
1961 amounted to $1,296.25 for the employees of Grand '
lodge and $1,903.75 for the employees of Grand lodge
agencies.
Note 6 - "California Freemason"
During the year ended June 30, 1961, subscriptions to
"California Freemason" together with miscellaneous
sales produced revenue of $68,471.66. Expenses of the
Correspondence Committee in publishing issues during
the year amounted to $53,436.84, resultin~ in an excess
of revenue over expenses for the year of '15,034.82, as
shown on Exhibit B.
Note 7 - Reserve for "California Freemason"
The 1958 Communication authorized the establishment of
t.he Reserve for "California Freemason" to provide
against the time when the cash receipts, due to the
prepayment of subscriptions, may not equal the current
expenses of publishing the magazine. The 1960
Communication appropriated $7,449.43 to be transferred
to the reserve, which was the excess of the cash receipts from subscriptions over publication costa for
the fiscal year ended June 30, 196o. This transfer
increased the reserve to $20,133.4o at June 30, 1961.
Approximately 274,ooo individual copies of ruture
issues of "California Freemason" were subscribed and
paid for at June 30, 1961, at rates of fifteen to
twenty-five cents per copy.
Note 8 - Contingent Liability
Under date of October 4, 1955, the officers of California
'Masonic Memorial Temple signed promissory notes with
six San Francisco banks for a total of $3,000,000.00.
Under authorization given at the 1953 Communication,
Grand Lodge became the guarantor of these notes.
California Masonic Memorial Temple owed $1,493,790.00
on these notes at June 30, 1961.

Note 1 - Basis of Accounting
.
The financial statements are stated on the cash basis ot
accounting on which basis revenue and expense are
recorded on the books or account when received and paid,
respectively -. Current operating expense bills applicable to the ;rear ended June 30, 1961 and unpaid at
that date were ot nominal amount.
Note 2 - Investments
Investments 1n securities purchased are stated on the
books and in this report at cost. Securities received
by- gift or bequest or by- assignment by residents ot the
home at Decoto are stated at estimated market value at
the time the securities are received or at the nominal
value or $1.00 i t the market value is unknown. In a
tew instances the carry-ing value of unlisted stoclcs
acquired by- girt or bequest has been restated at the
per share value ot the underlying assets ot the comp&Jl1'
which is believed to be less than the market value.
Note 3 - Notes Receivable
Notes receivable arise from the sale or real estate
assigned to Masonic Homes of California by residents ot
the home at Decoto and from real eatate received as
gifts or bequests by the Homes or the Pel"lllllllent
Endowment Fund,
Jfote 4 - Other Assets
Other assets consist of paid-up life insurance policies
and real estate assigned to Masonic Homes or California
by residents of the home at Decoto or received as girts
or bequests by the Permanent Endowment Fund. The life
insurance policies and parcels of real estate are each
recorded at the nominal value or $1.00 tor accountabi lity-. Payment by- Masonic Homes of loans previous}7
obtained by- the assignors on life insurance policies or
on real estate and or lite insurance premi1111s are added
to the nominal value.
Note 5 - Land, Buildings, and Equipment
Land, buildings and equipment are recorded at the cost when
originally purchased and no depreciatio n ot buildings
and equipment has been provided tor 1n the accounts.
Replacemen ts ot original items are charged to one ot the
Reserves tor Special Purposes establiahed by the Board
of Trustees.

Note 4 - Reserve for Renewal·s and Replacements:
During the year ended June 30, 1960, the Trustees
authorized the establishment of a Reserve for
RenewaJsand Replacements and the annual addition
thereto of a sum equal to one per cent of the
annual gross income of the Temple. The addition
for the year ended June 30, 1961 amounted to $1,036.
The Reserve has not been funded.
